A comet came among the stars; It did not "come it " strong; But though its tail was rather short, The people watched It long. Some robed a glass to see the thing. Some did not take the trouble, W bile some so many glasses raised, They saw the comet double. They watched it as it came and went. And some men, wondering, said. It looks just like another, for Its tail springs from its head. "Like many a story, too, it seems; You need but look a minute, Your eye ean pierce quite through the tail, And see there's nothing in it." With fiery eye and tail erect It sped on day by day; It would not face the Dog Star bold, Nor lap its milky way. It did not dare to bait the Bull, 'Twould not abate its speed To crack a joke with Gemini. These twins of heavenly breed.. Its enly object seemed to be, To make its tall increans ; So it for Ursa Minor made. Resolved to try bear's grease. THE SCIENCE AND ART DEPARTMENT.— The twenty- eighth report of the Science and Art Department of the Committee of Council on Education has just appeared in a Blue Book, together with numerous appendices. The fol- lowing is a summary at the cicae of the report.:—" 'The number o/ persons who have during the year 1880 attended the schools and cla,ses of science and art in connection with the Department is as follows—namely, 60,871 attending science schools and classes in 1880, as against 59,519 in 1879; and 837,308 receiving instruction in art, showing an increase upon the previous year of 41,864. Atthe Royal School of Mines there were f.:5 regular and 175 occasional students; at the chemical department, Science Schools, 245 students; at the metallurgicallaboratory, 79. At the Royal College of Science for Ireland there were 20 associate or regular students and 38 occasional students. The lectures delivered in the lecture 'theatre of the South Kensingen Museum were attended by 4,702 persons. The evening lectures to working men at the Royal School of Mines were attended by 1,800 persons, beim,. 626 more than last year; and 230 science teachers attended the special courses of lec- tures provided for their instruction in the new Science Schools at South Kensington. The various courses of lec- tures delivered in connection with the Department in Dublin , were attended by about 736 persons. The total number of I persons, therefore, who received direct instruction as stu- dents or by meane a lectures in connection with the Science ' and Art Department in 1880 is 906,171, showing an increase as compared with the number in the previous year of 44,150, or more than 5 per cent. The attendance of the Art and *Educational Libraries at South Kensington and at the Na- tional Library of Ireland in 1880 has been 81,184, a decided increase over that of last year. The museums and collec- tions under the superintendence of the Department in Lon- , don, . Dublin, and ' Edinburgh were last year visited by 2,332,443 persons, showing a decrease of 167,321 on the number in 1879. It should, however, be observed that the , number of visitors to the South Kensington Museum shows , a large increase, the number being for 1879 879,395, and for 1880 981,t363. The returns received of the number of visitors at the local art and industrial exhibitions to which objects were contributed from the South Kensington Museum show an attendance of 696,511. The total number of per- sons who during the year 1880 attended the different insti- tutions and exhibitions in connection with the Department has been upwards of 3,935,155. This total, compared with that of the previous year, presents a decrease of 8,552. The expenditure of the year, during the financial year 1880-1, exclusive of the vote for the geological survey, which was £21,717 12s. 11d., amounted to £312,963 17s. 103." THE ELECTRIC LIGHT IN THE WORKING OF COLLIER. lEs.—On Tuesday afternoon Etrneck Colliery, near Hamil- ton, belonging to Mr. John Watson of Earnock, was the scene of an interesting ceremonial which may well, says the Scotsman, be said to mark a new era in the mining annals. In proceeding to win the rich mineral wealth of his estate, Mr. Watson determined that, in respect of fittings ma- chinery arid general appointrnerts, it should be a model, and he has been highly successful in giving practical effect to his aims. Among other things, he early resolved to, if at all practicable, substitute the electric light for the ordinary mede of illuminating the workings, and, after investigating the various systems, he decided on giving that of Mr. Swan a trial. Accordingly, since April last, Messrs. D. and E. Graham, electrical engineers, Glasgow, have been engaged , fitting up the Swan incandescent lamp, with modifications to adapt it for safe use in the mine, and on Tuesday the in- auguration of the new light tool: place in the presence of a ' large company of leading gentlemen from Glasgow, Hamil- ton, and the west. Arrived at the colliery about half-past one o'clock, the visitors were received by Mr. Watson, and after a brief space spent in inspecting the three magnificent winding and fan engines, the Unibal fan, and the framework for screening the coal, they were conducted by Mr. James Gilchrist, manager, down into the workings in the ell seam at a depth of 118 fathoms. Here at the pit bottom, in the roads and at the face, twenty-one Swan lamps, were burn- ing, giving forth a brilliant, steady flame, the luminosity of which, while sufficient to supply the desired light, had none of the disagreeable intensity associated with most systems of electrical lighting. Besides the pear-shaped Swan laum;in which the glowing or incandescence is carried on in vacuo, there is an outer lantern, the invention of Mr. David Gra- horn, consisting of a strong glass globe, air-tight, protected with steel guards. Etch lamp was also connected with two differeet forms of Grab 4.111',4 patent safety air-tight contacts and switzhes for cutting off and letting on the current, the effect of which, it is believed, would be to render the lamps quite safe, even in the iy-esence of explosive gas. At first the intention was to employ the fan engine to drive the dynamo-electric machine or generator, but this was departed from, and an engine of 12 horse-power was erected in the workshops on the surface for the purpose. From the gene- rator the electric cables, two in number, are conducted along the roof of the workshops over ordinary telegraph poles to the pithead of No. 2 shaft, and thence down into the work- ings. From the ridge of the wonlishops to the pithead, a distance of several hundred yank, the cables consist of or- dinary copper wire, n. ia diameter; inside the workshop and below the ground, to allow of their safe handling, they are composed of insulated wires; while on the way down the shalt they are enclosed in a galvanised tube. Near the bottom of the shaft branches are taken off to supply light to the principal roadways and to the ha4lage engine-room, the main cables be carried into one of the sections of the mine, a distance of half a mile. After a careful inspection of the lamps at the pit bottom the .party were photographed in three groups, with the aid of the electric light, by Mr. Annan, of Glasgow, who may well be credited with the dis- tinction of being the first to exercise his skill in the bowels of the earth. They were then led to the haulage engine- room and int ) the workings, where they witnessed the effects of the light. At the latter point, while the course of visitors were at a safe distance, a shot was fired, bringing down a large mass of coal. Having spent fully an hour be- low ground, the party returned to the surface, where carri- ages were in waiting to convey them to Earnock Mansion louse, where luncheon was served.

ME FORCE OF MIGINATEsE.—They worked a racket on young Griph at his boarding-house recently. They detected thine raiding the pic closet, and found that he had got away with a mince pie, some cookies, some doughnuts, and some .cheese. The landlady and her daughter together resolved •on vengeance. They waited till Mr. Griph had devoured the foodthat he had taken and made his appearance in the sitting-room. Than the landlady said to her daughter— ." Mary,,yon know that mince pie that we made out of the meat we bought of the strange butcher, and which proved 't be mule meat?" "Yet, mother." "What did you do with it ?" "Pat it aside te give to tramps." That made Griph, who overheard, uneasy. "And Mary, you know those cookies that the cook carelessly spilled the kerosene over. What did you do with them?" "Pat them with the pie." Griph recollected that there was a queer taste to ethosemsokies, and kind of felt like a man who had just -started in on the miserieo of a first sea voyage. But he tried to shake.the feeling ea. "Arid Marv," centinued the old lady," you-know the cook carelessly aiad some very bad eggs to make some doughnuts. Where did you pat the doughnuts ?" 4‘ I pat the doughnuts aside for-tramps, too; and I guess when they come to eat 'em they'll think they've swallowed an earthquake:" Griph felt that he had. ;The seasick feeling seemed to grow instead of shaking off. Hi grew pale adehivered. The ladies were delighted. "Mary,, said the old lady," when you give those things to the tramps don't give them the cheese) that's with 'em, for I pat poieod in to kill rats?' Then 6 Huh wanted to be sick. With melancholy howl he sprang up, rushed up to his room and took an emetic that nearly brought his feet up. And he I had a chill and a headache, and went to bed and stayed there for two days. Tau CRRONICLES OF Eum—One Mayor was expelled 4‘ for slighting his election and taking a frolic into Scotland" —a fatal' frolic as it turned out, for he was stabbed to the heart in a gaming-house broil. Another Mayor had to resign "through losses ateea and land," and the court of aldermen net only discharged him "without the least fine," bat" inspired with charity," sent him ten pounds for his immediate relief. Next year six large grampuses were taken in the Etember, and the casks containing their blubber impounded by the Mayer as admiral of that estuary. Another year is signalised by a murder, another by the beautifying of the Exchange, and soon. In 1684 the charter was surrendered by Judge Jeffreys. but afterwards a new one wee graciously granted, "to the incredible joy qf the town." Trouble arose before very long, for .the aldermen, declined to lend themselves to royal interference with the freedom of their elections: so his most gracious Majesty. James 11., by way of giving them a taste of his.paternal . correction placed 1,200 eoldiers, mostly commanded by Popish officers, at free quarters of the town. These "lambs" frolicked and wantoned after their fashion, treating tbe citizens worse than dogs. So they lorded it till William of Orange landed at Torbay, when the Protestants rose one night and made prisoners of the Roman Catholic officers. Since the end of these.transieut troubles the town appears to have done little else but increase and multiply, blessed with a history at once prosperous and uneventful. Walls, gates, castle, have disappeared, docks have been enlarged oe dug, houses re-built and re-built again, and the town "has long enjoyed the proud title of the third port in tbe i;ingelom, London and Liverpool alone taking precedence." 'The population of the borough at the present time some- what e:s.ceeds 150,000.—" Our Over Countev" for Ausrit. A GRANDFATILEft'S LEGICY.—" When I was a little boy," Raid a gentleman one evening, "1 paid a visit to my gran father, a venerable old man, whose black cap and tassel, blue breeches, and huge silver knee-buckles, tilled me with great awe. When I went to bid him good-bye he drew me betireen his knees, andiplacing his hand on rov head, said, Grandchild, I have one thing to Say to you. 'Will you re- member it?' I stared inta his-face and nodded, for I was afraid to promise aloud. 'Welt,' he continued, 'whatever you do, do the best you can.' This, in feet, was my grand., father's legacy to me, and it has proved' better than gold. I nervier forgot his words, and I believe I have tried-to act upon them. After reaching home, my uncle gave Marcus and me some weeding to do in the garden. It was Wednes- 'day afternoon and we had laid our plans for something else. Marcus, fretted and ill-humoured at his disappointment, did not more than half do his work, and I began pretty much like him, until grandfather's advice came into my mind, and I determined to follow it. In a word, I' did my best,' and when my uncle came out I shall never forget his look of ap- probation as his eyes glanced over my beds, or the four- pence be slipped into my hands afterwards as he said the work was well done. Ah ! I was a glad and thankful boy, while poor Marcos was left to drudge over his beds all the afternoon. At 15 I was sent to the academy, where I had partly to earn my own way through the course. The lea- eons came herd at first, for I was not fond of study, but my grandfather's advice was my Motto, and I tried to do my best. As a consequence of this, though I was small of my age, and not very strong, my mother had three offers for me before the year was out, and nd one from the belt merchant of the yillaleveh'elai whose store was considered very desirable. t my ye oCwhnurch I tried to do the Lord's work as well a3s I diet been tempted to leave the Sabbath prayer meeting, and often, when I have school or let a hindrance keep me from the good thing, my grandfather's last or discouraged in any can, have given me fresh courage, 'Do the best you and would again try." Here, then, was the key to this man'socneaorafcter. He is con- sidered one of the best business men cne of the best officers of the Church o orhbebet citizens, of the poor, one of the best neighbours, fatlieers, elltsfbraiennddss, friends; in a word, he is nniversallv beloved and expected. And what is the secret of it all? He always tried to do the hPst that he could. Let every boy and girl take this for their motto. Acted upon, it will do wonders for you. .It will bring out powers and capabilities which will surprise and delight yourselves and friends. A Louis IltslNG9.—At one of our village matches I re- member happening to say that, the man then batting was having a good innings. This harmless remark was at once r. baked by a reference to days gone by. " Ah, well," said an old man, "it isn't nothin to an innings I mind a man has-in' at *The Wells' (Tunbridge Wells) time as I used to go carrier to The Borough'—he was in three days, he was, and never was out." I signified my admiration. "Yes," added the man, "I know it was three days, for I mind he was in when I went by with the broad-wheel waggon to London, and he was in when I came back." It was in a single wicket match, it is true, so the man said • still, my recollections pale before his.—" Sussex Folk and Sussex Ways," in Leisure Hour. THE DREAM OF ECG= ARAM.—This weird and strik- ing ballad will retain a permanent hold upon our literature. Its realism and dramatic power stamp it indelibly upon the mind of the reader. The strange career of Engene Aram furnished Lord Lytton with the ground-work of one of his best-abused and yet most popular novels. In defending his choice of such a subject for treatment, the novelist observes, in a preface to the edition of "Eugene Aratn" issued in 1840_:—"1he_gu11t of Eugene Aram is not that ota vulgar ruffian; it leads us to views and considerations vitally and wholly distinct from those with which profligate knavery and brutal cruelty revolt and displease us in the literature of Newgate and the hulks. His crime does, in fact, belong to those startling paradoxes which the poetry of all coun- tries, and especially of our own, has always delighted to con- template and examine. Whatever crime appears the aberra- tion rand monstrous product of a great intellect, or of a nature ordinarily virtuous, it becomes not only the subject for genius, which deals with passions, to describe; but a problem for philosophy, which deals with actions, to inves- tigate and solve; hence the Macbeths and Richards, the lagos and Othellos." There is much to be said, however, in favour of the tragedy or the ballad—as opposed to the novel—being the best and most graphic medium for convey- ing such a story as that which has conferred an unenviable notoriety upon Eugene Aram.—Fyvliz "Cassen Illustrated British Ballads." ai LACxerctAsnarth to RatsßeaEvEmfi N MaInLdLMERI7 known. NU never so glutted with labour as it was on Saturday, 4 . as tatting ie this neigh- Monday, engagements bourhood will become general oe could not be delayed, and a reduction'awages as compared with the declining ones of last season ha J to be submitted ep,3 to. The very best English labourers, up ta every class of harvesting work, were engaged at-from 20s. to 235. a week, with meat; binders, to live in the horse, re secured at from 108. to 185. a week, or 185. to 245. to keep themselves. There was a large amount of labour left disenglEed- How THE STC-CH OF THE FARM NAT BE IN4REASED,""" The following recently appeared in the Sussex Aertiter —The conclusion has long since been formed by, almost 'general agreement that the best way to make farming. pay is to keep more stock en the land, and produce larger qultr tides of meat; but, although the advice has been urged on, farmers for a dozen years or more to attend to this branch of husbandry rather than to corn growing, the agricultural returns show that during the recent years there has been little or no increase in flocks and herds, taking the country generally into vier. Laying down more land to grass is not at all calculated to increase the number either of sheep or cattle. The growth of more root and green crops, and making their produce heavy by large applications of arti- ficial manure, ought to do so, but somehow or other it does not according to statistics. About a quarter of a century ago there was a general belief that British farthing was making great headway in this direction, but what with turnip failures, cattle diseases, drought years the decima- tion of flocks by liver rot, and other causes, it the numbers of sheep and cattle go up one year they are down the next, and in the aggregate there has been little or no increase for some time past. The truth of the matter appears to be that husbandry of this kind requires a vast amount of capital to keep up the steam. And while the generality of our farmers never had sufficient means fully to meet its requirements, they have been worse crippled in resources than ever dur- ing the past half dozen years owing to the bad times. Next to growing heavy root and green crops, and,employing large quantities of artificial food in their consumption, utilising the greater part of the straw raised on the farm as food for stock, instead of a mere waste produced to litter them with, would afford facilities for larger numbers of stock to be kept than almost anything else. Straw may not be a highly nutritive substance at the hest, but it forms a capital element in the winter dietary for other richer materials to be intermixed with. Employed in this way it serves as a substitute for hay, and it is just here where the economy of making it serve as food would enable largely iftclined num- bers of stock to be bred, reared, and fattened. Straw cat into chaff and mixed up with root pulp forms excellent winter food for all kinds of cattle, and also for sheep and horses, when occasion serves. In fattening stock, oilcake, malt meal, or any other auxiliary rich nutritives may be added in any quantities. Hay not being needed, the cost and labour of haymaking might be saved, and the grass which used to be mown would of course support much larger numbers of stock in snmmer. The habit of utilising straw in this way give farmers a greater security to keep up the numbers of their sheep and cattle when there are indifferent root crops. The pulping system is a great economiser at such times, and, by making use of it, very small crops have been made to last a long time. The modicum of pulp which can be spared is mixed up with a large bulk of chaff, afford- ing a base for the artificial food deemed necessary to be added. Shrewd intelligent men have not only been known to sustain the numbers of their flocks and herds in winters of great scarcity for roots, by adopting these tactics, but on the pinch have kept sheep as well as cattle for weeks and even months together on straw chaff and artificial food, without any roots whatever. There were, indeed, instances In the winter of 1865, and subsequently in the winters suc- ceeding the drought years of 1868 and 1870, of flocks of sheep being kept wholly on dry food from November until April, with the exception of such rough grass as could be picked up by a daily run over stubbles or grass fields. Farmers in other parts of England would do well to take a lesson from the Cumberland and Westmorland men to enter- prise in cattle feeding. Mr. Little, in his interest* report many otyhaelm Angn rti counlityn gr an ln gSnomc gi e agty 'fan nd" turrenta In niis on their management, which appears in the last half-yearly vg toal teals that all the straw their arable lands produce, but the grain too— oats there commonly taking the place of wheat in the ro- tation and being the chief corn crop. One farmer, when questioned by Mr. Little as to whether he never eold any grain, scoffed at the idea, and said he made all his corn "walk to market." Boos IN Wistfreh.—Any farmer can have eggs in spring. Bat only those who care for their fowls can have eggs in mid-winter, when they are worth five or six cents apiece. We recently saw a flock of fifteen hens that had averaged seven eggs a day through December and January, and were still laying at the same rate. The owner had sold 5 dole. worth of eggs a month besides those used on his own table. When hens can be made to lay in this way there is no doubt about the profits of poultry keeping. Anyone who wM carefully attend to the following rules may be equally fortunate. To get a plentiful supply of eggs in winter young hens are neeessary. Pallets hatched in April or May will prove most satisfactory. The hen house must be warm and kept clean. Provide plenty of 'fresh water al- ways. A variety of food is necessary, but wheat and-screen- ings should be the main feed. Corn has more fattening than egg producing properties, and should be fed sparingly. Buckwheat is valuable feed for hens. Oats are not worth much, but will do to make out the variety. Feed in the morning a warm mess of meal, .middlings, or-something of that sort, but feed no soft feed after the middle of the day: Only dry grain should be in a hen's crop upon going to roost. Fresh meats must be fed. Lard or-tallow scraps are good; both can be bought at the soap factories, the former costing 2 dole. and the latter 1 dol. per hundred. Scrape should be broken and soaked over night, warmed and fed in the morning. Meal may be added. Hens also require vegetable food. Carrots are best; chop as fine as kernels of corn, and about twice a week add a few onions. For shell material use oyster or clam shells, both browned and raw. Break them fine. Keep plenty of fine sand where your hens can have full access to it. nother important considera- tion is, make no sudden change in your manner of feeding. —New York Herald. SEWAGE FAHNING.—By the recent census we have seen that many of our large cities are rapidly increasing in popu- lation, and, therefore, the difficult problem of what is to be done with town sewage becomes daily of greater importance, for in proportion as the inhabitants increase, so in like man- ner does the sewage. According to the present dangerous and wasteful method generally adopted in this country, all the refuse is discharged into one of the nearest rivers, and, consequently, even now there is scarcely a stream which has not been injured more or less from this cause, whilst if this state of things is allowed to continue we shall soon have all our fairest rivers completely polluted. Considering the vital importance of the sewage question to every nation, we were in no way surprised to find that Dr. Alfred Carpenter's invitation to inspect the Beddington Sewage Farm was last Saturday week cordially responded to by many members of the International Medical Congress. The farm, which is about 450 acres, belongs to the Croydon Local Board of Health, and is irrigated by the sewage of some 63,000 per- sons. This crude sewage on leaving Croydon passes through a kind of sieve, which removes rags, sticks, paper, &c., after which it goes direct on to the land without any other treat- ment, for from 12 to 24 hours at a time, and is then run on to a second and sometimes a third field before it finally leaves the farm and enters the river. Irrigation has been almost continuous for some 21 years, except on two or three .occasions when oats were grown, for in that case the land Is not sewaged until the crop is taken off. Rye grass seems to do best, and one field has been cut three times already this year, whilst a fourth crop is now being obtained. In addition to rye grass, however, there was also ordinary grass and some wheat, cabbages, ece. A number of horses were to be seen grazing which are not the property of the Local Board, hut are kept there for a time by their owners, who find that when out of health they quickly recover and gain strength on the farm. Many of the cattle, however, were bred on the farm, and look in perfect health, whilst the lee which was eaten for luncheon, and pronounced excel- lent, was fed on sewage grass. Perhaps the most striking proof that the vicinity of a sewage farm is not unhealthy is shown by the children at Beddington Female Orphan Asylum, who all look the picture of health, although they live in the midst of the farm; and also the low death-rate at Beddington gives striking evidence that the chief argu- ment which has been raised against sewage farming, namely, that it is injurious to health, does not hold good.—Land and Water. A serious fire occurred on the farm premises of Mr. Mar- riott Hall, at Thorpe Salcan, near Kiveton, on Thursday morning, by which damage was done to the extent of nearly £lO,OOO. Reports from New York agree in stating that there will be a great diminution in the quantity of American wheat available for export to Europe this season. The Commercial Bulletin puts the deficiency as high as 100 millions of bushels, but this will probably be found to be an exaggera- tion. A letter from Philadelphia explains that whilst there will undoubtedly be a short crop this year, America will still have a very large quantity of wheat to sell in Earpoe, and next year, should the weather be favourable, vast tracts of land w ill be brought into cultivation by the "vast num her" of German farmers who have landed at New York this year, and are pushing their way westward.

A movement is on foot m Liverpool for presenting the Mayoress with a handsome silver cradle. On Monday a railway employe named Boyce, aged 33, married, and residing at Swansea, murdered his child, aged three years, by striking it on the .heafi:with a hatchet. The man had been drinking. The South Staffordshire/Miners' Association was on Tues- day dissolved in consequence of the miners not being able to contribute to the funds, owing to the depression in trade. At Leicester, on Saturday, a servant girl named Lizzie Broughton, in the service of a publican, whilst lighting a fire, poured some petroleum upon it. An explosion followed, and the girl was burnt to death.. John Rowan, an Irish farm labourer, while en his way from Selby to Liverpool, where he intended sailing for America, was robbed in Leeds of £2s—all be had—by two women with whom he west drinking. None of the money

has been fond. As a girt was going to her work at the north end of Pres- ton, she observed the lead body of a child, partly covered with rage. She at once informed the police, and a constable zemoved the body to the mortuary. It is so far decomposed as to be rendered unrecormisable. . • .

,An inquest has been held at East Coker on the body of a lad tamed Alexander Marsh, son of a farmer, who died from injdries received when leaping a hurdle. A spike entered his groin, and he lived in great agony for several days be- fore death put an end to his sufferings. The Secialists in Switzerland, having been forbidden to hold a congress at Zurich, have written a threatening letter to the Federal Tribunal, in which they say they have enough dynamite tO Slow up half Switzerland, and that a conflagra- tion will begin there that will burn up the world. The Central Committee of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants for the promotion of the nine hours movement has lust resolved " That'the memorial asking for the cessation Of nine hours as a working day should be sent to the variod.li boards of directors at the earliest Opportunity." the various barristers ,appointed to hold revision courts over the country, for the purpose of revising the lists of voters who are entitled to elect members to serve in Parlia- ment, will hold their courts to hear county claims between September 20 and October 31, and will take borough claims between September 15 and October 31. An American paper says that Dr.aTanner is not dead, and has not been to Amsterdam, where he is circumstantially reported to have met his death under curiously dramatic circumstances. The doctor has never been out of the United States, and is said to be in training for another starving feat, which he promises shall last over 90 days. Mr. Joseph Cowen, M.P., in acknowledging the receipt of a resolution passed by the Newcastle branch of the Land League, expresses his regret that the labours of the few in- dividuals who sympathise with that -cause have not been more successful. "it was," he adds, "with extreme regret that I heard Mr. Forster'e declaration that the Government did not intend to release the prisoners.". Four hundred Aberdeenshire farmersmet on Monday at Irisch to consider the agricultural depression. A resolution was passed" That the depressed state of agriculture should claim the serious ;attention of all concerned, with a view to devise an immediate remedy, and that the chief remedy is to'be found in a, readjustment of the present rent paid for land." A large committee was appointed. Mr. Atherley Jones, barrister at law, who was requested to allow himself to be nominated by the Leeds branch of the Land League as the Home Rule candidate for Leeds, has sent a reply, in which he says that at this particular junc- ture he would, under the circumstances, hardly feel justified in accepting the invitation and opposing the re-election of Mr. H. Gladstone. The new Primitive Methodist College in Alexandra-road, Moss Side, Manchester, erected at a cost of over £B,OOO, was opened on Monday. Mr. Henry Lee, M.P., presided at the opening ceremony. From a report which was read there appears to be a balance still awing on the building account of £1,670, but this will be reduced by subscriptions which have been promised to the amount of £7OO. A pedlar named Alfred Gough has been arrested at Chesterfield in connection with the murder of a little girl named Eleanor Windle, whose body was found on Monday half way between Chesterfield and Brimington in a planta- tion. The child accompanied Gough on his way to Brim- ington on Saturday, and the man was seen to be illtreating her. Nothing further was seen of her until Monday morn- ing, when the body was found in the thicket. The child .had been strangled with a rope. There were sixteen British and foreign wrecks iof which eleven were British, one being a steamer, reported during the past week, making a total of 1,050 for the present year, or an increase of 170 as compared with the corresponding period of last year. The approximate value of property lost was £2,800,000, including British £2,300,000. Three vessels were lost off the coasts of the United Kingdom, four off Holland, one by collision, one abandoned at sea. Forty-five lives were 108 L. BITING AND DEVOURING THE CHURCH.-At a meeting of the Rochester Diocesan Conference, Canon Phillips is re- ported to have said: "He considered that, so long as they bit and devoured and prosecuted and imprisoned one another, they could never do the work that the Church of England was called upon to, do. And then there was a ques- tion of waiting two years before they moved. He thought the Church was always too late, and if they were to wait two years, who knew what might happen to the Church of England in two yearar—Liberator. A PROCRASTINATING BRIDEGROOM.—An interesting wed- ding took place a few days ago at the Parish Church, Cleverlon. The bride was a well-known resident of ..the place, and the bridegroom the son of a late hotel proprietor. In a dashing turn-out the fair one arrived with her friends at the sacred edifice: There was, however, no expectant bride- groom, and the anxious moments seemed hours as the bridal party waited and waited. After a long delay, and still no bridegroom appearing, one of the party hurried off to look for him, and he was found leisurely proceeding in his working dress tower& the church, apparently quite oblivious of any anxiety his tardiness was creating. "Never mind," said he, "like a cat's tail—always behind." Reports have been received from every county in England., and from eight of the Welsh counties, as to the probable results of the harvest. The Mark Lane Express summarises these returns, 353 in number, as follows:—Wheat, over average, 23; average, 159; under average, 171. Barley, over average, 103; average, 186; under average. 53. Oats, over average, 28; average, 97; under average, 217. Beans, over average, 19; average, 74; under average, 171. Peas, over average, 55; average, 160; under average, 53. The barley crop, as last year, is the best of the cereals. A large proportion of the corn is still out in the fields, and a great deal is vet uncut. The small yield of wheat is attributed by Bell's Messenger to indifferent cultivation, the number of farms that are unlet, and the low price of wheat, which has made its cultivation cease to be profitable. TWO CASES OF ATTEMPTED MERDER.—At Wolverhampton, on Tuesday, Thomas Ellis was charged with attempting to murder Mary Sheward, an elderly woman, with whom he had cohabited for about 14 years. On Saturday prisoner quarrelled with Sheward, and, seizing a knife, hacked her about the face with it, afterwards cutting his own throat in several places. Prisoner was reminded. The woman lies in a critical condition, but says she wants Ellis released. —The Newcastle-under-Lyme' magistrates. on Tuesday, committol a man named Hickey, a labourer, to the Stafford- shire Assizes on a charge of attempting to murder his wife. On the night of the 18th inst., the prisoner was at home, when his wife came in under the influence of drink and abused Vim. He therefore rushed at her with a clasp knife and stabbed her indiscriminatelyMnflicting six gashes about the face and neck. He immediately afterwards gave him- self up at the police station and confessed his crime. THE CHURCH DEFENCE INSTITUTION IN FAVOUR OF BIS- ESTABLISHMENT.—It is startling to find that, so soon after the spurt made by the Church Defence Institution to check the falling off in its income, the committee of that body have actually declared their intention to support a measure of Disestablishment ! It is, however, only in the city of London and the object of the movement is to pull down the useless city churches, and to employ the surplus funds towards meeting the spiritual wants of the populous metro- politan districts. Nevertheless it is, we repeat, startling to find that, just as Bishop Magee has been denouncing Liberationists for being "eager " to facilitate the conversion of churches into factories and drinking saloons, the Church Defence Institution declares that it also is eager to afford facilities for building warehouses and shops on the sites of consecrated edifices in the city. After this the institution will have to revise a good deal of the language it has used about the palling down of Dissenting chapels. The expla- • nation of this proceeding we take to be this—these wasted edifices and endowments in the city of London are felt to be a discredit and a weakness. to the Establishment, and, that fact being seen, there is anxiety—tardy though it be— ! to remove the source of danger. And then there is a large amount of money at stake, and it is wished to secure its re- appropriation to ecclesiastical purposes before the arrival of the dreaded day of Disestablishment. Well, that is a point upon which the disestablishers have something to say, and we think the time has some for them to say it.—Liberator. THE IRISH LAND BILL. It may be useful to recapitulate brieflyk and in its broad and general bearing, the total effect of the Land Bill, which has this week been passed. In its details the bill is um doubtedly complicated and difficult to understand. Looke&

at, however, in a comprehensive way, its complications van- ish, and its salient characteristics stand out in prominent relief, just as the small inequalities in a landscape, which seem so prodigious to the traveller in the valley, grow less, and finally disappear altogether when viewed from the height of an adjacent hill. Taking this kind of bird's-eye view of Mr. Gladstone's second experience in pacifying Ireland, we fond that what the bill accomplishes may be summarised in the following manner, which it is hoped will help persons who have consistently refused to follow all the endless bend- ings and windings of clauses, sections, sub-sections, amend- ments, amended amendments, and amended amendments re-amended, to comprehend with tolerable accuracy what I the Land Bill is which Parliament has just added to the I statute book.

In the first place, it must never be forgotten that Irish farmers are in their main characteristics supposed to be like farmers dii the world over. They want to live in peace and comfort, each man under his own vine and fig-tree, with reasonable assurance that he will not be unfairly treated, either by being ejected from his holding or being forced to pay his landlord an exorbitant rent. It was just these ob- jects that Mr. Gladstone proposed to carry into effect in 1870 and again in 1881. There were landlords who, prior to 1870, had undoubtedly run up rents unjustifiably, and carried out evictions capriciously; therefore in that year Mr. Gladstone's fiat went forth to the effect that if a landlmd chose to evict a tenant he must pay "compensation for disturbance." Landlords, however, in some instances have taken advan- tage of that provision in an unexpected way. They found a convenient loop-hole, and crept through it with consider- able agility. They ran up their rents so high as to make it impossible for farmers to pay, and thus got rid of inconveni- ent tenants, without the trouble of evicting or the need of paying compensation. The obvious remedy was to fix a rent beyond which the landlord cannot go. This is exactly what the present bill does. On this novel, unheard of, completely un-English, yet needful provision, which enables a Court to pronounce what is a fair rent for a particular holding, the whole merit of the blll, as Mr. Glad- stone himself acknowledged, virtually depe ads. It is the hinge on which everything tarns. Two at least of the far- mers' "Three F's" the bill grants—namely, "Fair Rent" and "Fixity of Tenure." Not absolute " fixity" in the sense that the landlord cannot for gross injury done to the land get rid of his tenant; but the complete feeling of cer- tainty on the part of the tenant that, during good behaviour, he will be allowed to plough and sow and reap and gather into barns without fear of capricious eviction. The last of the "Three F's" is " Free Sale." This is a peculiarly Irish institution. Some persons, the Marquis of Salisbury among them, contend that this means giving the tenant the right to sell that which he never purchased. Others, in- , eluding the members of the Government, urge that if the ; tenant has not purchased his right in his tenancy by money, • he has paid for it with the sweat of his brow, and has an indefeasible interest in it. Looked at a little more closely still, and taking the "Three F's" in their order, this is what the Land Act will precisely effect:

1. Free Sale.—What the tenant has to sell is the " good- will" of his farm. This something over and above the fair market value of his holding. It is the value of the tenant's improvements, plus the sentimental interest that he has acquired by living on the land for a number of years, plus the increased value which land in Ireland possesses compared with land elsewhere owing to the fact of the ex- treme competition for a bit of soil existing among all true followers of St. Patrick. In Ulster the tenant has always had the customary right to sell this goodwill, and the Act of 1870 gave legislative sanction to the custom. The Act of 1881 goes further, and extends the Ulster custom all over Ireland. An Irish tenant may now sell his goodwill to anybody, with this proviso, that the landlord has a right to object to the newcomer if all the improvements on the estate have been made and "substantially maintained," not by the tenant, but by the landlord himself. The obvious result of the legislation of free sale is that the outgoing tenant receives a large sum of money, while the incomer is depleted to exactly the same amount, which cripples his resources and leaves him proportionately less able to meet his rent and to expend capital on developing the land. 2. Fair Rent.—As we have pointed out, the defect of the last Act was that landlords could run up their rent to any extent, and thus force tenants to leave. They did not "evict ;" they merely compelled tenants to "resign." The Act of 1881 allows any Irish tenant to go to "the Court," meaning the Civil Bill Court of the particular county in which helives, and ask it to fix what is the fair rent for him to pay. The landlord can also go to the Court with the same request. But how is the Court to fix that shadowy and uncertain thing, a really " fair " rental for a tenant to pay? Luckily, the Court is not left entirely without guidance as to the principles upon which they are to proceed. They are, in fixing the rent, to take into account "the interests of the landlord and of the tenant respectively." Then they are also not necessarily to lower the rent because the tenant has had to pay a large sum for goodwill, or tenant-right, when entering into the tenancy. The Court may, under certain circumstances, if it likes, do so; but the Act ex- pressly states that "the amount paid for the tenant-right is not to be alone, of itself, a reason for reducing the rent." I Then it practically come to this, that the Court has simply I to go on general principles of justice and equity in deciding what rent is a "fair rent." When it has fixed that rent, a "statutory term" of fifteen years commences, (hiring which it is impossible for the landlord to raise the rent, or to evict his tenant, except for what is called a breach of the "statu- tory conditions ; that is to say, during this fifteen years of safety to the occupying tenant the only acts by which the tenant can imperil that safety are sub-letting without the landlord's leave, failing to pay his rent, committing "waste," and other analog( us misdeeds. 3. Fixity of Tenure.—This is the natural and necessary corollary of fair rents. For what possible good can there be in allowing a tenant to pay a moderate rental, if he is liable ta, be turned out at a moment's notice? This boon of fixity—or, as Mr. Gladstone prefers to call it, security—of tenure, is given by the 15 years' term noticed above. Dur- ing that 15 years the tenant is to be one—.and by far the most irremovable of his landlord's "fixtures." Thus en- dowed with the three substantial benefits of liberty to sell his tenancy for what he can get, security against excessive rents, and security against evictions, the Hibernian farmer is right in supposing that there is "a good time coming." But the question naturally arises, what is to happen to those , tenants who never trouble the Courts about their rents? , Are they to be left out in the cold, with no protection, or • only the confessedly inadequate protection afforded by the , Act of 1870? We take it that in the majority of Irish tenancies tenants will appeal to the Courts. Those who do , not will be protected in this way, that if turned out they can claim compensation for disturbance, levied at a far higher rate than before, from their landlord, as well as com- pensation for improvement, and they will have a right to these two compensations even though they are evicted for not paying rent. There are one or two supplementary provisions of the Act which require a word of exposition. Emigration is to be facilitated by State grants in aid. The reclamation of waste lands is to be encouraged by the same method. Lastly, there is the extremely important provision for creating, in a small way, a body of peasant proprietors, already attempted by the "Bright clauses" of the old Land Act. The present Act authorises advances to tenants for the purpose of purchasing their holdings. If bought out and out at once, as much as three-fourths of the purchase. money can be advanced by the Land Commission; if the land is burdened with a "fee from rent "—in other words, with a yearly payment to the landlord—then half the pur- chase-money is all that can be supplied out of the public purse. These being the grand, cardinal, and salient points of the measure which has occupied Parliament for the major part of the session, it now only remains for the Irish land- lords and the Irish tenants to work together in a spirit of conciliation, so as to reap the greatest amount of benefit, both for themselves and the country, which the bill is capable of producing.

Jupiter is now very conveniently situated for observa- tion, being not far from the Pleiades and rising soon after ten o'clock. The great red spot which has attracted so much attention in recent years continues as large and well-defined as before.

Mr. -William Simpson has received a commission from the Queen to paint an historical picture of the review of Scot- tish and Border volunteers which is to be held at Edinburgh on August 25th, as a companion picture to one painted of the recent Windsor review.

In the course of the excavations for the new fort at Lier in the neighbourhood of Antwerp, a number of bones of ex- tinct animals, mammoths' teeth, and the almost complete skeleton of a rhinoceros have been dug up. It was in the same district that, in 1760, was found the immense blreleton of a mammoth which is preserved in the Natural History Museum at Brussels.

After next week the comet will move rapidly to- wards the south, and will therefore not be visible much longer in these latitudes.

frofessor Lawrence Smith has drawn attention to a re- markable property in the meteoric iron of Santa Cattarina, in Brazil. This meteoric iron contains 66 per cent. of iron and 34 of nickel. Very small fragments were slightly affected by the magnet, bat if flattened on a steel anvil with a steel hammer they became very sensitive to the magnet, and by heating them red hot they became yet more highly magnetic._

Mr. D. T. Lawson, of Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, has been exciting considerable attention by some experiments which he has been making on the causes which lead to the bursting of boilers. His hypothesis, which appears to be confirmed by a very striking result obtained, is that cold water in- jected into a boiler of super-heated steam will occasion a 1 violent explosion. We fail to see in what this differs from Boutigny's experiment of causing water to explode by pro- ducing the spheroidal state, and then dropping cold water into it.—Athenerl2n.• VALUABLE ph,COVEET YOB TE2 HArn.—lf your hair is turning grey or white, or failing off, me “Tite Mexican Hair Renewer," for it will positively restore in every ease Grey or 'White hair to its original colour, without leaving the disagree- able smell of most llestorers." div.head: correspondent from Sydney writes the follow" Ang interesting letter to a contemporary:- – – –
div.p: A correspondent from Sydney writes the follow" Ang inter- esting letter to a contemporary:- - - -

The public of Australia have for several v'eeelts past been on the tiptoe of expectation concerning Jae results of the counting of heads in the various colonies.. The simultaneous numbering of the inhabitants of a Croup of communities such as this might at any time b,a expected to yield much that was both interesting and irAtructive. But special im- portance is attached to the, present census, inasmuch as during the decade since 'he last enumeration radically dif- ferent fiscal policies hat been pursued by the two leading colonies, and it was •aniversally felt that the outcome would shed light upon an issue that had long been obscure. In 1871, the population of Victoria was 731,000. It is now ascertained to be 855,000. The increase in the ten years is therefore 124,000, or 17 per cent. In 1871 the population of New South Wales was 503,000 ; it is now 750,000—an increase of 247,000, or nearly 50 per cent. The estimated, population of Victoria at the time of the present census was 930,000, so that 75,600 people have departed from that colony in the decade without being registered in the Custom House. But the worst feature of the data in regard to Vic- toria is that the actual increment is less than it would be if immigration and emigration had exactly balanced each other. The excess of births over deaths ;during the ten years is computed at 146,000; in reality, therefore, so far from the Colony of Protection having gained by immigra- tion, she has lost no fewer than 22,000 souls by excess of departures over arrivals. In the meantime, the Free Trade Colony, contrariwise, has added 106,000 to the number of her inhabitants by excess of immigration over emigration. So far the teaching is plain enough. Nor does further in- vestigation of the returns yield support for conclusions of a different nature. Leaving Sydney and Melbourne out of the question the increase in New South Wales is from 366,000 in 1871 to 520,000 in 1881, or over 42 per cent.; while in Victoria the increase is only nine per cent. In other words, Melbourne has been growing at the expense of the country districts—the producing industries of Victoria have been paying tribute to the manufacturing. A more remarkable verification of the doctrines of political economy
would be hard to discover. Yet the advance M Melbourne

is proportionately mach less than that of New South Wales as a whole, and very much less than the growth of Sydney. During the decade the population of Melbourne grew from 206,000 to 281,000—a notable and gratifying progression, only it swallows up three-fifths of the increase for the whole of Victoria. The advance of Sydney, however, was from 136,000 to 222,000—an increase of 86,000, but not much over one-third of the increase for the whole of New South Wales. The growth of the Free Trade capital was, there- fore, much larger than the growth of the Protection capital, notwithstanding that the process in the latter instance was accelerated by a fiscal policy which impelled the people to forsake the plough and the shovel and flock to the city of manufacturers.

We have seen that the actual population of Victoria is smaller by about 75,000 than the official estimate and that the census indicates a net loss by emigration of 22,000. But the figures tell an even more dolorous tale. In round num- bers the estimate stood thus: Population in 1871 Increase by births over deaths 1871-81 Increase by immigration at ports

929,000 About the gain by excess of births over deaths there can be little doubt. If there is any error under this head, evidently it is on the side of understanding the facts; for, as Mr. Hayter, the Government statistician of Victoria, himself says, many births escape registration, while no deaths except secret murders can. Nor can it be disputed that the gross number of arrivals registered actually did land in the colony. The gain clearly has been made, but it has not been kept. The deficiency of 75,000 people must be taken as representing a number who have turned their backs upon Mr. Berry's " working-man's paradise." And a legitimate inference is that the mass of these emigrants were male adults—bread winners—the working men whom the Protec- tionists say their policy attracts. For men with wives and families do not readily move off to fresh fields and pastures new. A fair conclusion is, therefore, that Protection and Berry ism have robbed Victoria of an innumerable swarm of her working bees, and consequently increased the percentage of her drones. The details of ages and sexes have not yet been published, so that this view only rests upon inference, but it will be matter for extreme surprise if it be not proved correct when all the data come to be seen. It was natural enough in these circumstances fora member of the Victorian Assembly to suggest that a committee of inquiry should be appointed to ascertain what causes have been at work; and it was natural enough for Mr. Berry and his Protection- ist following to scout the idea. An investigation of the causes might have led to the disclosure of unpalatable , truths; and then the business was being done with tolerable efficiency by the Press. Not the least significant of the comparisons that have been instituted is one relating to the natural increase in the two colonies. For a long while pub- lic attention in Victoria has been directed to the paucity of marriages in that community, and various causes have been assigned for the condition. The marriage rate there for several years past has been 11: per thousand smaller than in New South Vales; and the birth rate has been nearly 4 per thousand smaller. Accordingly we find in the latter colony, with a population averaging about 200,000 less than the former during the ten years, the excess of births over deaths aggregates fully 140,000. Of course there is stili some difference of opinion as to how much of the disparity in the growth of the two colonies is due to the disparity of their fiscal systems. The Protectionist orgains in Melbourne argue that the arrest of progress in Victoria is to be accounted for by the decadence of the mining industry, which they say is in no way traceable to the li,gh tariff, and by the comparative small- ness of her territory. But this theory is evidently wrong. The Victorian mines are not worked opt, and to contend that a fertile tract .18 extensive as Great Britain is fully populated with 850,000 people is simply absurd. The truth is that the cost of mining has been increased in an enormous ratio by the efforts of the Government to establish manu- factures by artificial means; and the sum remark applies to the agr cultural industry. The energies of the people have been diverted from the natural channels of industry into the purely adventitious openings formed by the erec- tion of a Customs barrier. Manufactures have been started, but at the expense of checking the development of the in- digenous resources of the land, and, since Victorian manu- facturers have no market for their wares outside of the protected area, the result is general stagnation. A fertile, innately wealthy, and sparely-peopled country that cannot keep her own children while neighbouring countries pos- sessing no greater natural advantages can absorb in- numerable people from abroad is certainly an anomaly, to be accounted for only on the assumption that there is some- thing rotten in the State. And here fact and theory support each other. The interest in the returns for the other colonies is not so great. As nearly as they can be at present ascertained, I they are as follow : Population Increase Increase In 1881. since 1871 per cent. Nov' Zealand 489,000 South Australia 277,500 Tasmania

No returns are vet to hand from Queensland. The enor- mous growth of New Zealand and the small increase in the population of Tasmania require some explanation. The first-named, as is well-known, has been following a "pro- gressive policy" with nnparalled energy and perseverance. She has borrowed immense sums, and spent the money in importing people and providing them with remunerative employment. So far, she seems to have retained the im- migrants, but lately there has been quite a large influx of navvies and other labourers into New South Wales from her shores. Tasmania has not advanced much during the decade, but this is because she has suffered several years of extreme depression. • She is now making a fresh start ahead, but the smallness and comparative sterility of her territory are inimical to a high rate of progress. Her mineral wealth is her main reliance, and this until within the last few years lay untouched, and indeed unknown. Victorian miners are now pouring across Bass Strait to ob- tain work in the gold and tin mines of the heart-shaped island; and in the ensuing decade Tasmania must make rapid strides. The outlook for all the colonies is bright ; but the single bright spot in the Victorian prospect consists in the fact that the results of the census have set her people thinking, and if they only continue to think for a while they are certain to eschew Protection and take a fresh de- parture in the way of progress.

After he has examined the country near the coast of the maioland of Africa with a view to the discovery of coal. Mr. Joseph Thomson expects to be sent by the Sultan of Zanzi- bar to Maltindarry, which is to be the centre of his future labours.

The Atheneum says the journals and letters of the late Caroline Fox, of Penjarrick, are about to be published. This gifted lady (a member of the well-known Cornish Quaker family) lived on terms of the utmost friendship with most of the notable men of science and letters of the day, and the forthcoming volumes will be found to be rich in recol- lections, conversations, opinions, and anecdotes of Mill, Sterling, Wordsworth, Coleridge, Carlyle, Bunsen, and others. A portrait of the author, etched by Mr. Hubert Herkomer, should add to the interest of the book, which is edited by Mr. Horace N. Pym.

With regard to the country at the south end of Lake Tanganyika, which Mr. James Stewart is hbout to open up by what is called the African Lakes junction road, Mr. E. C. Hore states that on a rich and verdant plateau the chief Zombe received him in a most friendly way at his large town of two thousand people, as also did the chief Kapufi on the beautiful Lofu River, with its many peaceful villages and gardens of unbounded luxuriance. Both of these chiefs expressed a wish to see Europeans settled among their people. These points will be occupied shortly by the London Missionary Society; and the Livingstonia missionaries hope to open a station among the Chungus (50 miles from the head of Lake Nyassa) at the town of Maliwanda, which Mr. Stewart visited in his first exploration of the country. Mambwe, between Bfaliwanda's and Zombe's, will then alone remain to be taken up in order to complete the line of settlements between the two lakes.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY.

ROYAL ASSENT.—The Royal assent was given by com- mission to thirty-one public and private bills (including the Irish Land Law Bill), the Royal Commissioners being the Lord Chancellor, Lord Mormon., and Lord Kenmare. THE NEWSPAPER LAW OF LIBEL—On the introduction of this bill, the Earl of REDESDALE objected to so important a measure coming up to their lordship's House when there were so few members present to consider it. He hoped it was not now intended to proceed with the measure.—The LORD CHANCELLOR said the bill had received the careful consideration and approval of the law officers of the Crown, and it was their intention to proceed with it.—Earl GRAN- VILLE added that not only had it received the consideration of the law officers of the present Government, but also of the late Government —The bill was then read a first time. THE WELSH SUNDAY CLOSING BILL.—The India Office Superannuation Bill and the Welsh Sunday Closing Bill were read a first time.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MoNnay. • THE FRENCH TREATY NEGOTIATIONS.—Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN, answering a question from Baron de Worms as to the Treaty of Commerce demurred to the assumption that the negotiations had failed. He preferred to say that they were suspended, and he hoped they would be renewed with the chance of a favourable conclusion. In answer to Mr. Ash- mead-Bartlett, he said that if the treaty fell through British trade would be conducted under the most-favoured- nation clause ; but Baron de Worms having asked whether, if the present treaty lapsed, the most-favoured-nation clause would not also lapse, Sir C. DILIIE said that was so, but the Government had three courses open to it—either to negotiate a most-favoured-nation treaty, a new tariff treaty, or no treaty at all.—The Report of Supply having been agreed to, the Appropriation Bill was brought in and read a first time. THE INDIAN BUDGET.-00 moving the House into Com- mittee on the East Indian accounts, Lord HARTINGTON wide his annual statement on the Indian finances. Dealing in the first place with the year 1879-80, for which the closed accounts have been received, he stated that these showed a revenue of £68.484,666, and an expenditure of £69,667,615, or a deficit of £1,182,949 as against a Budget estimate de- ficiency of £1,355,000. The revenue had increased by £3,922,000 over the Budget estimate, and the expenditure by £3,750,000, the chief improvement being in opium to the amount of £1,900,000, and productive works ; while there had been an increase in war charges and frontier railways of £2,532,000. Ile regular estimate for 1880-1 gives a revenue of £70,783,615, and an expenditure of £77,003,382, showing a deficit of £6,219,767. But the revenue includes two out of the five millions granted from the British exche- quer towards the cost of the Afghan war, the other three millions being credited to the revenue of 1881-82, and there is also an increase of no less than £1,218,000 on the opium revenue, £309,000 in excise, and £351,000 in customs. On the other hand, there is a deficiency in the land revenue of £295,000, and there is also a charge of £5,132,000 for war expenditure. Passing to the year 1881;2, he stated the Budget estimate of revenue at £70,981,000 and the expendi- ture at £70,126,000, showing a surplus of £855,000. As compared with the regular estimate for the previous year there is a diminution in the charges for war and frontier railways of £11295,000, and, allowing for This relief, the ordinary Budget is worse by £4,221,000. Of this an esti- mated falling off of the opium revenue accounts for £2,000,000, the provision for famine insurance, inserted as expenditure, accounts for £1,450,000, and £BOO,OOO occurs under other heads. Deficiencies are expected under the heads of customs, telegraphs, exchange, &c., but there will I be an improvement of £687,000 on the land revenue and £789,000 on provincial balances. The cost of the war, in. eluding the frontier railways. up to the end of 1880-1, ex- ceeded £20,000,000, or double the amount of Sir J. Strachey's estimate in February, 1880. The total charges of the war exceeded £23,000,000. But for the war, during the last four years there would have been surpluses of revenue exceed- ing £9,500,000. He regretted that the condition of the revenue necessitated the continuance of duties upon the coarser kind of English goods. Though unable to make ' any remissions of taxations, he regarded the state of Indian ' finance as prosperous and satisfactory.—Mr. STANHOPE ex- pressed his disappointment at nothing having been done to reduce the military and civil expenditure.—Mr. R. FOWLER moved the appointment of a Select Committee to enquire into the financial and general administration of affairs in India.' —The motion was seconded by Sir G. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TuEsnev.

NEWSPAPER LIBEL BILL.—Lord WAVENEY having moved the second reading of the Newspapers (Law of Libel) Bill, Lord REDESDALE complained that their lordships had had no time to consider this measure, which was a very impor- tant one. He had been unable to procure a copy of the bill until ten minutes before their lordships met that evening. He hoped the Government would not press the second read- ing.—Lord NORTHBROOK hoped their lordships would not hesitate to read the bill a seccnd time. The measure, while protecting the propiietor who published in his newspaper an accurate report, did not protect the person who spoke libellous matter.—The bill was then read a second time. THE WELSH SUNDAY CLOSING BILL—On the motion of Lord ABERDARE, the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sun- day (Wales) Bill was read a second time.

div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TuEsDAY.

-- - - THE AGRICULTURAL DEPRESSION.—Mr. GLADSTONE, answering a question from Mr. J. Howard, said he hoped the Richmond Commission would soon report, but apart from this upcertainty, he could not, at this time of the year, give any assurance that a Land Bill to meet the un- doubted depression of agriculture in England and Scotland would be a part of the programme of next session. THE PREMIER AND MR. ASHMEAD-BARTLETT.—On the second reading of the Appropriation Bill, Mr. ASHMEAD- BARTLETT proceeded at some length—and occasionally called to order by the Speaker—to canvass the foreign policy of the Government, on which he moved a vote of censure, as tending to the dishonour and disintegration of the Empire, and the isolation of England in Europe. Chiefly, be dwelt on the sacrifice of the German alliance bequeathed to the present Government by Lord Beaconsfield, ridiculed the exploit of the "concert at Dulcigno, and desiared that in the Greek affair our Government had played the part of a firebrand. He repeated also his condemnation of the aban- donment of Candahar, and the apathy of the Government to the advance of Russiain Central Asia, and criticised severely the history of the " Peace with Dishonour" in the Transvaal. Mr. GLADSTONE, speaking in a sarcastic vein, in the course of his reply, said: I shall dispose of Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett's charge by asserting everything he denies and denying everything he asserts. (Laughter.) I think the applica- tion of that succinct forrrrulary will nearly dispose of the whole of the oration we have heard. But it will leave him and me in a position of mortal combat. (Laughter.) It is paififul to me to be put in that position with relation to the hon. gentleman. The hon. gentleman has a great deal of human feeling. At various periods of his speech he referred to the deep pain—l don't know if he used the word anguish —(laughter)— to the deep and excruciating pain he knew he was indicting on me. (Renewed laughter.) He did this with a kind of feeling that approached commiseration, for which I can assure him I am truly thankful. As to the nature of that pain, however much I may suffer I will en- deavour to bear up against it as well as I can until the hon. gentleman on some other occasion gives me my quietus by another oration as pungent and convincing as that he has delivered to-night. (Laughter.) The hon. gentleman says that Cyprus gives us another command over the route to India.—Mr. A. BARTLETT : Over the land routes of the fature.—Mr. GLADSTONE : Oh! over the land routes of the future! (Laughter.) The hon. gentleman can see a great deal further into the future than any of those who sat around him or ought to have sat around him. What a pity it was he could not muster a single member of his party to the ernfie first tnd be illuminated by his discourse. (Laughter.) div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 27, 1881. SCHOOL FLOWER SHOW AT ST. f PRESCOT BOARD OF GTJARDIANS. HELENS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 27, 1881. SCHOOL FLOWER SHOW AT ST. f PRESCOT BOARD OF GTJARDIANS. HELENS.

ter)—into the minds of civilised countries, in order that the digestion of the various cultivated races might dispose of them in a better manner—(loud laughter)—than to offer any argumentative answer to speeches such as those he has delivered to-night. (Hear, hear.) The hon. gentleman is young, he takes great pains, he has plenty of time to gain instruction, and plenty of time to unlearn and' cast off errors. Let him apply that time to good purposes, and let him learn this, that if he wants really to make an impression upon the world, to give aid to his friends or inflict disaster upon his adversaries, the very first lesson he must learn is to restrain his universal and sweeping propositions within the bounds of fact and actual experience, and submit himself to be taught by lessons of the world and lessons of the day, and to learn and know that moderation, reserve, and consiclera•- tion for those with whom you have to deal, and the endeav- our to bring your proposition into exact conformity with the circumstances of the case, is for him, and for everybody else, the -very first condition to any substantial and durable success. (Loud cheers.)—The Bill was read a second time. HOUSE OF LORDS.—WEDtiESDAY.

_ THE FOOT AND MOUTH DISEASE.—The Earl of KtmnEn- LEY, in reply to questions, said foot and mouth disease did not prevail to any great extent in England, the number of cases being 49 in one county, 35 in another, and so forth. He further said that no pains would be spared by the Privy Council to prevent the spread of the disease. MrscEtteNEors.—The Regulation of the Forces Bill, the Newspaper (Law of Libel) Bill, and the Sale of Intoxica- ting Liquors on Sunday (Wales) Bill went through commit- tee. The Expiring Law Continuance Bill was read a third time and passed. The Irish Church Act Amendment Bill, for transferring all the powers and duties of the Irish Church Temporalities Commission to the Irish Land Corn- mission, was read a second time. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

- - THE Hatt or SCIENCE.—In reply to a question by Sir Henry Tyler, Mr. MIINDELLA said the science and art classes at the Hall of Science, London, were conducted by Dr. Aveling, assisted by Mrs. Besant and the Misses Brad- laugh. The Hall of Science was a peculiarly secular school under the superintendence of a highly respectable commit- tee, one of whom was a clergyman of the Chiarch of England. Dr. Bryce, the inspector, reported that "the instruction was good and the classes conducted with the utmost propriety." Mr. Mumlella said that, under these circumstances, he saw no reason why the Education Department should not re- cognise these classes.—Sir H. TYLER gave notice that early next session he would move that, in the opinion of this House, the Hall of Science is not a fit and proper place in which instruction should be given in science and art, and that Mrs. Besant and the Misses Bradlaugh are not fit and proper persons to be employed in the instruction of science and art under, any department of the Government. THE IMPRI4ONMENT OF CHILDREN AT DURHAM. —Re- plying to Mr. Macfarlane, Sir WILLIAM IlaucounT said he had no doubt that, in accordance with standing instruc- tions, the case of some children being sent to prison by the Durham magistrates for stealing apples would be reported to him without delay, and if the facts justified such a course, he would at once order their release. THE NEWLY-ELECTED MEMBERS.—Mr. Herbert Gladstone took his seat on his re-election for Leeds, and Mr. Buchanan took his seat for Edinburgh, both being received with toud cheers. THE WHITEBOY Acrs.—Mr. T. P. O'Comcort moved the second reading of the Whitebov Acts Repeal Bill, asking the House to be assured that the Acts were no longer necessary for the maintenance of order in Ireland.—The SOLICITOR GENERAL for IRELAND opposed the motion, and took ex- ception to Mr. O'Connor's contention. Mr. ARNOLD said that Ireland had a right to demand either separation from England or equal laws.—Mr. HOPWOOD advised that the motion should not be pressed to a division, but said he thought an effort should be made to weed eut such of the Irish statutes as ought undoubtedly to be abolished.—Mr. I O'Com•ron offered, if the bill was read a second time, not to press it further this session; but the SOLICITOR GENERAL for IRELAND had no authority to agree to this proposal.— On a division the bill was rejected, the numbers being:— For the second reading, 25; against, 44. -

THE ELEOTORAL BRIBERY AT WIGAN.—Mr. ARTHUR ELLIOTT asked whether the Government were prepared to make any suggestion to guide the House as to what course should he pursued in regard to the issue of a new writ for Wigan.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL said that there had been no case in which the House had not issued a commission where a report such as that of the Judges in this matter had been made. As far as he knew, the Government had not con- sidered what course should be taken. The responsibility of moving a new writ rested with the Opposition; but when the writ was moved for he should call the attention of the House to the evidence given before the Judges and do all he could to counteract the vote of Saturday last, which seemed to be founded on. no precedent and guided by no principle, and was likely to have a very evil effect. Mr. A. O'Donnor, who said the Irish electors of Wigan determined the election in that borough, moved for the issue of a new writ, and Mr. Finigan seconded the motion.-The ATTORNEY GENERAL therefore asked the House to postpone its judg- ment upon this motion.—Lord HAUTINGTON said it was im- possible that the House could give adequate consideration to the question now. The motion was eventually with- drawn. CATTLE DISEASE.—Mr. MUNDELLA reverted to the state- ment he made a few days ago as to the outbreak of foot and mouth disease in Lancashire. He said that a report from the Veterinary Department showed that state of things in this country at this moment was as follows :—ln the Ac- crington district there had been one outbreak, affecti th roe ' animals; in the lower Blackburn district 23 outbreaks, affect- ing 346 animals; in Clitheroe 11 outbreaks, °fleeting 44 animals; and in great Harwood one outbreak, affecting one lanimal. The total were 41 outbreaks and 394 affected animals—not the alarming condition of things which have been represented. COMPENSATION TO EDMUND GALLEY.—ID answer to Mr. Joseph Cowen, Sir W. HARCOURT said he hoped compensa- tion to the amount of £l,OOO would be paid to Edmund Galley. THE APPROPRIATION BILL.—The Supreme Court Of Judi- cature Bill was read a third time. The Appropriation Bill was also read a third time, after attempts had been made by several Irish members to get up a discussion on certain grievances; and the House adjourned until to-day (Satur- day) afternoon.

On Thursday, a flower show was held in the Assembly Room, Brook-street, in connection with the Congregational Sunday Schools. Flower shows have in recent years become very popular, and the votaries of the goddess Flora have greatly increased in number. Flower shows are an estab- lished institution now, and there is unquestionable evidence that the village or town flower show which comes once a year has had the effect of promoting a healthy Spirit of rivalry and competition amongst gardeners, and tended to a cultivation of love of flower rearing which Must necessary Prove beneficial. In the summer of 1870, after the West of England Conference at Exeter, in which the desirability of encouraging the love of flowers in the minds of Sunday school scholars had been incidentally referred to, one of the delegates promised to supply packets of seed, and did supply them to one or two persons, specially for the scholars of Sunday schools. These packets were given in April, two to every scholar who applied for them; seeds we.`e set and tended, and the efforts of the scholars were plalfily seen and appreciated in a few months afterwards in the collection of the various plants and flowers that they had been at the pains to rear. Sunday school flower shows have since been held in various parts of the country. The suggestion that a flower show should be held in connection with the Congre- gational Brook-street school emanated from Messrs. Jamesa Marsh and C. Sharpies, the superintendents of the school, who laid the matter before the teachers. The teachers gladly accepted the suggestion, and with their combined efforts, together with the efforts of the scholars, the flower show of Thursday was got together, and the collection of the various plants and flowers was really cmditable to the scholars. It. should be stated that many pots were exhibited but not for com- petition by several ladies and gentlemen connected with the church and school. Of course, St. Helens, from a combina- tion of causes which will be familiar to most of our readers, Is not celebrated like Aranjuez, in Spain, for its many beau- tiful gardens, but the love of flowers it can be said is not an unknown quality amongst its people. To further develop this love of flowers the teachers of the Sunday school in question have made and are making endeavours; and in all probability an exhibition will take place yearly. In April last 120 packets of seed were given to the scholars, but many of them failed, and the persons holding those packets were allowed to exhibit plants, provided they had been registered fully a month before the time of exhibition. One side of the table, which occupied almost the entire length of the room' bore the flowers that had been' raised by the seed, and the rest were plants that had been in the house or garden a month, and plants tic which bad been sent for exhibition, but not for competition. 14e following ladies and gentlemen kindly lent specimens :4Mrs. Roughsedge, Messrs. Moxon, Hams, Jordan, Etheridge, and Thomas Birchall. The fol- lowing ladies worked energetically to make the exhibition a success :—Miss M'Coll, Miss Marsh, Miss Sharpies, Miss Ada Sharpies, and Miss Thompson. The judges were Mr. Middleton, gardener fer Mr. Richard : Pilkington, of Rainford Hall; and Mr. Pike, gardener for Mr. H. S. Hall, of Denton's Green. There were about 200 plants In the room. In the afternoon the attendance was small, but in the evening there were a good many present and the company was enlivened by music rendered by several young ladies. The Rev. R. J. Ward distributed the prizes which consisted of books. A refreshment stall was stationed at one end of the room presided over by Mr. Bamford of the Market Cafe.
