THR APPOINTMENT OF ASSISTANT OVERSEER FOR WITISTON. A letter was read from the Local Government Board ask- _ ..

ing for the observ-a-tion-s—of the Guardians upon an enclosed copy of a petition rrom the ratepayers of Whiston against the appointment by the Guardians of Edmund Range, as assistant overseer.—Mr. TIMER: The question is whether we hhve to consult the ratepayers every time.—The RAN: I presmna that the appointments rest with this Board whatever tlw inhabitants may say about it.—Mr. TYREE : And if you once give way, you will have further difficulty. —The Rey. J. BARNACLE :Is there any special reason why there should be a change?—Mr. LEATHEEBAEROW: The question is whether or not their wishes have to be respected a little instead of being shelved.— The CLERK :The memorial from the ratepayers was laid be- fore the Board.—Mr. LEATRERBARROW : And taken as read, —not read.—Mr. RANSOM: I suppose there is no reflection upon the clerk. It was not read I suppose because it was not worth their while going through it.—Mr. LEATHER- BARROW: There is no reflection upon Mr. Hartley.—Mr. MEADOWS: If it has been the custom to see the ratepayers about such matter it had better be done.-The CLERK: There have beet similar difficulties in other unions.-Mr. LEATHER- BARROW said the objection of the ratepayers of Whiston was that applicants were not taken on their merits at all; but the selection of a man was a foregone conclusion, it being agreed on certain conditions to vote for so and so. There were gentlemen present who promised to give their votes before they came into the room.—Mr. BOBELL : It was a compro- mise, I suppose.—Mr.LEATHERBARROW : Yes, it was.—Mr. MEADOWS: I never did anything of the sort.—The Rev. T. CHAountas thought it was highly undesirable to have the discussion renewed. It appeared to him that the petition of the ratepayers did not receive the attention It ought to have had.—lt was desirable that no petitions should be received at all, it should be made known.—Mr. HALL moved that the guardians had no observation to make on the matter.—Mr. JACKSON seconded the motion, and said that'the opposition to the appointment arose from a joke, one old man having said, "if Leatherbarrow had been there they would not have had their own road," and it was through Mr. Leatherbarrow that all this fuss about nothing was caused.—Mr. LEATHER- BAREcm : It is no joke at all when you show papers round.—Mr. JACKSON said he did not show one. The reso- lution was carried.
..:0-17-ARDIANS ASKED TO APOLOGISE TO THE WORKHOUSE MASTER.

A letter was read from Mr. Bicknell (the master), referring to what passed at the last meeting, and which he said had caused some trouble. He was sorry that the imputation had been cast upon him that be would be "blowed" if be provided the Guardians with luncheon, though he admitted having felt angry.—Mr. CHAMBERS thought, and he was sure others would think with him, that the master had acted rightly in' bringing that statement before the Board. He hoped the three Guardians present would certainly make some obser- vation in regard to that statement. It was only due to the master that the chairman of the Revision Committee should apologise to the master, and the Rainford Guardian (Rev. J. Barnacle) should say a few words of apology with regard to his part of the discussion, and lastly, Mr. Fidler with respect to the remark as to the master being " blowed." It was no doubt a slip of the tongue. Having spoken of the excellent qualities of the master, he said one of the qualifications of a gentleman was to apologise if he had wounded the feelings of the lowliest man.—Mr. MEADOWS considered the master was to be commended for the way in which he had acted. He was told to engage another person, but he found hi had a pauner in the house who could assist them in preparing the luncheon without pay. There was no doubt that the master of a house like that could not do without pauper help. If he did they would have to have paid officers.— Mr. RANsobr, though he had a great opinion of the master, considered he was very much to blame in acting in the way he did at the last meeting, and not providing luncheon.— Mr. HALL considered the communication very unwise, and it was also vervrunwise for Mr. Chambers to ask them to apologise. If the master had told the committee that the woman was of great service to him she would not have been sent away, but as for apologising he should certainly never do anything of the kind. (Hear, hear.)— Mr. FIDLER expressed his regret that the matter had taken the course it had, as he thought a great deal of the master; but still his opinion of the transaction had not altered a bit. —Mr. Chambers was rising to speak, when Mr. FIDLER sub- mitted that he was out of order.—Mr. Caearnmas : I want to make an explanation.—VotcEs: "Chair."—Mr. BAR- RACLE expressed his surprise at the action of Mr. Chambers. He certainly should not apologise, because he had nothing to apologise for. He made a few jocular remarks about not having a substantial breakfast, and he was only stating facts.—Mr. CHAMBERS asked if Mr. Barnacle did not say that the Guardians were to the best of their ability honestly and fearlessly trying to discharge their duties, whilst the master was helping to spend the ratepayers money.—Mr. BARNACLE had not the slightest recollection of having said anything of the sort except the first expression as to doing their work fearlessly and honestly.—Mr. thumesas moved a rote of confidence in the master.—Mr. HALL moved an amendment, that no such motion be put.—Mr. TYEER moved that the master's explanation was satisfactory.—Mr. CHAMBERS seconded this and withdrew his motion.— Carried.

Before the election of relieving officers, the CIIA.IRMAI; said the business would be private, and asked the reporters to retire.—The reporter for a local newspaper kept his seat, and declined toga out as the matter was of great importance to the ratepayers, and said he could not under the circum- stances think of leaving the room.—Mr. FIDLER said he was very sorry that the reporter should take that stand.— Mr. Jackson became very; excited and left the room.—Mr. FIDLER asked the Chairman to rise to the occasion or dis- miss the meeting. The CLERK: You don't mean to say that you will give way to a reporter? He sug- gested that the Superintendent be sent for to re- move him in a proper manner. The Clerk afterwards said he did not suppose the reporter had instructions from em- ployers to treat the Board in that manner.—The REPORTER said his employers cou Id not know that the matter was of so much importance.—Mr. FIDLER said he could not understand the reporter taking that course as he was a very respectable man.—Mr. GILBODY : I will tell you what it is,—between the master and reporters we are coming to a nice pass. If masters are to be reporters and reporters masters I think it is time to retire. This will get into the Globe, and perhaps into the Balloon.—The REPORTER asked if there was any special reason in the case for the business being transacted in private any more than in any other case of the same kind.—Mr. TYRER said he would decline to answer that question.—After Mr. Ranson had had an interview with the reporter, Mr. Pants said be would move that the reporter be net permitted to enter the room again.—Subsequently the master and the asylum attendant entered the room, and stood facing the reporter. The Guardians shouted" away with him "(not crucify him)," away with him," and ultimately chucked out the reporter a la Bradlaugh. Mr. W. Bullock, of Prescott was appointed relieving officer for the Sutton district, and Mr. F. A. Harrison, of Halebank, for the Eccleston district.

THE MANCHESTER UNITY AND THE RAGISTRAR OF FRIENDLY SOCIETIES:A difficulty has arisen in conse- quence of the Registrar of Friendly Societies having refused to register some of the alterations of rules made at the last A.M.C. of the Manchester Unity, at Southport. The direc- tors deputed Past Grand Master Pownall arid Past Grand Master Holmes to wait upon the registrar. After a long conference, all the rules were registered in a modified form except one. This required any lodge with a deficiency in its management fund to make it good within six months from the 31st December of the year in which the deficiency arose, by an equal levy on all the members, to be paid before the following 31st December. The registrar refuses to allow any time for the payment of such deficiencies in the management fund, on the ground that to do so would be to condone an illegal act. The directors therefore urge lodges in this position—and they say there are many such—to take immediate steps to raise a management fund, and thus place themselves in a legal and proper position. EXTRAORDINARY JOURNEY OF A RUNAWAY TRAIN—On Sunday evening, about nine o'clock, whilst a train of eight carriages was being shunted at Holstead Station on the South-Eastern Railway, near Sevenoaks, it started down the incline on the road to London without the engine. It con- tinued its course, increasing its speed as it ran through Chelsfield, Orpington, Chiselhurst, and other stations. A telegram was sent to all stations, and at the junction above New Cross the signalman with great presence of mind put over the points and sent the train into the sidings to Brick- layers' Arms Goods Station, where it continued its rapid pace through the network of me4ls, and reached the loco- motive department, running into a dead road, knockinm down the wall, and entering the premises of Messrs. Oastle; and Palmer, tanners, doing considerable damage to a wooden building and a quantity of machinery therein. Two carriages were completely smashed and others more or less damaged. Five children belonging to the station master at Halstead had a marvellous escape. They were in a carriage in the i centre of the train, and travelled with t to London, receiv- ing a severe shaking, but in no other way being any the worse for the adventure. The father followed on the engine which should have been on the train, and it is needless to say that he was overjoyed upon finding his chil- dren unhurt.

ST. HELENS COUNTY COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. Thompson, judge. A HORSE Tnansecriow.—Andrew Makin corn miller, ol Blacknrook, St. Helens, sought to recover £4O 13s. 3d. from a farmer named Fletcher.—Mr. Massey appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Swift represented the defendant.—From the evidence of the plaintiff it appeared that one of his men informed him that Fletcher had a mare that would suit him very well, and in consequence of that he went next day to see Fletcher at the stables. He asked Fletcher if he would allow him to see the mare out, to which Fletcher replied that if he bad come half an hour sooner his son would have run the mare out, but he was an old man and could not do it so well. Fletcher said the horse had been standing up a long time, and was very fresh. Makin then asked him why the mare had been standing so long, to which Fletcher re- plied that the mare was too light for a heavy cart, and he did not want to ruin her. He further said that if plaintiff wanted it for a spring cart it would suit very well. Wishing to see the mare in action he asked Fletcher to move her about, and Fletcher this time said he was frightened as the mare jumped upon him. In answer to other questions Fletcher said the mare was a good worker, perfectly sound, and was well-known amongst the Staffordshire hounds, as she had hunted several seasons. Whilst there Makin observed the feet of the mare to be covered with rags, aud in explanation of this Fletcher said he had damped the mare's feet a little to keep them cool as she had not been working for a con- siderable time. Makin did not doubt the honesty of Fletcher at the time as he had been in the habit of doing business with him. The same evening Fletcher a pulled up ".aaar Makin's house, and some conversation ensued between the two, and plaintiff's servant (George Anders) relative to the merits of the mare. Fletcher informed Anders that the mare was a first rate one and perfectly sound, and was well suited for plaintiff's spring cart. A. bargain was then struck between Makin and Fletcher, the latter arranging to take £23 in corn. &c., and Makin's horse, which was valued at £l5. Fletcher proposed that Makin should send every sack of corn the same night, and after some discussion on this point Makin consented to send as many as he could get ready, and he did send a larre quantity. About ten o'clock the same night Makin met Anders and Parr, his two men, coming from Fletchers with Fletcher's mare in the cart. He examined the mare, and found it to be quite lame. He went with it the same night to a surgery but was unable to see a veterinaryourgeon. On the following morning he spoke to Fletcher about it, and desired him to take it back ; but Fletcher laughed and said "You will have to make the best of it." Fletcher further remarked that he had been " done " many a time himself.—John Shaw Menzies said he found the mare suffering from inflammation orthe feet. She could not work, and was only fit for the slaughterers.—By the Judge : If the mare had not thus been disabled she would have been worth £3s.—The defence was that there:had been no false representation or any breach of warranty, or any liability whatever. It was simply a "swop " between two tradesmen. Plaintiff had never asked defendant for a war- ranty, and if be had .one would net have been given. It was contended there was no unsoundness at the time of the exchange.—W. H. Roughsedge veterinary surgeon, said on the 14th December last, before the transaction was made, the mare was under his care for lameness. There was' a bargain with him that if the mare was not cured he should receive no money. He returned the horse cured; and received the money..-. Wm. Garton Dixon said he had frequently seen the mare, and the mare was perfectly sound.—Hir Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff for £33, a counter claim by defendant of £4 6s. Pd., amount of provender not having been delivered being allowed. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. T. P. E. Thompson. IMPORTANT CASE AFFECTING BANKRUPTS A.ND CREDI- TORS.—WiIIiam Birchall, auctioneer, sought to recover £3O 4s. Bd. from James Goss butcher, St. Helens.—Mr. Thomas appeared for the defendant and said they did not admit the debt.—His Honour: But there is a judgment against him.— Mr. Thomas: But we have filed a petition.—Mr. Massey: I appear for the plaintiff. The application is for an order to pay so much per month under the old judgment. The plaintiff in November, 1880, obtained a judgment in the Liverpool district for (altogether with costs) £3O 4s. 80 and immediately before obtaining that judgment, the defendant, Goss, who is a butcher in St. Helens, filed his petition for liquidation or composition. The creditors ultimately resol- ved to accept a composition of 2s. 6d. in the pound—is. down and Is. Gd. in six months after registration. The plaintiff opposed these resolutions, not being satisfied with the bona fides of the creditors in the action.—His Honour: But he did not succeed.—Mr. Massey: No, he did not. The first instalment was paid at the proper time and the second instalment was due in June, 1881. For that second instal- ment the defendant Goss, with two sureties, gave a promis- sory note, dated June, 1881, and the date of payment was distinctly to be 21st June, 1831:—" We jointlyand severally promise to pay to William Birchall £2 Gs. Oct ,value received, signed James Goss," and two sureties. On the 21st June, the time the note was payable, it was not paid, and therefore We say that our debt is revived; and we are now entitled to ' ask that the whole should be paid, under one of the rules.— His Honour: That seems so, unless—Mr. Massey: Oh, it cannot'be denied for one moment that this money has not been paid, and I cannot understand the defence here to-day. —Mr. Thomas: It is quite true that the defendant filed his petition. The plaintiff was presentat the creditors' meeting, and there was no opposition whatever. The promissory note was given to all the creditors for the second instalment, and amongst others, to plaintiff for his portion, £2 Ca. 00. This is a promissory note payable to order, and I maintain it should be presented for payment. Ills a negotiable instru- ment and we expected it should have been paid. We paid all who brought their notes at the appointed time, and they were all paid with the exception of plaintiff in this action. Being the only one left, Goss went to the solicitor's office and offered to pay. Plaintiff's solicitor would not accept the money as it was overdue. But I say that we have three clear days grace allowed. The note was presented for pay- ment, and we are still willing to pay it. This is an attempt on the part of the plaintiff to claim advantage over the other creditors.—Mr. Massey admitted that they had three days' grace allowed, but Goss did not come until the Saturday; he ought to have come on the Friday night.—His Honour: , The question seems to be, whether, having given the pro- • missory note you are bound to give it up, or that they are bound to present it. It may 'be that the resolution was te acer:t these piece l Qt paper, Mr. Massey: No, air; if your hononf will look at the bottom of this note, you will see that it is not made payable to any particular place, Therefore there is no place at which to present.—His Honour asked Mr. Massey to refer him to an authority, and this having been done His Honour said Goss had to find out his creditor.—MP. Massey: That is my case. The note was due on the 24th.—His Honour: And it was not paid on the 24th 7—Mr. Thomas: There has been no intention to de- fraud.—His Honour: But he has lost the benefit of his compositiori as respects his debt.—Mr. Thomas: The money was paid to all the others.—His Honour: It was the busi- ness of the debtor to find him out.—Mr. Thomas: I say the note is payable to order; it is a negotiable instrument.— His Honour: Can you find me an authority that it is pay- able to order ?—Mr. Thomas: There is nothing to prevent him from passing that hill away to somebody else. We had no means of ascertaining where this bill was, and we are willing to pay the £2 6s.—His Honour: I think it was the business of the makers of the note to take steps for paying it, and they did not do that, and therefore the debt is revived. I give judgment :for the amount.—Mr. Massey asked for £1 a month. The defendant was a butcher carry- ing on business in St. Helens. and was in a large way of business—Mr. Thomas said his client was only doing a small business, and was heavily in debt. His client put himself to great inconvenience to raise the composition by borrowing the money. He was insolvent at the present time, and could dot possibly pay £1 a month. He knew of a similar case in which one penny a month was paid.—His Honour ordered ss. a week to be paid without costs. CLAIM FOR RENT FOR LAND TINDER A. LEASE.—John Harwood, John taorton, and Francis Dutton, as mortgagees lof ona Nancy Roscoe, and Miss Roscoe, as mortgagor, for Iwhom Mr. Reid, of Bolton, appeared, claimed from a defen- dant, for whom Mr. Riley appeared, the sum of £l3 4s. 101 for rent of some land in Boundars-road.—Mr. Reid said the defendant had the land under a lease.—Mr. Riley said there Was a preliminary question whether there was not a question of title involved in the case to disentitle His Honour to proceed with it. After the counter part was executed before the ortginal lease was tendered, which, in fact, had never been tendered, it was discovered that there was a charge of some hundreds of pounds payable tO the Cor- poration of St. Helens in respect to streets which immedi- ately joined upon the land, and las contention was that it was an encumbrance, having regard to the Improvement Act, to disentitle the people to grant such lease. The question was, whether they had a title to make the lease under the circumstances.—His Honour thought the case in respect to the matter mentioned by Mr. Riley; was good against the defendant, who could in his own turn have a remedy against the people whe granted the lease; and he gave judgment for the amount with costs. TAMPERING WITH FIOURES.—HeRry Houghton, provision dealer, of Sutton' for whom Mr. Riley appeared, sought to recover £8 2s. for goods supplied to James Bothwell collier, who was formerly in business on a small scale at Collins Green.—Mr. Swift appeared for the defendant.— Plaintiff said the last payment was made ica March, 1880, since which time he had sold the defendant goods, the last being obtained in April, MO.—Defendant admitted part at the debt, and produced bills which were minutely examined by His Honour, who pointed out several instances of figures having, been tampered, apparently with the intent to defraud.—Mr. Swift said he was afraid under the circum- stances that he could not proceed with the case. After the auspicious appearance of the papers it would be useless for him to do so. After a pause, Mr. Swift said he hoped be was - not doing wrong in abandoning the action.—His Honour: I think you are doing very rightly in not support- ing your client in something that is clearly a fraud committed by somebody.—An order of 103. a month was made. Eiouos Lints TO LLST LIFE Tl.—John Morris, wine and spirit merchant, Liverpool-road, St. Helens, sras sued by a Mr. Hall, a traveller, for the price of 5,000 labels marked "gin," " whiskey," 4c., at 7s. 6.1. per thousand.— Plaintiff said he called at defendant's house some time ogo, and after some conversation defendant gave him an order for 5,000 labels, to be printed according to the judgment 'of ihe traveller, which was the usual custom. The greater part of the labels were marked a whiskey," because there were more whiskey bottles in demand than any °then—Defendant said the order was given for 500 labels, because 5,000 would last longer than his life would last, and would be enough for all the publicans in Liverpool-road for ten years—Plaintiff said he scarcely ever took an order for less than 5,000; and he called James Lawrenson, who said he overheard plaintiff

and defendant talking about the order. Defendant objected to 5,000, then plaintiff said be would eend3,ooo, but defendant said he would not have them. He really did not know what , the order was.—His Honour: Then you might have stayed at home. (Laughter.)--Defendant called a witness, who said he was in defendant's vaults, and he beard the parties arguing for an hour and a half. He beard defendant say, "You may send me 500, but if you send any morel will not have them. '--His Honour: I think you have been too pressing, Mr. Hall, and I shall nonsuit you. You may make what arrangement you can. • AN AGFIEENENT NOT TO BID IN OPPOSITION AT A PRO- PERTY SALE—In this case Robert Broome was the plaintiff, and Wm. Berry, an old man, the defendant. Both are farmers in the neighbourhood of Farnworth.—Mr. Swift said the action was brought to recover a sum of money agreed to be given by the defendant to the plaintiff in consideration of his not bidding against the defendant at a certain sale of property byauttion.—His Honour: Surely that is illegal. —Mr. Swift said that at first sight persons not cograisant might think the legality of that was questionable, and thinking that His Monour would mention that, he had en- deavoured to be ready to satisfy His Honour that it was not illegal. Mr. Swift then read from Lord St. Leonard's book, "One person may legally bind himself not to bid against another ;" and Mr. Dart in the fifth edition of his book in 1876, on precisely the seine sub- jade page 108, referred to the same case. Mr. Dart's propo- sition in the fourth Jurists new series, page 1,290, said : "It appears that an agreement between two persons not to bid against each other at an auction is legal, and forms a valuable consideration for an agreement, giving to the party withdrawing his opposition at the auction pretension over other property." Mr. Swift want on to say that on the 28th September in last year there was a sale by auction of lease- hold property at the Black Horse Inn, Fa: nworth. Plaintiff and defendant were there. Defendant asked plaintiff what he thought of the property, to which plaintiff said " What do you think of £900." Defendant then said "Do you think so much," and the conversation ceased for a time. Subsequently, when the bidding was going very slowly, Broome said "I will give you £lO or I will take £lO not to bid." Berry said "I will give you £10." The bidding, however, was proceeded with, and again Broome said "1 will give you £20," to which Berry said "1 will give you £20," which Broome accepted and drew up an agreement (produced) in these terms :—" I hereby agree to dive to Mr. Robert Broome £2O in consideration of not bidding against me, and I give 20s. on account now." That was signed by Berry, who bought the property.—Defendant said the agree- ment was for £lO, and although he signed the agreement for £2O lie did not know at the time. He had no business to do it as he could not see very well.—lt was said on behalf of the plaintiff that the defendant knew very well that the agreement was for £2O as he promised several weeks after to pay it, and suggested that plaintiff should take £9, which was refused by plaintiff.—His Honour made an order for the amount to be paid forthwith, His Honour remarking that he could not resist the cases cited by Mr. Swift as to the legality of the transaction.

div.head: ANNUAL LICENSING SESSIONS AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: ANNUAL LICENSING SESSIONS AT ST. HELENS.

The annual Licensing Sessions for this division was held on Tuesday, at the police court, before Mr. W. W. Pilking- ton (chairman), Mr. W. L. Evans, and Colonel Gamble. The police-superinteadent's report showed that during the year 648 persons had been summoned for drunkenness, as compared with 574 of last year; 687 were apprehended for drunkenness as against 545 last year; total 1,335, as com- pared with 1,119 last year. The number of publicans pro- ceeded against were 9, as against 4 last year; number of publicans convicted 8, last year 3; beersellers proceeded against 6, as against 7 last year, 5 convicted, being the same in number as last year. At present there are 173 public- houses, being two more than at the same period last year; there are 171 beerhouses ; last year there were 175, and the number of grocers dealing in wines and spirits is 8, as against 8 last year. A' BEERSELLER FINED'ON TIIE LICENSING DIY. Mr. Swift said that on the list of transfers there was the name of Edward Cusack, who applied for the license of the lady whom he had married to be transferred to him. He (Mr. Swift) was against him, an he was not surprised at Cusack not appearing. Perhaps their warships would allow the question of that license to stand over. Cusack married the woman who kept the beerhouse in Brook-street; he had never been approved of, or consented to by the owners of the property; he got temporary authority because his character aprareti to be good, but now he was brought into the police °thee for being drunk, and fined that very morning, lie had never had the license transferred to him, and the owner of 1 the property never thought he ati; the right man fcr tha, place.—To stand over to the adjourned'sessZA

div.head: VIE BED CAT TO DO FUETKEE PENANCE.
div.p: VIE BED CAT TO DO FUETKEE PENANCE.

Mr. Swift appeared to support the application of John Dean. He might congratulate their worships upon the light- ness of the list of the new applications. There were three altogether, and there was not one of them that was really a new application for a full license. With regard to Dean's application it was not a new application, as some of their worships would remember. In 1873 a man named Roughley went to live at the Red Cat with a good character, but during the progress of the house-warming he committed what appeared to the magistrates to amount to a serious offense, and was fined £5 for permitting drunkenness ins October, 1873. He kept the house without any further complaint until the licensing meeting of the following year, and then when he came up to have his license renewed the magistrates refused it. He had to leave the house, and at that time they made application in the names of other per- sons who had gone into the house, and were willing to keep it, but the magistrates did not think that the time had arrived for renewing the license of the Red Cat. It had been without a publican's license since 1874, consequently it had had seven seven years' penal servitude—(laughter)— and the only use made of the house had been to sell beer to be consumed off the premises. It would not be for him to say, even if he felt disposed, that the punishment was too severe, but he submitted that the man was fined, deprived of the license—lost it so far as he was concerned, left the premises, and now that the house had been without its license ler a full period of seven years, he asked their wor- ships whether the time had not arrived to properly re- new the license to that old-established country public-house. The license was turned off for the offence of one man who was not the owner, nor the brewer, but was a tenant tempo- rarily, and his offence should not be further visited upon the owners or the property. It had already been a great loss to them, and now after this seven years interregnum he respectfully asked that the license be granted. John Pye, of Windle, is the owner, and Mersrs. Greenall had it on a lease.

AN OLD HOSTARY Ti) BE PULLED D 371.1. Peter Slade applied for a provisional order for the removal of a full license from the Eccleston Arms, Prescot-road, to premises about to be built at the east side of the Eccleston Arms.—Mr. Swift .supported the application of Peter Slade, who was at present,and had been for the last six years, tenant of the Eccleston Arms, but which was better known by its more popular name of "The Nogs." Their worships might know that it was the old house which stood :between Crop- pers Hill and Bird i'th Hand, on the right hand side going towards Prescot. It had been there longer than living memory extended, the date upon it being 1740, and it had been built for that purpose and used for that purpose ever since. As their worships knew the tramways were getting laid, Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., the owners Of that old house, were prepared to pull it down, and in its place erect a new, and in all respects an improved house close by the site of the o'd one. There was intended to be a new road out from Pi escot-road down towards Knowsley-road, and the new howl.. would stand at the corner. The house proposed to be boot eouhl cost, independently of the value of the land, £2,500. They would see from the plans which he submitted that all the sanitary requirements insisted upon by their worships had been duly attended to; and the rooms were large enough to be commodious and numerous enough to satisfy the wants of the neighbourhood, and altogether in the place of the old house there would be the substitution of a new and improved one. The plans and building lines had been approved by the Corporation; and the pulling down of the old building and the erection of the new would allow the public road to be widened.

AN OUT-DOOR LICENSE. Edmund Yates, applied for a license, for sale of beer to be consumed off the premises in Ormskirk-road, Rainforcl. Mr. Swift appeared for the applicant, and said their worships would remember it was one of the cases in which the appli- cant NM given a title by law to have a license. &imposing his character was good and the premises of the requisite annual value. Both of these conditions existed hi this case.

they are insensible to that which by any other member would be keenly felt as the deepest disgrace. No sooner have they been thrust back into their proper corner of political obscurity than they have darted out again and resumed their antics. Since Mr. Gladstone has got the Land Bill out of his hands, he has taken rather more notice of the gad- flies of the House than he could before, and has given them cause to know that he possesses unimagined powers of caustic humour and cutting satire. Wisely, Mr. Gladstone has treated the Churchills and Bartletts not with serious answer, but with good-humoured, pitying contempt. His new style of light and glancing ridicule reminds us somewhat of the " chaff "of Lord Palmerston in his best days. It is I rather less dry and loftily-disdainful than that Lord Harlington developed last session in dealing with the same parties. It is much less elaborately cynical than Sir Wm. Harcourt's style. Lord R. Churchill had a good taste of the Premier's humour not many days since, when he compared him to the insect that can tickle and buz around one, but has not even a small power of stinging. Mr. Healy's turn has come since. But the most exquisite bit of satirical oratory the session has yielded was the short speech in wnich Mr. Gladstone polished off Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett on Tuesday night. No newspaper reader who relishes a series of witty sallies should miss that. Those who heard it say that in the mode of its delivery it was even more irresistibly laughable than in the language used. Ashmead-Bartlett was (to use an Americanism) fairly squelched. The brother-in-law of the Baroness Burdett-Coutts had taken upon himself, with im- mense arrogance, the position of the leader of the Opposition to review the acts of Government during the session on the motion for the second reading of the Appropriation Bill. His speech was long, wander- ing, and absurdly wild in assertion and extravagant in expression. It was, indeed, a miserable hash. Mr. Gladstone could not pretend to reply personally to so grotesque an indictment; but he turned the steam of his wit, like the jet of water from the pipe of a fire- hose, full upon the conceited young man, and after playing upon him for a few moments, he was left limp, drenched, and unhappy, with every atom of the starch taken out of him, whilst the) House was con- vulsed at the sight of his taking down. It is pleasant to have a Prime Minister who knows how most effectually to give even an Ashmead-Bartlett his quietus.

Ir is almost impossible to exaggerate the serious- ness of the present agricultural outlook. Our hopes of a bountiful harvest, which had been raised by the reports of the state of the crops that had reached us, have been dashed to the ground by the cruel per- sistency of the cirenching rains of the last few days. Instead of enjoying bright skies and hot sunshine, and grand blue skies and August splendour, we are the victims of a pitiless downpour, of a murky firma- ment, rough winds, swollen rivers, and drenched lands. The cut corn stands sodden and wet, and the farmer has been looking out day after day during the past week seeing no glimpse of ripening sunshine to brighten his prospects. A short while ago we were assured that the wheat crop of this year would be ten per cent below the average yield. The almost con- tinual rains we have had since must have made a serious addition to the unfavourableness of that calcu- lation. What corn there is has had no chance of ripening, and unless the next few days bring us sea- sonable weather we shall have to add another bad harvest to the already long list, and class 188 r with the years of disaster which have broken the fortunes and *ell nigh broken the hearts of so many English farmers. This is indeed a very serious prospect. It is only too quickly brought home to us what:a bad harvest means. The middle and the working classes in town and country are so intimately dependent one upon the other in this country that anything which affects the prosperity of one affects the prosperity of both. If the continuous run of bad seasons cuhriL- nates in a poor harvest this year we shall all feel the pinch of it in the coming wint3r. Already the price of flour has gone up, and there is every reason to believe that this unwelcome advance is not all that we\ shall have to pay for the gloomy weather and sunless weeks of August. Reports from the great corn-growing tracts of America state that. the yield out there is below the average, and, considering how largely de- pendent we are upon the States for our food supply, this aggravates the unpromising character of the situation, and fills the hearts of the poorer bread- winners with consternation and dismay. The im- portation of grain from America has saved us during the last few years from famine, and yet there are people who advocate a policy that would rob the poor people of this enormous boon merely that the English farmer might get more for his wheat. But we would impress upon our readers that the remedy for the ills of agriculture does not lie in that direction. There is a remedy, and it will have to be tried. Bad weather, of course, we cannot control, and the laws of natr-43 we cannot :influence, but the Land Laws can be altered so as to relieve the poor tenant of some of the burdens which handicap him so heavily. The agrarian problem in England is surely becoming as acute as it has been in Ireland, and these suc- cessive bad harvests are bringing into vivid relief the hard and intolerable conditions under which our English farmers have to carry on operations. The next great measure of a Liberal Government must be to simplify the Parliamentary system so as to make it equal the demands of the present day; but as soon as that is done, the relations of landlord and, tenant will have;to undergo :a'' searching inves- tigation and substantial reform. Unless the Eng. lish farmer is to sell out and emigrate to a country where he can farm under fair and reasonable con- ditions, something must be quickly done to ameliorate his condition here. He is borne down by losses of bad seasons simply because he has started at a terrible disadvantage. Good seasons are certain to come again, but they will be of little use to him unless he can be put on a better footing from that which he occcupies now. If a wet season concentrates attention on this subject, and brings home to us the urgent necessity of a re- form, it will not be the unmixed evil which, in our shortsightedness, we Are prone to think it. We fear this year's harvest is doomed. As we write the rain still patters unceasingly on roof and pave- ment, and unless the new comet begins to shed its benignant influence at once the sprouting ears too look forward to a winter of high prices' corn will be past recovery, and we shall have wisdom and in such gsnrnands that acwitey coa nf threealAmise tit-hceompeelLrtlaeswiss sea League and the stupendous folly of those crack- brained 'politicians who want to cure all ills by tax- ing the poor man's food.

(3- FERRY BOAT ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. INQUEST YESTERDAY. Iternoon, an inquest was held at the Mersey proad, by Mr,-,C. E. Driffield, county coroner, of Mr. Geo 7-• :-Treacy, a clerk employed at the „ilphur and Jopper Works, Widnes, who was on Wedne ay afternoon, whilst crossing the river is the r zorn ferry boat, which was struck by a thit ''.:ceased was knocked out of the boat. Mr. was Ach respected, and belonged to a family hold- od ltloi in NVidnes. Great interest was taken in I:eee.lngs, as it was supposed the question of liability -,ensation would be settled at the enquiry. Mr. solicitor, appeared on behalf of the relatives of ; Mr. Ferrand, from the solicitors' department, -;_lreet, Liverpool, represented the London and North- astern Railway Company; and Mr. Christopher, the Avner of the flat which struck the ferry boat, was also present. Mr. T. Birchwood Imison acted as foreman of the jury. Mr. Wm. Treacy, of 143, Mersey-road, said he was a book-keeper at Messrs. Hutchinson and Company's chemical works. Deceased was his son, and 24 years of age. He had for nearly 12 wears been employed at the Tharsis Sulphur and Copper Works, Widnes, as a clerk, and he lived at 119, Church-street, Runcorn, with his wife and two children. He was drowned on Wednesday afternoon in the river Mersey, whilst crossing in the ferry boat to Widnes. Deceased was found the next morning on the Lancashire side of the Mersey, about five o'clock, about half a mile from the Widnes Hospital, and taken to his (witness's) house.

Thomas Hulse, of Terrace-road, opposite the promenade, said he was a waterman. On Thursday morning, about ten minutes to five, he was on what is known as the bank, about half a mile from the Hospital, and looking for deceased's body, in company with some other men. One of these, named Robert Sutton, saw something which he thought was deceased, and on going to the place they found it was Treacey, whom the night's tide had driven up the river. De- ceased was on his face and without a hat. He got a" hatch" for the purpose of putting him upon it, but as the place was a very "rotten" one, he experienced considerable diffi- culty in drawing the body out of the mud. They put the body en the " hatch " and took it to the house of his father, on the Widnes side. Deceased was there examined, and a silver watch and other articles were found upon him. There was a mark on deceased's face, as if he had received a blow. Deceased's watch was stopped at 1-18 p.m. Henry Cox, Loch-street, said he was captain of the ferry boat plying between Widnes and Runcorn, and which be- longed to the L. and N. W. Railway Company. He had had charge of it since Christmas, when his partner fell ill. Previous to that time he was mate. He had always been accustomed to the river. On Wednesday afternoon, about five minutes past one o'clock, he left the Runcorn side, with six passengers, being assisted by a man named Thomas Lea. At this time a flat was coming from the Runcorn side of the river, and she and the ferry boat were both on one tack. The flat came out of what was known as the Wood-end deep, and , was trying to get through the bridge to the West Bank dock.] The ferry boat had pas-sed the first pillar, and was near the second from the Runcora side, when he observed the flat coming after them. The passengers then wanted him to keep his vessel before the wind, but as the flat was going quicker than they were, he (witness) could not bear his boat before the wind, "as he was afraid of giving him the meet- ing." The flat kept coming closer to them, and he shouted out to the captain to heave her round astern. However, instead of doing so, the flat ran right into them, at about two yards from the boat's stern, and knocked them round. At this time he did not observe that Treacy had fallen over- board, and, in fact, he did not know until he was told. Im- mediately afterwards he heard some one on the ferry boat shout out that there was a man overboard. Finding "it was a near thing," he called to the people on the flat to heave her round and go under the ferry boat's stern but ' they did not do so. If the captain of the flat had slackened his helm a little bit' he would have run clear of the ferry boat, but he made no attempt, but " came right at them." He could not tell how the deceased got overboard. .lle shouted out to the people in the boat to be sure to remain sitting down. As soon as the flat had gone clear of them, they having got round its stern, they braced the sail up and tried to pull as hard as they could towards the drowning man; but it blew so hard that they could not reach him. They saw deceased fighting with his hands, as if he could not swim, and immediately afterwards he went down close to the centre pillar on the Lancashire side of the river. They could not throw deceased a rope, owing to his being on the wrong side of the ferry boat when he fell into the water. This was owing to deceased falling into the water on the Runeorn side, and the ferry boat ;coming round on the Widnes side. The reason why the flat ought to have given way to them was owing to the ferry boat not having any chance of doing so. The reason why the ferry boat could not go behind the flat was that it was too near. Cross-examined by Mr. Husband : It was blowing very hard at the time, and Ithe flat had sail up, too, and was going head to the wind. The flat was going faster than the ferry boat, as it had its sail up and going with the tide. He was quite willing to admit that some of the passengers wanted him to go round the stern of the boat, but he was frightened of giving the flat a meeting, as that would have caused a far worse accident. Hardley (fish- monger, Regent-street, Runcorn,) was in the ferry boat, I and said to him, "Go round her stern," to which he replied "It is too late; if you turn her, our boat will run right before your bow." Hardley said two or three times that they had better go under the stern of the flat ; but be did not hear him say that the flat captain could not do what he liked with his vessel on a day like that. It was, however. just as true that he (witness) could not do what be liked with his boat in such weather. He did na, to the best of his recollection, say to Hardley "To with him ; -we are not going up the river for him." The flat was about 100 yards off when they saw it coming in the same direc- tion as the ferry boat. He (witness) had that distance to decide whether he would go forward or get astern. Both the vessels had their helms ported. A young man named Thos. Williams had charge of the helm. Williams was not paid wages by the railway company; be was lately a coachman with Dr. Robinson. He did not ask Williams to take charge of the helm, but he did so of his own accord. He told him how to steer. He was afraid of going up the river fur fear of running into the flat. The Coroner (to witneee) : You had better have run into the flat than the flat into you. Witness: No; because it woubi have sunk us to have "given the flat the meeting." Cross-examined by Mr. Husband: Have not you lost the use of your sight e, little? Well, a little.—Do the railway company know that? They know my eyes are a little blood- shot.—How long have you been employed by them ? I have been 30 years at the ferry, and I never had an accident be- fore.—What age are you? lam just turned 60, sir.—How long have you been affected in your sight? A good many years.-1 suppose you have never heard of any complaints having been lodged about the way in which this boat has been managed? No, sir.—Did you ever command a flat? I have been with one, but I was never captain of one.— Would it hems difficult matter to steer this flat, which was light, about the river with the wind coming up so strongly? Well, they cannot manage a light flat as they can a loaded one; but if he had just "slacked his tiller down" a little bit, she would have gone clear of our stern.—And if you had "slacked your tiller down" a bit, would not you have gone clear ef the flat? No, sir; our boat would have gone right against it. Our vessel would not turn round like the flat.— You had 100 yards to do it in? Yes, but we could not do it in that distance; it was blowing too hard.—ls this boat of yours licensed as a passenger boat? I don't know.—ls it a boat used only for carrying luggage? Luggage and passengers; but I believe it was built on pur- pose for luggage —Now, after this accident had happened, how long would it be before you were told there was a man overboard? Before we got round her stern he was at one side of the boat and we at the other. We brailed our sail up and got the oars out, but we could not do anything. —Before you got your oars out the captain of the flat had got into his little boat and was after the man? Yes; he could pull that boatquicker than we couldonrs.—The ferry boat did not go after him then? We tried to get after him, but three of us had not strength enough to pull the boat to him—When you got on shore what sort of language was used to the parties who had been in the fiat? I asked the steerer why he had not "heaved her round," and he said he could not do so, because be wanted to clear the pillar. In answer to the Inspector of Police, the witness said they had not any ropes, or anything on board the boat for the purpose of saving life, in case anyone fell overboard. They had never carried ropes for such a puipose since he was con- nected with the ferry. The only ropes they ever carried were those used to fasten up cattle. They had "a grapple" with them on this day, which they should have thrown to the deceased if they had had a chance, but he wan on the other side of the flat. In fact, if they had keen on the same side as that upon which deceased fell out, they would have saved him.

By a Juryman: The flat ran against one of the pillars of the bridge in order to get clear of the ferry boat. At the close of his evidence, the Coroner asked the wit- ness if he could sign his name to the depo,ition. Witness No, I cannot; nor write "nother." The Coroner: I thought that all captains had to do that. I am afraid that when the London and North-Western Rail- way Company pat you in the position you occupy they meant the ferry for luggage and not for passengers. Witness: Yes, sir.
In answer to another question as to what the corrpiny had done with the passenger boat which used to run, itu, ss said it was at the ferry but yet.

A Railway Official, -who Was present, apparently waiting the arrival of Mr. Ferrand, who had been detained, said that when the witness stated that the ferry boat was a' lug- gage boat merely, he did not know what he was talking about. In fact, witness had only occupied the post of cap- tain a very short time in place of the old captain, Harrison, who was at present sick. Mr. Whitley (juryman) said be had crossed the ferry for 17 years, night and morning, and he knew that there was one boat in the possession of the company which it was understood was used for luggage, and that only. Whether the boat out of which the deceased was thrown was the one , or not, he could not say. I Thu Coroner: Really, I think that we may take it that 1 this boat was for luggage 'and passengers alai". ' Joseph Foden, captain of the flat Adelaide, referred to in the above evidence, said it was used for the conveyance of soda and ash, and beleoged to the Liverpool and St. Helens Lighterage Co. At the time of the accident the vessel was going to the West Bank dock. Alter the witness had given

I evidence as to the position of th'h two vessels at the time of I the accident, he said that when he observed that Cox was determined to go ahead of the flat, he pushed down the helm so that the fiat came head to wind. They had crossed to Runcorn side, were they tacked, and were returning at the time of the accident, meaning to go through the north arch of the bridge. The ferry boat was coming across from the Runcorn side, and in advance of the flat. Cox shouted and made a motion as if he intended to

----- heave round. He (witness) also motioned to the effect that the flat was for West Bank dock. Cox's boat kept coming on, as if he was determined to go ahead of the flat. The stern of the last-named vessel caught the other on the quarter, and then there was a call of " Man overboard." He saw deceased in the water' and threw him a rope, which went round his head, but be made no attempted to take hold of it. He then went aft and got in the flat's boat, with which he sculled to where deceased was. He was only about a yard from Tracy when he went down, but was decidedly of opinion that it would have been an easy thing for the captain of the ferry boat to keep clear. During cross-examination the Coroner said to the witness: You will have it that she struck the flat, though I think I I have got it from you already that you struck her. In answer to further questions, witness said thAt Cox could have ported his helm and gone on the Runcorn side of him (witness), or he could have clewed the sail up and let him go ahead of him, but he did neither of these things. The only chance he (witness) had was to put the helm hard down to prevent her going right over the ferry boat\ The flat afterwards ran against the north arch of the bridge, and afterwards went ashore. When witness got on shore Cox began to curse him. In reply to Mr. Ferrand, witness said he had given this evidence to Mr. Husband before coming to the inquest. By Mr. Husband: He did not think Cox was drunk; he should not like to say so. The Coroner: Why don't you answer his question straightforwardly? In reply to Mr. Ferrand, witness said he knew that Cox had been employed at the work for a long time. The Coroner: Yes, but he says that his sight is getting worse.
Mr. Ferrand : Yes, everybody's sight gets worse as they get older.
The Coroner: lam afraid he has a poor set of eyes in his head.

Thomas Lea, Egerton-street, Runcorn, said ha was mats with Cox, and gave evidence to the effect that he thought the course of action which his own captain took in the matter was correct. He, however, said he did not know whether he should have taken the same acti JR had he been placed in similar circumstances. He denied having heard Hardley say to the captain, " Go round her stern." Ile had seen as many as 20 persons in the ferry boat. In answer to the question whether the captain was a tem- perate man, he said he could drink pints of ale and he could leave it. The Coroner: He cannot do both. Whether does he drink pints of ale or leave it? No answer.

Mr. Husband: Is it not a well-known fact that if a person wants to go over that ferry the best plan is to give him a pint? Witness: Well, I don't know. Mr. Ferrand: I suppose latmen as a rule do like beer. Witness, in reply to further questions, said he did not think it right that a stranger should be allowed to steer a boat.

Thomas Ogden, a hand employed on the flat, also gave evidence strongly condemnatory of the course adopted by Cox, the captaia of the ferry boat. He was decidedly of opinion that the boat had several chances of 'getting clear, whereas the flat upon which he was had none, owing to the strength of the current and the force of the wind that was blowing. Arthur Hardley, 51, Regent-street, Runcorn, said he was a flatman (he also keeps a fishmonger's shop), and was going across in the boat to his own vessel, which was at Messrs. I Gossage's. He said to the captain of the ferry boat "Henry, you had better go under this flat's stern, as he cannot do as he likes with an empty flat." "Goto with him," re- plied the captain, "we are not going up the river for any man." The young man at the helm said, "Shall I keep the tiller up ?" "No," answered the captain, "keep your helm where it is." Witness supposed the captain was afraid to go up the river for fear he should have to put an oar out and pull the vessel down again. He did not know that the man was in the water at all until he got drowned. He considered the accident a piece of neglect on the part of the ferry boat. He took off his hat and coat ready to swim, and went to the bow of the boat clear of everybody, for at a time like that they drowned every one in the struggle. Not a word was said about passengers keeping their seats. Cox never opened his mouth about it. Deceased's legs were knocked from under him by the blow given by the flat, and then be went over- board.

In answer to a question as to why he did not attempt to rescue the deceased as he could swim, he said it would be impossible to rescue the deceased owing to him going to the other side of the vessel, and he could not get to him or he would have jumped over for him. There was no one pull- ing tke oar to get there only himself, and the captain of the vessel did not know what witness was puffing about. The captain could have avoided the c6llislon by twice the length of the boat, as be had plenty of steerage way. It was the rule for a vessel going before the wind to give way to a vessel on the wind.

The Coroner instructed the jury that there was no criminality on the part of anyone, and therefore they could confine their judgment to the simple facts of the case as to how deceased met his death, because the matter would come up again in another court.

The jury, after consultation found a verdict to the effect "that the deceased met with his death by drowning, owing to the negligence of the man in charge of the ferry boat.", They recommended the London and North-Western Rail- way Company to provide a life-buoy or some other appli- ance, so that if anyone fell overboard it could be used. Mr. Ferrand : It is the first accident in 30 years. The Foreman: That does not make it less blameworthy. I can say for myself that they have been more lucky than wise. It is not their fault if people have not been. drowned oftener. The enquiry then concluded.

LOCAL NOTES. For eccentric composition and orthography the following letter, recently received by a farmer from a bucolic neigh- bour, is a kind of curiosity :--"Sir,--I shoald feeel Obliged Canard off Vv enthsdaemY. an WMillontadaky if you tak better Car of yore horces they tresspas rnee and _s_d h eas _utr gbraepeknesvheeer psopletgsif Sunnotdai trululy-7, I am credibly informed that the sender of this document was a farmer in a respectable position. It is evident to me that there existed a strong necessity for School Board education in the district in which he lived when a boy. Apart from his original literary style one cannot but admire the forbearance of the writer of the letter, for though his neighbour's horses have invaded his domain and have apparently been unremittingly engaged in breaking his sheep's legs Sunday, Monday, and Wensday," he con- tents himself by mildly intimating that unless the nuisance is suppressed he will tak Car "of the unwelcome intruders. This is a spirit of Christian charity that is truly refreshing to meet with in these degenerate days. A large number of persons in addition to teetotallers will agree with me that the practice which prevails so largely in this district of giving children spirits medicinally is open to

grave question. Lancashire people, however, are not the only ones that adhere to this custom. One day last week a boy between five and six years of age living at Cottesbrooke took some of the medicine on his own account, and was seized with convulsions and died soon afterwards. This unfor- tunate case will serve to show not only the undesirableness of allowing young children to acquire a taste for alcohol, but also be a warning to parents not to leave bottles contain- ing dangerous liquids about carelessly. The weather has not been very favourable during the last week, but there is some hope. An Alexandria correspondent says that a new comet is visible, being below the ear of Ursa Major. Surely we shall all fervently hope that this latest celestial visitor will have a look at Grea Britain. We want something to drive away these dull skies and the monotonous downpour of drenching rain. And what more calculated to do it than a comet? At the time of writing this we appear to be living in the month of November instead of what is gener- ally the finest month in the year. There is a considerable amount of satisfaction to be derived from the statement that the tail of the new comet is larger and longer than even that of the comet of June. Surely this will be sufficient to alto- gether reverse the present meteorological conditions! The correspondence which has lately appeared in your columns, Mr. Editor, relative to the Frodsham Bazaar catastrophe, has given rise to much comment in Frodsham and the district. Some of the Nonconformists appear to be very indignant at the statement made by your first corres- pondent as they contend that not the slightest bigotry has ever been shown by them towards the Church party with whom they are on the best terms. That such is the case may easily be gathered from the fact that the Wesleyans lent their school room to the vicar for his Lent services with the utmost readiness, and I am assured that both they and the other Nonconformists in the parish are only glad to be able to render the good vicar and his flock any assistance in their power. 1

Strolling up Main-street, Frodsham, one day this week, I could not help noticing the progress that has been made in the place during the last few years in the way of improved dwelling houses and shops. There are, however, two or three very unsightly buildings towards the upper end of the street which appear to be in a very dangerous condition, and the removal of which would add to the safety as well as the improved appearance of the street.

With the great increase of activity which is manifested in the amount of enterprise displayed in various directions, I am not surprised to learn that a novel experiment is about to be tried by a firm of tailors in this town. I expect that the details which I am about to give will be read with much pleasure by some of our young cheap swells, for it will affect the weakest point of their susceptible natures. The fact is that the tradesmen I refer to are stated to con- template introducing the practice of letting out suits on hire at so much per annum, the clothes to be returned at the expiration of a certain period. If the hirer has two suits a year he will have to pay perhaps £3 for the use of them, if he has three suits he will pay £5, and if four suits £5 10s.; for it must be obvious that the wearer of four suits would injure them but slightly, and ought therefore to expect to have the benefit of a con- siderable reduction in the charge. All the clothes have, of course, to be returned, and the tailor will dispose of them in a manner best known to himself, either hiring them out again at'a lower figure or selling them to the second-hand clothes dealer who chooses to make the highest bid. The sy stem has been in vogue in Liverpool, London, and other large towns for some length of time, but whether it will be so successful here remains to be seen. At all events young Crutch and Toothpick will have something to be thankful for. FLACCUS.
The Rev. S. F. Collier, of Runcorn, who has spent four years as a student at Didsbury Wesleyan Methodist Theolo- gical Institute, has been appointed district missionary for Kent.

ANOTHER WIDNES CHEMICAL WORKS OFFERED FOR SALE.—A few days ago Messrs. J. B. and B. Leach, of Liverpool, offered for sale, by order of the liquidators, the Lugs laic Chemical Works, formerly worked by Messrs Wells and Galloway. The premises cover 9,760 square yards of land, and are held for a term of 900 years, subject to a ground rent of £lOl 13s. 4d. per annum. There was a good attendance at the sale, but no bid was made. IMPORTANT TO TRAVELLERS.—A WIDNES CASE.—At the Wigan County Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. W. W. Ffoulkes, judge, the Appley Bridge and West Lancashire Corn Company brought an action against Charles Lloyd, one of their travellers, to recover the sum of £37 10s., the price of 20 sacks of flour. Some time ago the company supplied 20 sacks of flour to a man named Thos. Campbell, of Widnes, but they were subsequently returned, and on the recommendation of the defendant sent to another Widnes man, named Mellewish, who did not pay for them. When the flour was sent to the latter, Lloyd wrote to the plaintiffs urging them to send it, and stating," I will be responsible." Mr. Ellis, who appeared for the plaintiff, argued that the letter made defendant the principal debtor and not merely a surety, and for the defence Mr. Beasley contended that Mel- lewish was the real debtor. His Honour held that defen- dant's promise that he would be responsible was a guarantee for the payment of the money, and said the document must be stamped. A verdict for the amount claimed was given, and the defendant was ordered to pay it in monthly Instal- ments of £5.

THE Rusconx BOWLING CLUB AT HALTON.—The first main of bowls in connection with the Runcorn Bowling Club this season came off on Saturday last, on the green of Mrs. Ormson, Norton Arms, Halton, for a pair of bowls and jack. There was a large attendance of spectators. The green was in capital condition. The event was limited to seventeen players, and that number was obtained before play began. Amongst those present were Mr. Dainteth, Mr. Robert Wright, Mr. Haddock, Mr. Lloyd, Mr. Moreland, Mr. Worrall, Mr. Sandbach, and others. The draw having been made, the first two to take possessioa of the green were Mr. Wright and Mr. T. D. Matthews, when the former won very easily. In the next round Mr. Dainteth and Mr. Wright were drawn together, when the latter came out the winner by five points. Some of the other contests in the various rounds were rather close, one being won by a single point only, and three by two points, but undoubtedly the chief interest of the main was centred in the play off for the bowls, by Messrs. Wright and Haddock. Some excellent bowling was witnessed, especially on the part of Mr. Wright, who won a very tight game by three points. RUNCORN, WESTON, AND HALTON WATER WORKS Co.—The following is the report of the directors and state- ment of accounts for the half-year ending June 30th:— "The directors have not so satisfactory a report to give upon the present occasion, partly owing to the long arid severe winter and to the great depression in trade generally. The sum received for water last half-year was £1,882 10s. fid., now it is £1,647 4s. 5d., showing a difference in the receipts of 8,235 6s. The increase of houses in this town, and a further demand for the extension of water mains to two large manufacturing works already given, will it is hoped with the revival of trade enable the shareholders to look forwar4l to a better account next half-year, which the directors fully expect to be able to give them. The revenue account shows a balance of ,E 513 135., including the amount brought forward from the previous half-year, out of which the directors recommend a dividend to be paid of £2 10s. per centum per annum, free of income tax, payable on and after the first of September ; this will absorb £270 16s. lid., leaving a balance of £247 168. Id. to be carried forward. The buildings, machinery, mains, and plant are in excellent condition ; the water in the well continues of good quality and as abundant as it has ever been, and shows no signs of diminution in the supply.—JonN BRUNDRIT, chairman of directors."

The Vicar took his text from Solomon 11-12, The flowers appear on the earth," an assertion, he remarked, which was true even at that late period of the summer, judging from the number and variety which met his eye in every corner of the church, to say nothing of the beautiful bouquet on the pulpit cushion, supplied by the kindness of some parishioner. Several lessons might be learned from flowers. First, a lesson of thankfulness to God, who, by scattering them on the surface of the earth, when they were for orna- ment and not for use, had provided for their pleasures as well as for their wants. The second lesson which might lee learned was of dependence upon God, the very lesson taught by their Lord and Master. The variety of flowers, some excelling in form, some in colour, some in fragrance, might remind them how each saint had his distinguishing grace; but just as the flowers bloomed wherever they were planted, so every Christian should do his duty in the station wherein God's providence had.placed him. At the close of the ser- vice the children filed out of their seats and deposited their flowers on trays, which were held at the entre/tee of the chancel by the Vicar and the Rev. J. J. Bryant, assisted by the churchwardens and sidesmen. Their example was fol- lowed by most of the congregation. Many of the bouquets were composed of the choicest flowers, most artistically arranged, exciting the surprise and admiration of all who saw them. They were presented in such quantities as to cause the ladies who undertook the task considerable time and trouble to arrange them on the steps of the altar, where they remained in artistic array until they could be forwarded on the following day to the respective hospitals. Sr. BEDE'S CATIEOLIC chapel, on Sunday, the Rev. Fath preached in the morning, and the Rev. West Leigh, in the evening. In the there was Mass, and in the evening a ro.ar. by Solemn Benediction. The collections the expenses recently incurred in p .intirg the church.

RUNCORN AND DISTRICT STARR-BOWRETT Over £28,000 worth of shares have now been take. this society, and on Monday eight new members The first appropriation, which takes place on Wedt night, at Runcorn Public Hall, is looked forward to wii. greatest interest. All who become members befort le, 3. inst. can participate in the appropriation. In at. p- of our columns will be found a review of a amphl specially dealing with the advantages offer . by suc societies.

THE COMING ELECIION OF COMMISSIONERS AT RUNCOIO —The annual election of five Commissioners in place of t' five retiring members takes place on Thursday next. ' five retiring members are Mr. George Marshall, Mr. J ,mes Dobson, Mr. J. R. Frith, Mr. Samuel Taylor, and Mr. J. J. Speakman. Besides the retiring members, who are eligible for re-election, the other probable candidates are Mr. W. J. Shore, Mr. W. Mellor, Mr. William Fisher, Mr. William Whittaker, Mr. F. A. Lake, Mr. James Curzons, Mr. R.

Wright, and Mr. George Gorst. We hear that there is a strong feeling among the friendly societies against the return of the two first-named of the retiring members. SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A WIDNES MAN.—On Monday, James Percival, who lived at Moor-lane, Widnes, and was employed by Messrs. J. Kirkham, erectors of chemical works, was working at Messrs. Pilkington and Son's Works, Moss Bank, Widnes, on Monday, when he stepped on a plank, which had been placed for the use of the workmen, which broke beneath his weight, and he fell to the ground, a dis- tance of 19 feet. Several of his ribs were fractured by the fall, and his shoulder blade broken. He now lies in a critical condition.

NELSON-STREET WESLEYAN MISSION SCHOOL, RTIN'CORN. —The first annual excursion of the teachers and friends of this school took place the other day at Sutton Hall, the residence of Mr. Lowe, and the Camden choir accompanied them. Previous arrangements had been made with Mr. Yarwood for the supply of conveyances for the occasion, and a large omnibus, qapable of accommodating from 35 to 40 persons, was engaged to which four splendid horses were attached. The route chosen after leaving Camden school was through Halton, Preston-o'-th'-Hill, Dutton, and Ashton. On arriving at Sutton, tea was provided for the party on the lawn. The party were driven home via Overton and Prod- sham, reaching Runcorn safely about nine o'clock.

THE FABITWORTH AGEICULTURAL SHOW.—Sir Andrew Barclay Walker has been invited to be the president of the Farnworth Agricultural Society for the ensuing year, and has accepted the position. The same gentleman has forwarded a donation of 25 guineas to the chairman of the committee, Mr. R. Whalley. Several well known judges of dogs have also offered their services to this old society free in con- , sideration of 1880 having been a bid year for the Farn- worth show. The prizes will conclude 15 silver cups, of which two will be of the value of £lO. and the rest of them from £3 3s. to £5. There: will also be the usual number of premiums. The entries close on September sth. We may state that Mr. Wh alley, who has madehis name famous in connection with local agricultural matters, took prizes value .20 guineas for the best Bull at the Ormskirk Agricultural Show on Wednesday. Mr. John Halsall, of Hale Bank, also obtained two prizes value 20 guineas, for Jumping.

r ADvaxcE OF THE BANE RATE.—Thc Bank rate of discount has been raised from 3 to 4 per cent. TRE REGISTRATION OF VOTERS.—The various bar- risters appointed to hold Revision Courts over the country for the purpose of revising the lists of voters who are entitled to elect members to serve in Parliament, will hold their courts to hear county claims between September 20 and October 31, and will take borough claims between September 15 and October 31.

LIBERAL CLAIMS IN SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE—In the division of South-West Lancashire, the following figures show the number of claims made in connection with the South-West Lancashire Liberal Association :—New property claims and re-claims, 2,100 ; objections to register and claims, 2,700; claims for £l2 list by persons omitted by overseers, 446.

MISTAKEN IDENTITY AT WARELINGTON.-011 Tuesday the Warrington police arrested on suspicion a man supposed to be Joseph Taylor, who is "wanted " for the murder of Ws daughter-in-law at Bradford. The police of the latter town have issued handbills containing a likeness of the murderer, to which the man arrested bore great resemblance. This likeness and that of a photograph previously issued are, however, quite dissimilar, and as the man was able to give a good account of himself he was set at liberty.

COWARDLY ASSAULT BY A SOLDIER AT PRESTON.—Yes- terday, at Preston Sessions, William John Chick, a soldier, was charged with violently assaulting Mrs. Richardson, a married lady. She was standing at her door, when the pri- soner came-up and, without a word of provocation, struck her in the mouth, breaking two teeth. She screamed, and he savagely kicked her about the legs. The chairman strongly denounced his cowardly conduct, and sentenced him to nine calendar months' imprisonment.

TUE SALVATION ARMY AT NORTHWICEL—The Northwich corps of the Savation Army had to undergo new experiences on Monday evening. They were marching and singing along Crown-street, to the music of an officer's fiddle, when an offended tradesman met them near his own door, and attempted to stay their progress with a cloud of flour. The "service" was temporarily stopped, and the incident caused a good deal of commotion; but, nothing daunted,, the reso- lute warriors in a few minutes resumed " operations," and went on their way rejoicing. Officers and rank and file bore unmistakeable traces of the little skirmish ; and as they journeyed along Witton-street attracted considerable atten- tion.

TRIP FROM EARLESTOWN TO BLAOEPOOL. The em- ployes of the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany's Viaduct Wagon Works, Earlestown, had their annual trip to Blackpool, on Saturday last. The employes, who numbered upwards of 1,000, left Earlestown about six o'clock in the morning reaching Blackpool in about an hour and a half. The excursionists were accompanied by the Earlestown brass band, which enlivened the proceedings of the day by playing selections of music. Favoured with fine weather, the many attractions of the "Brighton of the North" were seen to advantage, the men having tickets of free admission to the Winter Gardens and Raikes Hall Gardens. The return journey was commenced about eight o'clock, and Earlestown was reached between ten and eleven.

THE REPRESENTATION OF WIGA.N—AII unexpected division in the House of Commons, taken at a Saturday's sitting at the fag end of a long session, has saved Wigan from the expense and turmoil of an election inquiry. The Attorney-General moved for the appointment of Commis- sioners to inquire whether corrupt practices prevailed in the borough, his motion being based on the report of the judges who tried the petition resulting in the unseating of Mr. Powell. It was explained by the Attorney-General that the judges in the case had reported that bribery and treating had prevailed. Under these circnmatances, Sir H. James considered that the House would be treading on dangerous ground if it went 'behind the judges' report, while on behalf of the Government he declared that if they neglected to make this motion, they would be abrogating that which was "almost a Ministerial duty." Mr. J. K. Cross opposed the Attorney-General's motion, pointing out tbat, compared with other boroughs, Wigan was a perfectly pure con- stituency. The hon. member mentioned that at the time of the election there had been a great strike in the Lancashire coal trade, which had left many of the electors of Wigan without wages and without food, thereby rendering them peculiarly subject to temptation. Many of the inhabitants were colliers, and while Mr. Cross admitted that they were "a dog-running, pigeon-flying, and Church-and-King-toving population," he indignantly denied that they were corrupt or open to bribery. Sir Hardinge Giffard also opposed the motion, at the same time challenging the statement of Sir H.lames that in these cases the opinion of the election judges should be taken as conclusive. On a division the motion was lost, thirty-seven voting for and forty-three against it.

TUE LANCASHIRE AND YOMISIZIEM ELILWAY COM. PANIC.—This company's half-yearly meeting was held on Wednesday. Mr. T. Barnes (chairman of the Board of Directors) presided, and; in proposing the adoption of the report, he said that it was a matter of disappointment that the company had to declare a dividend of per cent, less than that of the corresponding half of last year. In common with all the principal railways, their expenses !had been augmented by the unavoidably increased cost of working 1 during the severe weather of the past winter. They had in- curred increased cost owing to the coal strike n Lancashire, I and they had the further cost of maintaining about 27 miles of additional line of way, and also of working some new branches. They were giving greater facilities and accom- modation than before, better carriages and more frelnent and faster trains, thus adding to the cost of working, in order to meet the public requirements and keep pace with their neighbours. The increased total receipts for the half-year amounted to £26,140; of this £5,485 was for passenger traffic and £20,216 for merchandise, minerals, &c. The total number of passengers carried was 17,698,547, an increase of 504,023, or nearly 3 per cent., bat the increase in the receipts was but little more than per cent. The average fare showed a diminution in every class, the average being 7.31 d. against 7.46 d., which to some extent accounted for the increased percentage of working cost. Compensation for passengers showed a decrease of £7,998, whilst that for goods showed an increase of £1,534. After a discussion on the management of the company the report was adopted. A dividend at the rate of 4f per cent, per annum less inciame tax was declared, and the balance of £15,917 was carried forward to the next half-year's account.
