GOLBORNE LIBERAL ASSOCIA.TION.

An association, which is intended for the organisation of the whole of the Liberals in Golborne and SUITS =ding district, has been formed. At the first meeting, which was held the other day, there was a good attendance, and con- siderable enthusiasm was manifested. Mr. R. Yates pre- sided; and after discussing the subject it was decided to form an association forthwith. Mr. John Unsworth, sen., was elected president and treasurer of the association for the ensuing year. It was also decided to elect the following gentlemen as vice-rfresidents :—Messrs. Davies, Yates, Howard, W. Jackson, William Mitchell, and Dr. Latham, of Ashton. Mr. John Travers was appointed to act as general secretary, Mr. James Dean, financial secretary, and Mr. C. Hall as political secretary. An executive committee of 18 gentlemen was also elected. Subsequently a vote of thanks to the Premier, Lord Granville, and other members of Her i Majesty's Government, for the valuable services they had rendered to the country in connection with the passing of the Irish Land Bill, was unanimously adopted; and it was' also resolved that copies of the resolution should be for- warded to the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone and Etrl Gran- ville. In reply ta this Mr. Hall, the politic d secretary, has received the following communication :—" August 22nd, 1881. Sir,—l am desired by D-frd Granville An) acknowledge, with his best thanks, the receipt of 4 copy of the loso'ution with reference to the Irish Lind Bill, which was adopted at a touting of the Golborne and District Liberal Association, held on the 18, h inst.—l am, air, your obedient servant, G. W. SPENCER Lrrarrow. C. Hall, Esq Ualtligh, Park Yiew, Golborne. GOLBORNE NEW LIBERAL CLUB.

------- In connection with the newly-formed Liberal Association for Golborne and district it has been deemed desirable by the leading members of the Liberal party here to form a Liberal dab. At a meeting held on Tuesday night, under the presidency of Mr. Unswortb, the questionof the erection of a suitable club-house was fully discussed, and it was resolved that a building for that purpose should be erected. In the interim, however, it was deemed desirable that a tem- porary building or rooms should be immediately taken. It was decided to float a limited lliability company, with a capital of £2,000, to be taken up in £1 shares, and we under- stand that the preliminary steps for the formation of the company have been taken, and that nearly 40 persons have already intimated their willingness to take shares in the company. The new company is to be called the " Golborne and District Reform Club Company."

I GOLEORNE CONGREGATIONAL CHERCH.—Special musical I services were held in the Congregatiotal Church on Sunday 'afternoon and evening list. The selections included Att- wood's anthem, " feack me 0 Lord," Hopkin's " Te Deum," 740zArt's " Quoniam," CØ Father" (Handel), "Kyrie Bleison," and the "Gloria." The rendering of these pieces gained a large portion of its success from the instrumenta- tion, which c.,n4sted of two first and two second violins, the viola, bassoon, flute, double bass, and harmonium, all of which tended not only to strengthen the vocal parts, but to add vigour and life to the entire pieces, which, taken as a whole, were highly appreciated. The Rev. R. Lambert, late of Wigan, delivered able sermons. Both services were well attended, and the offertory realised £7 2s.

THE PARLIAMENTARY REVISIONS.—The revision of the lists of voters for North-East Lanceshire will commence on September 28. The first townships to be taken are IValton and Ribchester. The Likrals have served about 1,450 objections. The Conservative figures are not yet to hand for the whole division. At Blackburn they have issued 200 objections, against 288 served by the Liberals. The Con- servatives have sent in about 500 objections and 700 re- claims on the Oldham lists of voters. The Liberal objec- tions are glightiv fewer than the Conservatives, as are also their claims. At Blackburn, in connection with the ap- proaching revision of the list of voters, there have been served by the Liberal agent 1,276 parliamentary and 1,701 municipal notices, and by the Conservative agent 1,021 pat liamentary and 1,323 municipal. There are 455 parlia- mentary and 575 municipal claims for Conservatives, and 213 parliamentary and 252 municipal claims for Liberals.

- HOUSE OF LORDS. - THE UN/VERSITLES STATUTES BILL. - Their Lordships assembled at twelve o'clock.—Lord Redesdale presided.-- Earl KIDIBERLET moved that the Commons amendments to the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge Statutes Bill be agreed to.—The MARQUIS OF SALISBURY moved that the amendments be disagreed with. The effect of the amend- ments would be to confiscate the independence sf these ancient universities.— The noble Marquis's. motion was carried by 36 against 13.

_ Tnz Passitca or SEVERAL Brus.—Tlue Irish Church Act Amendment Bill was read a third time. The Appro- priation Bill was read a second time. The Standing Orders were suspended, and the Bill was committed read a third time and passed. The Supreme Court of Judicature Bill— the Commons' amendments to the Bill were agreed with. The Solent Navigation Bill was read a third time and passed. _

• THE SERVICES OF OFFICERS. - Lord STILkTENSITL't having called the attention of the House to the injury to the States resulting from imperfect records of the services of officers, whereby such services remained un- rewarded, while others were unduly recognised, Earl Mon- LET said the complaint was groundless. Their Lordships adjourned at one o'clock.

div.head: LATEST SEWS.
div.p: LATEST SEWS.

George Crowley, a Protestant suspect recently arrested in County Waterford under the Coercion Act, has been liberated. The Guardians of Waterford Union have resolved to give preference to Irish manufacturers wherever practic- able in receiving tenders, and to ask all other Irish Unions to do likewise.

Last night's Gazette announces that Her Majesty has been pleased to confer the Victoria Cross upon the Rev. J. W. Adams, late chaplain to the Kabul field forces, for hav- ing extricated and rescued some men of the 9th Lancers, who had fallen into a deep fiullah while the Afghans were tiring and rapidly closing on them.

GREAT RAILWAY DETENTrorr.—Passengers and Volunteers were arriving at Glasgow (North British Station) yesterday morning at four o'clock. The Glasgow Highlanders being among the last, they .were mud to the knees, and many speechless with cold, having been thirteen hours wet to the skin. Many were unable to:attend business yesterday, and it is feared there will be a large amount of sickness.

THE STAFFORDSHIRE STRIKE.—After being on strike for nine weeks for an advance in wages, upwards of 20,000 nailers resumed work yesterday at an advance of 20 per cent. In Rowley, Ralesowen, and other districts the nail warehouses were visitcd early by operatives eager to obtain work, and the greatest excitement prevailed. About 10,000 operatives resumed work at Sedgley a fortnight ago at the same advance.

MR. GLADSTONE AND THE SCARBOROUGH LIBERALS.— Replying to a resolution passed by the York and Scar- borough Liberals, at a meeting held at Scarborough, Mr. Gladstone says it has been very gratifying to him to read the cordial expressions of their confidence in the Govern- ment, and he is sure that those who were present on the occasion would share the satisfaction of Her Majesty's Ministers at the passing of the Irish Land Bill. YELLOW FETER IN A LANCASHIRE REGlMENT.—lBteili- gence reached Plymouth yesterday that yellow fever prevailed to an alarming extent at Barbadoes. The 4th West India Regiment (now styled "Ist Battalion Lancashire Regiment ") has lost many men, and the entire regiment has been marched to Gun Hill. Colonel Fraser (Royal En. gineers) and Mr. Cousins (Commissariat), also Mrs. Robin- son, wife of the Governor, are dead. There are fifty cases in the town of Bridgetown alone, and dysentry prevailed extensively among the blacks.

The review of Scottish Volunteers by the Queen at Edin- burgh on Thursday was completely spoiled by torrents of rain. Forty thousand volunteers were present, under the command of Major General Macdonald. Her Majesty was accompanied by Princess Beatrice and the Duchess of I Edinburgh' and was very heartily cheered by the large multitude of spectators, who, notwithstanding the heavy rain, waited on the ground until she arrived. Mr. Herbert Gladstone ha; written a courteous but for. cible letter to Mr. Healy in reply to one addressed to him by the member for Wexford. Mr. Gladstone admits the sin- cerity of the motives by which Mr. Healy is animated; but says that "nothing can possibly justify, in his opinion, the man, deeply, conscious though he may be of the wrongs of his fellow-countrymen, who in cold blood advises the poor ignorant tenants to take the law into their own hands, to decide, perhaps, on the impulse of a moment, whether or no they are unjustly treated, and to commit acts which the law of every civilised country calls murder." SERIOUS STATE OF GENERAL GARFIELD.

The following telegram was received yesterday morning at the American Legation :—" President has lost ground to- day. Some of the symptoms this afternoon and evening are of the gravest character. The condition of the swollen glond and of the pulse and temperature suggests serious and alarming complications. Ms mind at intervals has been somewhat crowded and wandering. His strength fails, but he still swallows liquid food, and apparently digests it. On this one fact rests the hope that is still left of a reaction." The hopeless tone of the,above telegram is believed te fore- bode the dissolution of the President, who, it is thought, is sinking rapidly.

WASHINGTON, Thursday Midnight.—Soon after the even- ing bulletin had been issued the attending surgeons began to notice a change foaphe worse in some of the President's symptoms. He became more restless, and his pulse rose to 120. He commenced to have hallucinations regarding his circumstances and surroundings at intervals, especially after waking from sleep. He talked incoherently, and seemed un- conscious of his situation. The appearance of the parotid gland gave reason for the apprehension of serious conse- quences. Little more could be done, however, than to con- tinue the applications already used. At 10 p.m. the President's pulse .began to subside, and he became quieter. At the time of the despatch of this message the pulse was 1124 and the President was asleep. His condition continues to be a subject of the gravest anxiety. The members of the Cabinet assembled at the Executive Mansion as soon as the intelligence of the President's increasing unfavourable symptoms became known, but they departed at midnight when the symptoms of the patient indicated that the crisis had not yet arrived.

MANCKESTER OOTTON.—An extremely disappointing market has once more to be reported, the chariness of buyers and the increasing anxiety of producers to secure new business being alike more marked than before. In yarn both the home trade and export demand has been meagre; prices are irregular, but id, decline from Tuesday is commonly quoted. Cloth is also slow of sale, and agents find stocks Increasing; buyers are able to fill any orders they have at a reduction of about lid. per piece, but the ameptance of lower prices has not so far led to any improvement in inquiry. I - LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS. Bacon in good request for th home trade, but slow for export. Hams dull. Shoulders strong. Beef rather more buoyant. Pork without change. Lard more freely offered. Cheese weaker in the absence of in- quiry. Butter in only limited demand. LIVERPOOL COTTON.—Spot: Only a small amount of business has been done, and the market is freely supplied. Quotations of American low middling an& upward and good Dhollemh are reduced 1-16 d per lb. Sales 7,000 bales, of which 1,000 bales are on speculation or for export. LIVRRPOOL Come.—There was a moderate attendance at our market to-day, and a fair business was done in wheat at an ad- vance of from ad to 4d per rental on the quotations of last Tuesday. Flour, which is about 3d per rental dearer than on I last market day is in good demand. A steady business has been done in Indian corn at full prices; new mixed sold at 65 2d to es 20, round at es aid to 65 6d per cental, In beans a fair trade has been transacted, Egyptian selling at is 10d to Bs, mixed at 7s 91 to 7s 10d per rental. Peas are in fair request, 75 5d to Is ed per cental. Oats are quiet. Oatmeal has realised an improvement of from 5d to Ed per rental on last Tuesday's rates.

div.head: FRODSIIAM.
div.p: FRODSIIAM.

SERMONS AT FRODSHAM BRIDGE.—On Sunday, specia sermons were preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel Frodsham Bridge, by Mr. Thomas Rigby, of Sutton Weaver A collection was made at the close of each service in aid of the trust fund.

FETE.—The further details of the cricket fete at Belle Monte on Thursday next are published, and the pro- gramme as settled offers many attractions, in addition to the beautiful situation of the grounds. The organ to be used in the recital has done good service in the Parish Church, Overton, having been purchased by Mr. Rigby when the work of restoration was commenced. THE WEATHER.—The unfavourable weather during the week has completely checked the harvest operations. A large quantity of oats has been cut, but the continual down- pour has prevented them being carried. The farmers com- plain that the potatoes are beginning to rot, and altogether the prospect is somewhat gloomy for agriculturists.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

ANNIVERSARY SErisroics AT ‘VINSFORD.—The anniversary of the Station-road Free Methodist Sunday School was held on Sunday and Monday, when two sermons were preached by Mr. R. Hatton, of Winsford, whose sermons, especially on "Charity" in the evening, gave great satisfaction. The proceeds of the Monday's tea and sermon collections cane to 1 between £8 and £9, which will put the Sunday school in good position for another year.

MONARCHY IN RELATION TO THE EMPIRE, rte. Sir,—When I penned Ty first letter upon this suhject it was not with the intention of entering into a discussion upon the relative, merits of democracy and limited mon- archy. I simply wished to call the attention of your readers to two little scraps which I thought were an interesting token of the value of the latter system in an Empire like our own, as it bound us all together in a common loyalty, and was a strong antidote to rebellion, and a powerful stimulus to unity. This, I thought, was a matter of con- siderable importance; and, were it the only argument in favour of the English monarchial system, I am inclined to think that we should be justified in maintaining that system, notwithstanding the strictures of your correspond- ent, Mr. John Peers. He evidently does not set much store by the colonies, and would, I gather, be prepared to run the risk of alienating them from our rule if only this bugbear of monarchy with its attendant taxation might be dsstroyed. But if he rightly apprehended the value of the colonial empire of Great Britain, he would scruple to take the slight- est step calculated to endanger its existence, and certainly would not grudge twopence three farthings, which is perhaps the amount we pay per head per annum towards the support of this monarchial system, with its accompaniments of loyalty and union. And that loyalty exists not only among Maori and Basuto chieftains, not only among our dark fellow subjects in various parts of the world, but in Australia a most gallant people delight to cailthemselyes "subjects of the Queen," and the same spirit in British North America exclaims: " Let the Queens legitimate authority as a constitutional monarch be assailed, and not- withstanding the lamentation of Burke that the age of chivalry was passed,' thousands of swords would leap from their scabbards to avenge her. Ay, and they would be drawn as freely and wielded .as vigorously and bravely in Canada or in Nova Scotia as in England. Loyalty! Love of British institution! They are ingrafted on our very nature ; they are part and parcel of ourselves!" Is loyalty such as that a meaningless phrase? No, it is a wonderful reality, which may be laughed at, but cannot be ignored; and, existing as it does, ha our possessions in every quarter of the globe, was I not justified in speaking of it as "one of the st (riga et of the ties of empire?" The full importance of empire to us I cannot here enter into, suffice it to say that it affords an outlet for our surplus population, and a field for our enterprise; that while France consumes British goods at the rate of 7s. Bd. per head, and the United States at 7s. per head, Australia and New Zealaud consume them at the rate of £8 10a. per head; that while during the past few years our exports to al- most every foreign country have decreased, there has been an increase of those exports to the colonies and India; that, as the Daily News says, it is a mistake to suppose that if Australia flew the Southern cross and Canada the Northern star, instead of the British flag, these advantages would re- main; and that "if England were deprived of her outlying provinces she would sink to the level of Holland." More- over, great minds look forward to a time when these benefits shall be quadrupled by the realisation of "the dream of the mighty federation of all the members of the English family," of which Mr. Chamberlain recently painted so glowing a picture. And if, pending the fulfilment of that sublime ideal, the British monarchial system goes so far as to secure the allegiance and the unity of the Empire, surely we can each manage to pay our proportion of twopence three farthings per annum towards its support. And, for that matter, does Mr. Peers think that our fellow-subjects in other lands would object to bear their fair share of the sum which we pay to support the Queen? I should think not, for it wouldn't amount to a halfpenny each. But there are many other arguments in favour of our monarchial system, to which for lack of time and space I can only just allude. That a millenial democracy might be better than a nine- teenth century limited monarchy I will not dispute ; but it is with the nineteenth century that we have to deal, and that the English monarchial system is the best adapted to our present requirements is to my mind self-evident. The Hon. T. D. M‘Gee says, "it combines all the good of mate- terial importance that has ever been discovered." It to a great extent ensures the loyalty and the unity of the Em- pire ; it imparts a permanency to our institutions which in republican states is altogether lacking ; "every grade of so- ciety and every interest in the country is represented in it society is secured by it; noble institutions are patronised by it ; eclat is lent to great and important national gatherings by it; its members work hard for the good of the country ; its soldiers can fight and die for a common sovereign as they could not for a republican section ; under its benign influence England has attained to a height of civilisation and liberty and glory at which " all the world wonders," and in it liberty cannot degenerate into license. Mr. Peers, with boundless philanthropy, remarks that one very strong argument against the system is that we are not justified in placing:human beings upon thrones and making demigods of them; but we do not make demigods of them, for they are "limited monarchs "—they are there, as Cowper says, " to administer, to guard, to adorn the State, but not to warp or change it ;" and if they forget that they are "limited monarchs," they will soon find that they are the reverse of demigods. And it is not, as Mr. Peers seems to imagine, "adoration of accumulated wealth" that makes us adhere to the British monarchial sytem. It is because our Sovereign does her duty, and is a Queen in the truest sense of the Word—a mother of her people—that we respect and love her; and when our sovereigns forget to do their duty no "accumulated wealth" will blind us. I have enu- merated a few of the benefits which are attendant upon our monarchical system, which Mr. Peers seems so anxious to destroy. They would accompany it to its doom. But let him not imagine that such a consummation, however de- voutly he may wish it, can be easily attained. The chances are that the change which he contemplates would be preluded by the horrors of a civil war in which the greater part of the empire might be involved, for, remember—" Let the Queen's legitimate authority, as a constitutional monarch, be assailed and ten thousand swords would leap from their scabbards to avenge her; and they would be drawn as freely and wielded as vigorously and bravely in Canada and Nova Scotia "—ay, and in other parts of tiesiworld too—" as in England." This may be sentiment; Mt it was sentiment that enabled the five hundred soldiers, of whom Carlyle speaks, to be sabred into crow's meat for a cotton flag not worth threepence; and I repeat, sentiment may be laughed at, but it cannot be ignored. And all this Mr. Peeve would be prepared to risk for the sake of the magnificent sum of twopence three farthings per annum; for the other benefits which we are told we should derive from the substitution of a democratic for our limited monarchical form of govern- ment are far too vague, shadowy, and prciblernatical to be calculated upon. It seems to me that the democrat bases his ideas, if he has any, basis for them, upon Ithe proverb Tex popitli, vox Del—the voice of the people is the voice of God; and if this were indeed the case then democracy might be the best form of government. But the voice of the people is not the voice of God. It is often the voice of ig- norance and the voice of selfishness. It gives forth an un- certain sound, and at the bidding of silver-tongued self- seekers it may be turned into the voice of Belial ! In Ireland the voice of the people was "Down with the land- lords! Shoot them! Fire their houses! Hough their cattle!" In Northampton the voice of the people was atheism. In the House of Commons the voice of the people was for a Land Bill from which the second estate of the realm had to eliminate some "glaring injustices," amid the execrationsof the vox populi; and now when the tumult has subsided, and the clamour is hushed, the still small,voice of reason, speak- ing through one of the strongest advocates of the Land Bill, has to admit that the House of Lords has improved and not destroyed it. Educate the popular voice; let justice be its cry and not self-interest; let enlightenment direct its vote, and not violent and unthinking and unknowing partisan- ship; let its patriotism be superior to the bribe of an intoxi- cant; let real liberty, and not the sham that too often hides itself under her sacred robes, burn in the hearts of the people; let "all the ends they aim at be their country's, their God's and truth's," and then the voice of the people may be the voice of God; the various checks and counter- checks which form the beauty of our system of government may become superfluous; and democracy may with some show of reason claim our consideration.—I am. 24th August, 1881. ARTHUR BENNETT.

LETTER FROM THE FAR WEST OF AMERICA. Dear Mr. Editor,—Thanking you for your former publi- cation I again drop you a few notes from here. Our coun- try has now been plunged in deep affliction at the attempted murder of our 'beloved President. Just as the nation was prepared for their great and glorious holiday, the fourth of July, the terrible news flashed across the country, and flags were lowered at half-mast. It would seem that every town and hamlet was buried in sorrow. Almost every one holds their breath as they ask how the President, that great and good man, is. Republican and Democrat alike have been shocked at the awful news, and day after day our telegraph office is besieged by those eager to learn the news. But thank God he is better, and is still improving though slowly, and it is the earnest prayer of thousands that he should be restored to his health. The great comet has been visible here for some time, although tot so plain at present as at first. The weather has been very hot, in fact warmer than ever s,nce we came here, so much so that men have not been able to work in the heat of the day. The harvest is already co nmenced, and now may be heard the sound far and near of the machines. Crops are, on the whole, good. Vegetables also will be plentiful. Bugs are plentiful in the potatoes, 13t we poison them to a certain extent, and thus save the potatoes. Our harvest machines are a great improvement. We have the self-binder, which is the latest and best machine. One man witp three horses can cut and bind 15 acres per day with this machine, the machine binding the sheaves with twine and dropping them on the ground. This used to be done with wire. We have had more thunder and lightning this summer than usual, the lightning being far more vivid here than any I don't hear of so much damage have seen in England, but I being done. We have had a good season, though, for crops. Small fruits do well here except raspberries, which seem to die. Last spring nearly all the peach trees were destroyed with the frost. Ihope that your harvest in England this year will be good, but inthe best of times farmers cannot do so well as out here in the Western States.—Yours truly, Bethel Farm, Hampton, JAMES SPENCER. Hamilton County, Nebraska, July 17th, 1881.

Mr. Thomas Dunn, secretary of the Cleveland Miners' Association, having forwarded to Mr. Gladstone a resolution of that association expressing indiglation at the action of Lord Salisbury in persistently striving to mutilate the Irish Land Bill, has received a reply thanking him for their ap- proval of the conduct of the Government, and expressing a feeling of certainty that they will share the satisfaction of Her Majesty's Ministers at the razsing of the measure.
PRESCOT POLICE COURT.

FRIDAY Before Mr. W. L. Evans. NEGLECTING TO SUPPORT HIS WIFE AND CHILD.— Henry Higgin, of Eccleston, was summoned by the Prescot Board of Guardians for having, since the 28th April, neglec- ted to support his wife and child, whereby they became chargeable to the Prescot Union.—Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Guardians, who prosecuted, stated that the prisoner was married to his wife, Sarah Higgin, on the 9th February, 1876, and he (Mr. Hartley) regretted to inform his worship that for a period only of four months did they live together as man and wife. The wife left her husband on account of ill-treatmena, and the latter had done nothing towards main- taining her and her child. Prisoner had been in fall work at a place called Middle, near Shrewsbury. He asked his worship to inflict the full penalty.—Mr. Blackwell (assistant magistrates' clerk) said that could not be done as there was only one magistrate present. The prisoner could not be sentenced to a term of imprisonment exceeding 14 days.— Mr. Hartley remarked that in that case the prisoner had better be remanded to the Petty Sessions as he thought the full penalty should be imposed.—P.S. Bull said be received the prisoner into custody at Shrewsbury on the previous Tuesday. He was informed that the prisoner had been in full work, earning 13s. per week.—ln answer to his worship, prisoner admitted having neglected his wife and child dur- ing the last twelve months. Had she been a prudent wife to him, that would not have been so, and he would not have been in that box. If his worship would show mercy and favour he would return to his work and take the child with him.—Mr. Evans: And what is to become of your wife? Prisoner: She was not so good a wife to me as she might have been. However, if she will undertake on oath to be the same to me as I to her, I will take ber back.—Mr. Blackwell : And supposing the Guardians consented to that arrangement, are you prepared to pay them the full amount they have given to your wife and child? I don't think—Mr. Hartley: I don't think any reliance can be placed upon the prisoner.—ln answer to Mr. Evans, Mr. Hartley said the wife and child had been in the workhouse since the 28th April, and the cost of main- taining them in the house since that time would be about £6.—Mr. Evans (to prisoner) : Are you prepared to pay that? Prisoner : I have not got it on me, but if you will give me a little time I will pay it —Mr. Hartley : If he will consent to support his wife and child I undertake to re- pay this money. I think I shall be justified in withdrawing the case. The Guardians don't want to send him to gaol if he will look after his wife and child.—Mr. Blackwell : We ought to have some guarantee that he will pay the money. —Mr. Evans: Can't you pay anything down? Prisoner: There is 1 3s. 7d. in the station.-3(r. Blackwell: Can you find a surety that you will pay this money? Prisoner : Yes, sir.—Mr. Blackwell :If he pays £1 down and gives security for the balance, that will do.—Mr. Hartley: The best thing would be for him to pay 105. down, and with the balance to take his wife and child to Shrewsbury.—Prisoner ultimately consented to take his wife and child out of the workhouse, and to pay the £6 by instalments of 3s. per week. He was then bound over in his own recognisances and discharged. ANOTHER CASE OF ABSCONDING FROM THE WORKHOUSE. —Mary Clarke, a young woman, was charged with having, on the 19th September, 1880, absconded from the workhouse and stolen a suit of clothes, value 163. ed.. the property of the Guardians of the Prescot Union.—Mr. Hartley prosecuted, and stated that prisoner was permitted to leave the house along with other inmates to attend divine service at Portico Chapel, Eccles- ton. The prisoner and another woman named Hunt did not return to the workhouse. The workhouse master hearing that the prisoner was shortly to be liberated from gaol, ob- tained a warrant for her apprehension.—Mr. W. H. Bicknell, the master, gave evidence in support of this statement, and the prisoner was sent to gaol for fourteen days with hard labour. WORKHOUSE ROBBERIES: AN IMPUDENT THlEF—James Richardson was charged with having absconded from the workhouse and stolen a suit of clothes; also with having broken into the engine-house and stolen lib of cheese, two pocket-knives, a key, and other articles, value £1 2e. 10d., the property of the Guardians of the Present Union.— Michael Costello, an inmate of the workhouse, said that ota the night of the 25th June, the prisoner slept in the same room as he did though not in the same bed. He missed him about five o'clock the following morning. Prisoner had taken his clothes with him—Humphrey Leather, another inmate, deposed that about half-past seven o'clock on Satur- day night the 25th June, he secured the engine-house doors and windows. On the following morning about half-past five, he found the cellar grid had been lifted and an entrance into the engine-house effected. He went into the house and on making an examination he missed two knives; a key, a pound of cheese, and other articles.—The prisoner: I did not go into the engine-house. The Master of the workhouse stated that on the 25th June the prisoner was an inmate of the workhouse and had been for some months. [Prisoner: Ten months, I think.] On the following day (26th) he missed the pri- soner, who had left the house without his authority. While an inmate the prisoner a as supplied with a pair of trousers, vest, shirt, stockings, boots, coat, and cap, value altogether £1 is. Prisoner had taken these articles with him. He next saw him in the custody of the police. He was wearing some of the articles of clothing be took with him out of the workhouse.—Thomas Berry, of Northends Farm, Tarbock, deposed to finding the prisoner lying down in a field of wheat on his farm on.the morning of the 11th instant, and to handing him over to the police.—P.S. Stevens said he received prisoner into mestody from the last witness, and, after searching him charged him with breaking into the engine-house at the workhouse and stealing the articles above-mentioned. Prisoner replied, " Yes : that's right."— Prisoner, who had nothing to say, was committed for trial at the Quarter Sessions.—Prisoner was then further charged with breaking into the engine-house on the night of the Bth or early on the morning of the 9th, and stealing two tin canisters, some tea, coffee, sugar, cheese, and tobacco, razor, shaving-brush, two chisels, a "scriber," and a comb, value 43. 01., the property of the Guardians.—Evidence vas given in support of the charge by Humphrey Leather and John Cain (inmates), Mr. W. H. Bicknell (workhouse master), Thomas Berry, and P.S. Stevens, and the prisoner was com- mitted for trial on this charge also.—He was then further charged with having, on the night of the 9th or early on the morning of the 10th, broken into the bread pantry at the workhouse and stolen a quantity of bread and batter, a cloth coat, and a pair of stockings, value 103. 61., the property of the Guardians.— William Boardman (inmate) said that on the evening of the 9th instant he left his coat in the bread pantry, and on going for it on the following morning he found it had gone. The pantry had been entered by the window The coat produced was the one he missed.—Richard Watkin deposed to locking up the pantry on the night of the 9th, and to finding that it had been entered, next morning. He missed about 30 cobs of bread and a pair of spectacles and case. The bread pro- duced was similar to that he left in the pantry.—Mr. Bick- nell also identified the bread as similar to that used at the Workhouse. It was marked with the Union stamp—Thee. Berry, farmer, Tarbock, stated that about half-past six o'clock on the morning of the 11th instant he found the pri- soner in a wheat-field on his farm. Prisoner was lying on the ground. He had a candle' which was lighted, stuck in the ground, and over the light he had fixed a tin containing tea. He had also a bag with him, but at that time he (wit- ness) did not know what was in it. iWitness told the priso- ner to pick up the articles and go with him, and the priso- ner did so. On the way to Huyton, and as they were passing Haisnead Park, the prisoner said "It's no use carrying the bag any further. I may as well do without it," and he threw it over the wall. Prisoner subsequently took a mason's hammer from his pocket and threw it also over the wall. He told P.S. Stevens where he would be likely to find something the prisoner had disposed of.—P.S. Stevens said that about half-past eight on the morning of the date in question he received the prisoner into custody from the last witness, who told him what had taken place on the way. Be afterwards searched for and found the bag and hammer, and in answer to his questions prisoner replied that they were the same he threw over the wall. The bag contained a large quantity of bread and two tins. He charged prisoner with stealing the articles, and he replied "I did not steal them ; there were three of us together."—He was committed for trial. THE ALLEGED THEFT OF A MATTRESS AT RUYTON.—Jas. Murray and Michael Murtay, two young men, were charged with stealing a hair mattress, value 155., between the 10th and 13th of the present month, the property of Messrs. Branch and Leete, auctioneers, Liverpool.—Henry Mundie, in the employ of Messrs. Branch and Leete said that on Wednesday and Thursday, the 10th and il.th inst. his employers sold by auction the household furniture and effects of the late Sir Thomas Birch, of The Hazles, Huy- ton. Previous to the sale it was witness's duty to mark off the different articles in the list. The mattress produced was one of the articles he marked. It was marked 64, and was sold on Wednesday, the 10th, to a gentleman in Liver- pool for 153. The mattress was left in the bedroom in which it was sold, and of which witness had charge. When he went for it on the 13th he found it missing—P.C. Morgan deposed to finding the mattress at the prisoner Murray's house in Moss-street, Prescot, and to am/reheat- ing the prisoners.—They were remanded to the petty sessions, bail being accepted. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. W. L. Evans. WOUNDING A WIFE WITH A TEA-POT.—Edward Newman, a dissipated-look;ng fellow, was charged with having, at Wavertree, on the 18th inst., unlawfully wounded his wife by striking her on the head with a metal tea-pot.-The pro- secutrix, Catherine Newman, said she was the wife of the prisoner and resided at 122, Heygreen-road, Wavertree. About half-past three o'clock on the afternoon of Thursday, the 18th inst., the prisoner came home in an intoxicated state, took up a looking-glass, and was about to take it out when she remonstrated with him, knowing that he had taken several articles out of the house and sold them for drink. Prisoner said," I have worked for them and I will do what I like with them." He then put the glass down and took up a metal tea-pot and threw it at her with great force. The tea-pot struck her on the left side of the bead, inflicting a wound and rendering her insensible. She went to the East Dispensary, where the wound was dressed by Dr. Orr, the house-surgeon.—George Newman, a son, also gave evidence.—Dr. Orr deposed to dressing the wound on the prosecutrix's head. It was about two inches in length, and extended down to the bone. It was a serious wound, but he did not anticipate any danger from it.—P.S. Townsh end deposed to apprehending the prisoner and to charging him with unlawfully wounding his wife, and he replied, " Yes. She struck at me, and I put up the tea-pot to guard the blow, and the pot struck her on the head."—On being formally charged, the prisoner said he did not wound his wife intentionally.—He was committed for trial at the quarter sessions.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. IN Suntans CHARGE AGAINST A PRE:, Hugh Hayes and William Ryan, grooms, being drunk, and the latter prisoner was with obtaining goods under false pretences tailor and draper' Eccleston-street, rresc, stated that about five o'clock on Tuesday aft Hayes in Derby-street in charge of a horse acc ing to Mr. Beamont, of the Royal Hotel. He and quite unfit to take charge of the horse. The • apparently been down as its knees were cut, a been overturned as it was very much damage or —Mr. Evans: Could he reply to you when yen to , charge? Witness: I said he was drunk and quite take charge of the horse, and prisoner replied the.: capable of taking charge.—Superintendent Berke, appeared Hayes set off on the day in question driv. other prisoner about the country in the cab referred to there was no doubt they had been in Broadgreen A drinking champagne, and it was very likely they had chain pag-ne with them as he saw a bottle on the road as he wa, passing, and there was also a bottle in tha cab when they arrived at Prescot. Ryan was in Mr. Spencely's employ up to Tuesday morning, when he was discharged and paid off, and he immediately afterwards went to Mr. Park's shop and obtained a quantity of clothing, telling Mr. Park to put them down to Mr. Spencely. On making inquiry Mr. Bar- ker found it was really a bad case, and be must ask for Ryan to be remanded for a week.—Mr. Evans: Was Ryan drunk 7—Superintendent Barker: Yes, sir.—Henry Park said be was a tailor and draper, and carried on business in Eccleston-street, Prescot. He knew Ryan. He came to his shop on Tuesday morning and asked to be supplied with two pairs singlets, two pairs drawers, four pairs socks, um- brella, overcoat, hat, and pocket handerchief. Thinking that prisoner was still in the employ of Mr. Spencely, and as he had before been supplied with goods, he supplied the articles to the prisoner, who told him to put the coat, hat, and handkerchief to Mr. Spencely's account. Had he knownlpat piisoner was not in Mr. Spencely's employ, he would 'ffot have supplied him with the clothing.—Hayes, who was only charged with drunkenness was fined 10s and costs or 14 days, and Ryan was remanded for a week, Mr. Evans remarking that he was charged with a very serious offence indeed, that of obtaining goods under false pre- tences.

div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. TrESDAY.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, Judge.
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. TrESDAY.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, Judge.

A TRANSACTION WITH I KINGSLEY HORSE DEALER. Mr. Thomas Fleming, team owner, 18, Vernon-street, Liver- pool, sued Mr. John Spruce, horse dealer, Kingsley, near Frodsham, for £l5, being the deposit money paid by plain- tiff to defendant on an agreement concerning a horse, which understanding, it was alleged, defendant had broken. Mr. W. D. Jolliffe (from the office of Messrs. Ashton and Garrett, solicitors, Frodsham and Runcorn) appeared for the plain- tiff, and Mr. Hitchen for defendant. Mr. Jolliffe said that on the 18th April the plaintiff, accompanied by Mr. Guy, veterinary surgeon, went to Helsby by train and there met the defendant, with whom they proceeded, in a trap, a dis- tance of seven or eight miles, to the place where Spruce kept the animal concerning which the action arose. After some conversation, plaintiff entered into a contract with defendant to purchase the horse for the sum of £7O. The conditions of the agreement were that plaintiff was to pay £5O, and to hand over a horse valued at £2O to Spruce. Plaintiff paid defendant £l5 on the bargain, and it was agreed that he should send the horse to the plaintiff the next day, and when he had received it, he should forward the animal valued at £2O. It was further agreed that at the end of one month from the date of the contract plaintiff was to pay the balance of the purchase money. On the day following the interview defendant did not send the horse as agreed, but wrote stating that he had to go away, and he would not trust to anyone sending it off. He also requested the plaintiff to go on working the £2O horse. The letter sent by defendant read as follows :—"lt is not convenient to send the horse to-day, as I have to go to a sale that I was telling you about, and I should like to box him myself. I don't know whether I shall not have to go again to-morrow, if the sale is not over, but you must keep on working with my horse until I send mine down." Plaintiff wrote in reply, asking .defendant to send the animal as soon as possible. On the 22nd April, plaintiff wrote again, on which defendant replied by asking him to go for the horse. Plaintiff said he should do nothing of the sort, but should hold him to the original agreement. On the 2nd May defendant wrote plaintiff requesting him to meet him at the Crown Hotel, Lyme-street Liverpool, but as the letter only reached him the night before, he could not break the engagements he had entered into, and was thus prevented from going to the hotel until a later hour than that fixed upon, the same day, when he found that defendant had left. On the oth May, defendant again wrote to the plaintiff asking him to fetch the horse, alleging that it had been arranged he should do so, but this was not correct.— Mr. Hitchen : Your Honour, in the face of this letter, I really cannot see what defence I can make to the action. The let- ter appears to be a distinct contradiction to the instructions I have received, and in the face of it, I really could not go on. My instructions are entirely different.—His Honour said the letter written by defendant certainly seemed to admit that he was to deliver the horse.—Mr. Hitchen: Defendant is not here to day, and I could not contradict that letter.—The Judge said that under the circumstances, there must be judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed. —Mr. Jolliffe: With full costs. How soon will he be able to pay P—Mr. Hitchen : I understand that his goods have been taken iu execution, and I must ask your Honour to make a lenient order.—The Judge made an order for pay- ment in 14 days.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday last. Pre- sent—Rev. Canon Barclay (chairman), Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. C. Rigby, H. Lowe, Joseph Knowles, jun., John Ashton, W. Jackson, James Darbyshire, W. Pickering, J. Weir, 11. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).

THE FRODSHAM WATER SUPPLY. At a meeting of the Frodsham Water Supply Committee, held on the 15th August, Mr. John Ashton in the chair, the Clerk read a report on the Frodsham water schemes which was carefully considered by the committee, and, after some discussion, it was resolved that the committee recommend that Mr. Bancroft be requested to furnish a report explaining his suggested proposal for driving a heading for water at Five Crosses, and an estimate of the probable cost of such undertaking; also, if any portion of the estimated cost of scheme prepared 14th March, 1879, inoiuded the cost of driving a heading, and if so the amount. It was further resolved that the Clerk communicate, and if necessary arrange, an interview with the owners, or their representa- tives, of the Lower Bradley Mill, and ascertain without pre- judice the amount of compensation which the said owners claim in respect of their water rights. The report was adopted. URBAN POWERS FOR FRODSITA3I. A meeting of tne committee appointed to consider the letter from the Local Government Board as to urban powers for Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship was held on the 15th inst.,when the Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board, dated 6th inst., from which it appeared that their Lordships were willing to invest the Authority with the following urban powers under the Public Health Act, 1875, in respect of the contributing places of Frodsham and Frod- sham Lordship; viz.:—Cleansing of streets and rem Oval of refuse (sections 42, 44) ; power to make bye-laws respecting new buildings, Ste. (sections 157, 158). The sections were read, and the Clerk pointed out that the Local Government Beard had not included the urban powers relating to slaughter-houses and offensive trades, and it was resolved that the committee recommend the Authority to request the Local Government Board to grant powers, under sections 112, 113, 114 and 115 of the Public Health Act, 1875, relat- ing to offensive trades, and se:tion 169 relating to 31aughter- houses, in addition to powers under sections 42, 44, 157. and 158 of the said Act referred to in their Lordships' letter. The Clerk produced copies of bye-laws adopted by other authorities, when the Chairman took the bye—laws relating to slaughter-houses for perusal. This report was also adopted.
RE-AFPOINTMENT OF MEDTCLL OFFICER. On the motion of the Rev. J. W. N. TANNER, seconded by Mr. JOHN ASHTON, Dr. Bride was re-appointed medical officer of health for 12 months at a salary of £l2O.
THE CLAIM AGAINST THE AI7THORITY.

Mr. BANCROFT, Engineer to the Authority, writing in respect to an account of £l9lls 2d from the Warrington Cor- poration, stated that he had ascertained from the gas man- ager that it was for alleged damage to gas pipes from the coal yard adjoining the Navigation yard at London Bridge for a distance of about 100 yards up the private road belong- ing teMr. Davies. This length of sewer was laid between his visits, so that he did not see the gas pipes himself, but Mr. Cooper, the clerk of the works, assured him no damage was done to them, and stated that the gas pipes were laid in such an irregular manner that the Authority's sewer had to cross three times.—lt was decided to communicate with the contractors, and take the necessary steps to protect the interests of the Authority under the contract.

PRESENTATION OF AN ORGAN TO PRESTON.—On Thurs- day, at a meeting of the Preston Town Council, a letter was read from Mr. Dewhurst, coalmine proprietor, offering to present the town with a large and costly organ, to be placed in the new public hall, now being formed On the site of the Preston Corn Exchange. The organ has to be completed by the Guild festivities, when the Prince of Wales is in- vited to lay the foundation stone of the new Free Library and Museum. The offer was accepted with thanks. _ITRDA_Y, AUGUST 27, 1881 FLORAL AND HORTICUL- STATE OF IRELAND. 'URAL SOCIETY. ,LOWN DOWN: DAMAGE DONE. Abition of this society was held on Friday, in Griffin Inn, in the occupation of Mr. J. Cronm- . The society is only a young one, and though ,es were slightly under the number of last year, the ty of the exhibits, more particalarly the plants and ers, were superior than those shown on the two former asions. There were, however, 133' exhibits, and the Av would no doubt have been a success, but for the un- ortunate catastrophe of Friday afternoon, which put an end to any bright anticipations of financial success, to be realised on the following day, which might have been in- dulged by the committee. There was a fine show of plants and flowers, but the former were mainly the exhibits of Mr. T. Swift, solicitor, of Mill Brook House, and Mr. Wala.sley, of Spritagfield House. In the vegetables and fruit classes, also, these two gentlemen exhibited, and carried off most of the prizes. Mr. Swift, and Mr. Walmsley, were particularly successful, their gardeners, who represented them being Mr. John Braithwaite, and Mr. Thomas Case, respectively. The prizes were confined to about half a dozen competitors, the two already mentioned and Messrs. Johnson, J. Topping, J. Anders, W. Rigby, J. Waring, R. Prize, J. Sephton, J. Spencer, and Aspinall. The following gentlemen formed the committee for carrying out the work : Messrs. Edward Marley, Thomas Waring, John Braithwaith, Thomas Case, John Anders, Joseph Top- ping, J. Sephton and H. Flowers. Treasurer: Mr..J. Sepia- ton. senior, Eccleston ; secretary, Mr. H. W. Braithwaite, Prescot. The unfortunate occurrence referred to was the blowing down of the tent in which the show was held. The judges were rather late in their work, and the tent had only been open to the public a little over an hour when the occur- rence took place, so that the committee had received very little at the entrance, and all hopes of holding the show on the following day was out of the question. Consequently, the show, financially, was a failure. About five o'clock, a few minutes after OUT representative had left the field, the canvas which had been augmented in weight by, the exces- sive rain so as to weigh nearly 30 cwt., was noticed to bulge in at.the side against which the wind was blowing strongly, and causing the stakes in the ground to show symptoms of unsteadfastuess. The visitors wisely left the tent, and at- tempts were made to strengthen the stakes. The tent ran parallel with the hedge of the field,and unfortunately its entire length against the wind. Ropes were tied to the hedge which was composed of thorn trees, but all efforts were in vain, for the tent was blown down upon its side, and the plants and flowers inside considerably damaged,some 'being irretrievably lost, amongst them being a few valuable store and green- house plants. The thorns to which the ropes were tied were torn up by the roots.

In his first public utterance since his release from confine- ment Mr. John Dillon, Mr., said his imprisonment was tempered by a set of rules which made it very tolerable. He spoke in language of warm admiration of John Devoy and Michael Devitt, and expressed a hope that if in the future far greater sacrifice and suffering should be asked from the Irish people than had been asked by the Land League there world be found thousands ready to venture on the paths which those men had trodden. He asked the people of Tip- perary never to forgive the present Government for its treat- ment of Ireland; and referring to a statement of Mr. Forster in the House of Commons last Friday said that "of all the base and cowardly pieces of slander that he had ever heard uttered in public that was the lowest and the basest and the most cowardly." Sir C. G. Duffy, in a long letter to the Rev. Canon Doyle on the Land Bill, says it recognises the claim of the long- excluded Irish race to the possession and control of their own soil, and if they had repealed the Union in 1843 a patriot Parliament would, he considers, have framed some such measure to keep peace in the -country they were com- missioned to rule. It amazes him that the people and their leaders have not a sort of maternal pride in This Act, for cer- tainly they were active partners in the production of it. Sir Charles expresses his conviction that what is still the fore- most and most urgent of Ireland's public affairs is to regain self-government. The tenant farmers in the Ards district of county Down are much pleased with the manner in which the Land Bill has been passed, and bonfires have been lit in various parts of the district to indicate their satisfaction at the success of the measure. The Ballyclare Tenants' Defence Association, county Antrim, have passed the following resolution : "We hail with gratitude the welcome news that the long- looked-for Land Bill will soon be the law of Ireland, and we return our sincere thanks to Mr. W. E. Gladstone and all those members who have stood so nobly by him in his great struggle for justice for the down-trodden farmers of Ireland." The chief warder of Limerick prison, where nearly sixty suspects are detained, has been suspended. It is alleged that he has broken the prison rules by allowing documents to be received by the suspects without having previously been inspected. Regarding Mr. Forster's analysis of the finances. of the Land League funds, the Irish World says that it alone has remitted £20,000 since the beginning of this year. A return giving the number of arrests for drunkenness on ' Sundays between May 2, 1880, and April 24, 1881, both days inclusive, shows that in Dublin there were 929 arrests; Cork, 385 ; Limerick, 93; Weterford, 86; and Belfast, 272; making a total of 1,765. In the counties of Ireland the total number of arrests was 1,922. On Tuesday the Land League of Kilbinane, the centre of the most agitated district in the south, emphatically pro- nounced in favour of the Land Act. Several of the farmers said they would not stand any nonsense, and they would not have any dictation on the part of people who told them to surrender their farms to Emergency men. They ex- pressed their determination to avail themselves of the Land' Act as far as possible. MR. BIGGAR ON THE LAND ACT.—Mr. Biggar, M.P., addressing a meeting of Land Leaguers at Deptford, on Wednesday, said the landlords of Ireland for a long period had had the government of the country in their hands, and had misapplied their privileges with disastrous results. The tiller of the land was entitled to its first fruits. Although the Land Act contained some beneficial provisions, it did not, he contended, go half far enough. Resolutions were passed denouncing the continued imprisonment of the sus- pects •, and'demanding their release; endorsing the princi- ples of the Land League; and expressing a belief that the continuance of the Coercion Act would lead to distur- bances. Serious rioting took place late on Tuesday night, at Rath- keale, where a number of cattle, seized for rent, were im- pounded. The police who guarded them were badly stoned. They charged several times. One man's rifle was taken from him, and the weapon of another was broken. A third was badly injured about the head by blows of stones. Con- siderable reinforcements, however, arrived, and the tumult subsided. _

div.head: STATE OF TILE HOUSE.
div.p: STATE OF TILE HOUSE.

The MASTER reported that there were 164 inmates as against 150 in the corresponding week in last year. There had been 11 men, 3 women, and 1 child vagrants relieved during the week. There were 29 boys and 27 girls in at- tendance at the workhouse school, and 12 boys, 20 girls re- ceiving industrial training. Out-door relief had been ad- ministered to 609 persons at a cost of £6O 18s. 11d, as com- pared with 636 persons relieved at a cost of £6l 3s. 9d in the corresponding period of last year.

div.p: THE COI7NTY HATES.

The CLERK said he had received a county rate precept for £1,833, which was £250 more than that of last year.— Mr. Lowe: Well, you must work away.—The CLERIC: The Guardians have no appeal. He remarked that he wrote to the Clerk of the Peace since the last meeting stating the at- tention of the Guardians of the Union had been called to a report of the proceedings of the Court of Quarter Sessions, held at Knutsford on the 27th July last, at which sessions the letter which he addressed to him on the 25th May last was read. Not having received any official communication on the subject since the sessions the Guardians had directed him (assuming the report referred to was a correct one) to ask if the subject matter of the letter had been referret to the Finance Committee. He was directed to call the atten- tion of the court and of the Finance Committee to several townships in which the rateable value was greatly in ex- cess of the basis for the county rate—in some cases more than 8d per cent. The Guardians :were informed, and believed that the whole of the discrepancies were not due to the increase in the assessments to poor rates or from new property, but to errors, which in some way crept into the basis as settled in 1873. He was further directed to say that the Guardians were not aware that a re-valuation of the county, referred, to at the last Quarter Sessions, was required, but were informed and believed that by the powers contained in the 15 and 10th Vic., cap. 81, ample powers were given to I the court to proceed to the formation of a new basis more in accordance with the present value of property in the county, and on a more equitable basis to the ratepayers, and that such new basis might be made at a comparatively small ex- pense. He had received the following reply :—" Clerk of the Peace's Office, Chester, 10th August 1881.—Dear Sir—l have received your letter of yesterday's date. The letter you wrote on the 25th May last was read at the Quarter Ses- sions, held at Chester Castle on the 27th June last. It was not referred to the Finance Committee, but some magistrate stated that the subject appeared to be one for consideration by that committee. There were no sessions held at Knots- ford on the 2:th July. Your letter of the 15th inst. shall be laid before the next Quarter Sessions, which will be held at Knutsford on the 17th October next, and if so ordered may be referred to the next quarterly meeting of the Finance Committee, which will be held in November next.—l am, yours faithfully, THOMAS ROBERTS."— The Clerk was directed to forward copy of the correspondence to the clerks to the unior.s he had been in communication with in refer- ence to the subject.

div.head: TIM ADDITIONS TO TE INFIRMARY.
div.p: TIM ADDITIONS TO TE INFIRMARY.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board transmitting to the Board two copies of an order authorising the Guardians to make certain additions to the Infirmary at the workhouse at a cost not exceeding the sum of £2,400. Ten tenders had been received for carrying out the work, and that of Messrs. Stelfos, Carter, and Rylands, of North- wich, was provisionally accepted.

A Cheshire correspondent writes on Thursday :—Rain has been falling in torrents throughout Cheshire since mid- night, and still continues. The Dee is rapidly rising, and threatens to submerge the surrounding country. The harvest is in a deplorable condition, and corn is beaten down and rotting from the excessive rainfall of the past week. ZAMENE.—It is a healthy sign of the times to note that within the last few years an extensive demand for non- alcoholic beverages has arisen. This has led to the discovery and perfecting in manufacture of a large variety of drinks possessing different degrees of merit. Holding a leading position amongst these, we can bear personal testimony to the excellent qualities of zamene, than which we have tasted nothing more agreeable and refreshing of its kind, and more likely to come quickly into public favour. A sparkling, effervescent non-intoxicant of agreeable colour and flavour, zamene unites gentle stimulating with tonic properties, being highly recommended by the medical faculty, both for the weakly and convalescent, and for every day consumption. PAINFUL DOUBLE ELOPEDIENT.—A case of two brothers, married men, with large families, eloping with a couple of younc; single women, is reported from Morley. The four left for Liverpool with the intention of embarking for America, but at the last moment the women were prevented from following out their intentions. Passage tickets were procured, and the parties presented themselves on board, but the doctors, for certain reasons declined to pass the women, and they had to return to Liverpool, and snbsequently pro- ceeded to their respective homes. The men, however, remained on board, and duly sailed with the vessel. After the departure of the neon from Morley one of the deserted wives discovered that her husband had procured a bill of 'sale in respect of his furniture. She was unable to provide the money at the proper time, and this and the conduct of 'her husband so preyed upon her mind that she became ill, and died in a few days, at the age of thirty years. MR. HERBERT GLADSTONE AT LEEDS.--The announce- ment was made at a meeting held in support of Mr. Herbert Gladstone's candidature at Leeds on Saturday that the Premier would visit the borough and address meetings on 1 the 7th and Bth of October. Speaking in response to a 1 resolution which expressed approval of his candidature and. ' confidence in the Government of which he had become a member, Mr. Herbert Gladstone referred to the negociations. for a renewal of the commercial treaties with France, and sai,l that the meeting might rest assured that Her Majesty'S. Government would not make any treaty which was worse or less advantageous than that which would shortly expire. if, lie added, the negodlations failed,, the Governmbnt could hardly be blamed, because the commercial classes had in- sisted upon haying good terms with France or no treaty at all. Referring to our foreign relations, he said that one of , the most satisfactory features of the foreign outlook was the L inereasing friendship which had arisen between this country and the United States. With regard to Ireland, whilst the . necessity for making arrests was to be deplored, the course taken by the leaders of the Land League rendered it almost impossible for the Government at present to release those held in confinement. The use of language such as that attributed to Mr. Healy, M.P.—which was nothing less than an incitement to commit murder—was fatal to the peace and prosperity of the countsv, and it was the duty of every Irish patriot to repudiate it and the men who used it. . div.head: LAND ACT RULES.
div.p: THE LAND ACT RULES.

A Dublin correspondent states that it is the intention of the Chief Secretary for Ireland to spend some time on the Continent, and he will leave before the end of the present month. His absence from Dublin will not interfere with the framing of the new rules unuer the Land 4ct, and the commissioners appointed under it will be fully engaged in formulating these. It is the intention to appoint four assis- tant commissioners, and no more 'at present. These will be barristers. Ererything will be in readiness for working before the let October, and Mr. Forster will return to his post before that date.

div.p: REVIEWS.

BRETON'S GREAT BOOK OF POETRY (London, Ward, Lock and Co.)—The ninth part of this volume contains selections of poetry from the writings of Matthew Prior, Addison, Swift, Pope, Tickel I, Garth, Brackmore, Gay, Green, Bishop, Ken, dm. THE PRACTICAL TEACHER (London, J. Hughes, Pilgrim- street, Ludzate Hill.)—This excellent magazine is admirably adapted to meet a want which must have been urgently felt by those engaged in educational pursuits. The part for August now before us contains ably written articles on "Health at school," " Anecdotal natural history," and " Practical lessons on insect life ;" also the pupil teachers examination papers for June, with model answers to every question, "Recent inspection questions in arithmetic, geography, grammar, and domestic economy," which must render it one of the most valuable publications which could be plaeed in the hands of teachers, monitors, and others. How TO SAVE (Preston, Richard Seed, Friargate.)—This is a small pamphlet written with the object of showing the operative and artisan what the author considers to be the best method of investing his savings, having special re- ference to Starr Bowkett Building Societies. The author assumes that a man has five shillings per week to invest suggests that he should take up "Four shares of £lOO each in a Starr-Bowkett Building Society, which will absorb 2s. per week for subscriptions. He has still .313.. per week to invest. For a year or two he may put this in a Post Office Savings Bank at 24 per cent. interest. He is now regularly disposing of his 55., and we will allow this to go on for say five years, at the end of which time let us suppose he gets an appropriation in his society, which places at his disposal £430, to be re-paid in 12i years at the rate of £32 per year. He looks out for a convenient lot of property, and, to put it reasonably, we will assume he makes a purchase of a lot paying 6 per cent, in- terest dear. Of course he might make a worse purchase, but he ought to look after that, for 6 per cent, clear is about what he ought to have. He therefore only gets £24 income from his property, wkilst be has to repay. at the rate of £32, or £8 per year (Ss. per week) more than he receive from the property. /row here is a difficulty, but one easily got over. He has in the Savings' Bank five years' savings of 3s. per 1 week, which vrith interest amount to £42. He may now cease to deposit his 3s. per week in the bank, leaving the £42 where it is, and his 35. per week along with his £24 income will just supply all the demands of the society. Thus his subscription of 2s. per week, and his repayment of £32 are just kept up by his ss. per week saying and the in- come from his property. This goes on for 124 years, at the , end of which time he has completed his repayments, and ' the property is free, but now as the repayments have ceased, the society-requires that he continue paying the amount of his subscription, not at the rate of 2e,,, per week but at the rate of his repayments, which for another year or two.he is well able to do. We find that he has paid in subscriptions during the fiVQ years before he got his appropriation, and during the next 121 years, the sum of £9l towards the full amount 3100 45., thus leaving only £lB 4s. or a few pounds less than his next year's income from the property, but we will allow the next year's income for this purpose. He has now been a member of the society 14 years. The society has still to run on 24 years during which time he pockets the income from the property, viz.., £6O, also his Sc. per week for 24 years and the year of his finishing up payments, amounting to £45 10s., and when a squaring up takes place we find he has property worth £400; income from ditto for 24 years, £6O; si. per week for 31 years, £45; cash in Post Office Savings Bank, £42; interest on ditto for 16 years at 2,,,,. per cent., £2O; subscriptions returned, £109; total, £616."

Instead of the ex- plosives in question having any connection with Fenian machinations, they are found talave been intended for use iota shooting gallery, their fictitious consignmeut as "boots wri shoes" being with the sole view of evadieg the extra Payment necessary for the carriage of explosivu.

div.head: IRON AND COAL TRADES.
div.p: IRON AND COAL TRADES.

BARROW-IN•FURNESS, Monday.—There is a steadier tone 1 in the hematite pig-iron trade, and sales of both Bessemer and forge iron have been made at more money. Some makers are asking as much as 60a, per ton at works for best Bessemer iron. Orders are very largely held, and extensive ] deliverlea have to be made to consumers generally. Stocks remain large, and have not lately been reduced. The steel i trade is very actively employed, and all the mills are running full time. There is a good demand from foreign countries, and home users are also purchasing freely. Shipbuilders have a very active business, and as the orders they have in hand are extensive, several months of brisk work are in store. Engineers are well supplied with orders, and those employed in minor industries are also busy. LANCASHIRE, Wednesday.—ldthough the coal trade of this district continues all through very dull, there is, if any- thing, a slight tendency towards improvement, and collieries here and there are working more time than they have been I doing of late, whilst stocks have not been going down at the pits quite to the same extent. In the house-fire coal trade there has been rather more doing in consequence of the colder weather, and conenmers are beginning to anticipate their winter requirements; the demand for other classes of fuel for ironmaking and general manufacturing purposes has also recently been slightly on the increase. There is, how- ever, not yet any generally increased demand to materially affect the market, and supplies continue largely in excess of requirements. Prices also continue very low, without any material change from last week, except that there is perhaps less disposition to force stocks at under current rates. The average prices at the pit mouth are about as under :—Best coals at Bs. to Bs. 6d. per ton, seconds, 6s. to 'is. according to quality, common round coal, for iron-making and steam pnrposes, ss. to ss. 3d.; good burgy, 4s. 3d. to 4s. 6d.; and good slack, 3s. 6d. to 4s. per ton. In the shipping trade a moderate business continues to be done, although generally it is below the average for the time of the year. and steam coals delivered at Liverpool and Gareton are not in the open market fetching more than about 6s. 6d. to 7s. per ton. For coke there is a fair demand, with the common qualities averaging about 9s. to 10s.. and the better sorts for iron making pur- poses, 128. up to 15s. per ton at the ovens. In the iron trade a rather quieter tone has been noticeable during the past week. In pig iron the business doing continues very limited in extent, and the market can scarcely be said to be so firm as it was. A few small transactions are effected on the basis of old prices, but buyers in want of iron appear as a rule to be holding back in anticipation of some downward move- ment in values, and it is not improbable that makers would be disposed to negotiate for anything like quantities if good offers were made. For Lancashire pig iron, delivered in the Manchester district, makers still quote 445. for No. 4 forge, and 455. for No. 3 foundry, less 21 per cent; but at these figures they are booking very few new orders, and in outside brands there is also very little stirring, with prices • in some cases slightly easier. In the finished-iron trade the pressure of inquiries has not been quite so great, but there is still a good demand in the market, and most of the makers- having fully as- much work in hand as they can get through at present, are very firm in their prices which in some cases are ss. per ton above what would have been • taken a few weeks back. The quotations for delivery into the Manchester district remain at £6 to £6 2s. 66. for bars, about,£6 125. 66. for hoops, and £7 15s. up to £8 per ton for ordinary merchant sheets. Amongst engineers there is a moderate improvement so far as the amount of work in hand is concerned, but new orders have still to be taken at very low figures. The lace Hall Rolling Mills, Wigan, were yesterday offered for sale by auction at the Mitre Hotel, - Manchester, but did not meet with a purchaser, the only - offer being a nominal bid of £9,000, and the property was ?, consequently withdrawn.

div.head: ESSENCE OF PARLIAMENT.
div.p: ESSENCE OF PARLIAMENT.

TUESDAY, August 16.—Quite an affecting parting with Mr. Rylands just now. Peter has gone home a sadder and a wiser man. Not even the excitement of pairing for the rest of the session with Randolph has raised his spirits. The session has been a blank to him, broken at the last by two acute disappointments following sharp on each other's heels. When the Liberals were in opposition, Peter had rather a good time of it. No week passed but he had some tremendous resolution on the orders, and frequently made a speech. Now, with his party in power, he is evilly en- treated when he would table a resolution, and howled at by his neighbours when he would make a speech. All this he bore with great patience, though he tells me, with tears in his eyes, no one knows what he suffered. But he saw re- ward almost within reach. When Grant Duff went to India, Peter felt that the only uncertainty was whether Gladstone would offer him the Under-Secretaryship at the colonies, or in the Home Department. Peter rather fancied the colonies, as offering a wider field for an imperial mind. Went and looked over the Colonial Office in a casual manner to make some inquiry, and thought Grant Duff's room very pleasant. Dreadful blow when a faithless and forgetful Minister passed him by. Fresh gleam of hope when crisis arose with Land Bill. Rumoured that if the Lords stuck out, Gladstone would make a fresh batch of Peers. "How would ' Lord Burnley' look ?" Peter said to me only last Friday night. "Or do you like Baron Thelwall ' better ?" Didn't know what was in his mind at the moment. Thought they were alternative titles for a novel. But all clear now. The Under-Secretaryships are filled; there are to be no more Peers; and Peter wearily wends his way homeward media- ting on man's ingratitude. It was in this humour that Randolph, who knows about " Mephistopheles " and "Faust," got hold of him and opened friendly negotiations by proposing to pair. Fancy from sometking Peter said we shall hear more of this next session, when the Fourth Party may appear with a notable recruit.—Punch.

div.head: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.
div.p: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.

THE FRIENDLY SOCIETY FRAUD.—Robert Saxon was charged with obtaining two cheques by means of false pre- tences, and also by means of a forged certificate.—Mr. Swift appeared to prosecute, and Mr. Riley defended.—Mr. Swift said the charges were laid under two different Acts of Parliament. The one relating to false pretences said, "Who- soever shall by any false pretences obtain from any other person any chattel, money, or valuable security with intent to defraud shall be guilty of a misdemeanour." That was under the Act of Parliament relating to property. The other Act of Parliament was one relating to forgery, "Whosoever, with intent to defraud,: shall demand, receive, and obtain any chattel, money as se,..urity for money, or other property whatsoever, in, upon, or by virtue of any forged or altered instrument whatever, knowing the same to be forged, or altered, shall be guilty, of felony." With regard to both of those Acts of Parliament, the mere pieces of paper upon which they were written were chattels, so that even if they did not represent any money at all the obtaining of those two pieces of paper would be an offence under the Act of Parliament: The prisoner was the secretary of a friendly society called the Shepherds' Return Lodge. That lodge was the branch of a larger society called the St. Helens Dis- trict of the Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds, Ashton Unity, and under the rules of the society when the wife or the widow of a member died there was payable out of the funds of the society towards the funeral of that wife or widow the sum of £B, and the practice was when a claim was made upon the society for the secretary to investigate the claim; and if he found it to be right, then to give a cer- tificate that the person who had died was the wife or the widow of a member who was good upon the books of the lodge. That certificate being presented to the secretary of the district, the secretary of the lodge would receive from the secretary of the district the required cheque, which would have to be signed by the treasurer, the master, and the deputy master, Without these signatures the certificate of the secretary was of no avail. In June,lB79, the prisoner went to Peter Ball, secretary of the distriet, and presented to hien a certificate stating that John Roughley's wife had died of, paralysis, on the 19th June, 1879, aged 78, and "that he is good on the books of our lodge." It professed to be signed not only by prisoner, but by Joseph Stirp, master, and Thomas Hill, deputy master. With that certificate in his hand the prisoner went to the secretary of the district, presented it along with a certificate of death of Esther Roughley; and upon the faith of the genuineness of that certificate he obtained a cheque for £§. He had then to get r the cheque signed by the treasurer ef the district, and by a ' trustee. He got the cheque originally from Peter Ball, and afterwards got it signed by Jacques, the treasurer, but with regard to Pickavance, one of the trustees, he never did get it signed at all. The pretended signatures of master and deputy master was a forgery, and there could be no doubt whatever that when prisoner presented that certificate he knew very well that it was a forgery because it was in his own hand- writing, and was signed by him in order to. support his cer- tificate. He bad to produce the certificate of death, and he did produce it properly signed by the res,istrar of the district. That certificate of death was obtained and made use of f raudu- I ently, because Roughley the person mentioned in it was really a member of two other societies with which the prisoner was connected, and the friondeof Roughley in re- spect to those two societies obtained properly from the regis- trar,,two certificates, which they handed to the prisoner, who in respect of those two certificates did pay to the friends,.thr monies due to them from the two societies. poring satisae their claims be had the certificates left inlffs hands, and I fraudulently made use of one of them in order to defral the society which was concerned in this case.
