div.head: TRAVELS IN THE EAST.
div.p: TRAVELS IN THE EAST.
BY A SOUTH-WEST _LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN.
[SP EC I A L.] No. XIII.

JERUSALEM. Our first experience of tent life was anything but agree- able ; the night proved very tempestuous, the rain fell in torrents, and we felt as if we had been suddenly trans- ported to our cold English climate. Flap! flap! flap! blew the tents, while the rain rattled against, and fell splashing around us, all night. To add to my exceeding discomfort I had noticed, before the lights were put out, that our tent pole, joined in the middle by a narrow brass coupling, was bent at the joint about a foot out of the perpendicular. My companions did not seem to heed it, but I do not think I got a wink of sleep. Our Arab attendants were, every now and then, as the storm increased, driving down the stakes and tightening the ropes; but did not succeed in driving out of my head that it (my head) or some other body's, was in momentary danger of being struck by the dislocated pole, or enveloped in the folds of the dripping tent ; not to say any- thing of being exposed in our night garments to the rage of the hyenas and jackals, whose yah-yahing was heard above the storm all night. And, by-the-bye, to vary the nocturnal entertainment, we were favoured with the presence of six young street curs, which had undertaken our defence, and kept up a ceaseless yelping in answer to the wilder beasts, doubtless to assure us of oar safety, and that they were duly earning the privilege of picking our bones. When we passed through the Damascus Gate early next day on our first visit to the city, I do not know that I was greatly horrified, although there was quite enough in the narrowness, filth, and darkness of the streets to produce such a feeling in a mind less prepared for what we saw. But I had read too much about modern Jerusalem to be in the third heaven of enthusiastic expectation. Bad as its aspect was I felt thankful it was no worse. The rain through the night had filled the rough uneven pavement with pools, and made its streets, if streets they can be called, even more miserable than they afterwards appeared. The best streets in Jerusalem are not greatly superior to the worst streets in our large towns in England. True, they are paved, while those in Cairo and Alexandria are not, but the pavement is of the roughest description. The biggest and squarest boulders are used for the gutter in the middle of the street, while the lesser ones, though fixed fast enough and jammed together, seem to have got jammed in a struggle for pre-eminence, or in their desire to dislocate the ankles of the poor pedestrian. The avidth of the streets seldom exceeds twelve feet. After you enter the Damascus Gate, and proceed a few yards down an 'open roadway, two of these narrow streets are before you, parting at an angle of 30 or 35 degrees. To reach the busi- ness part of the city you take the one to the right, and soon find yourself threading your ray under gloomy arches, opening now and then at the crossing streets so as to admit the light. As in Cairo, some of the open ones are shaded with mats or palm leaves, which are intended to spread from roof to roof, supported by bamboos and other rough sticks, but which hang down like so many torn banners, leaving the noon-day sun—the only one that has any chance in these narrow thoroughfares—to stare right down through two- thirds of the pretended screens, and see 11 that is going on. The bazaars are miserable affairs ; stall-like shops display their meagre wares, and, not unfrequently, thick volumes of smoke issue from their doorways. Camels, ponies, mules, and asses, laden so as nearly to fill the street frem side to side, pass to and fro, making it exceedingly difficult and dangerous for foot passengers. No such thing as a cart or carriage, or even wheelbarrow, is ever seen or could be used in the streets of Jerusalem. The first opening you come to in this dismal passage is the Via Dolorosa, running up to the hill to the right quite open' but proceeding to the left under arched houses, such as we have now left behind. By some it is called "the way of the thoss." It leads directly through the city from east to west, and is a sort of out-door sanctuary or repertory of relics, sup- posed to be connected with the crucifixion, so numerous are the shrines before which the pilgrims pay their homage along its route. There are no less than 14 points of interest, called praying stations, which I think I must enumerate. 1, The Arch of Ecce Homo; 2, The place where the cross was laid upon Christ; 3, Where Christ sank under the weight of the cross the first time; 4, Where it is said Christ met His mother; 5, Where Simon began to bear the cross; 8, Where St. Veronic wiped the sweat from the Saviour's brow; 7, The house against which Christ fell the second time He sank down; 8, Where Christ turned and addressed the women; 9, Where Christ sank again under the croa. The rest of the stations are within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and are: 10, A circular stone standing on which it is said Christ was disrobed; 11, Where He was nailed to the cross; 12, Where the cross was raised; 13, Where He was taken down from the cross; 14, The Holy Sepulchre itself. Not satisfied with historical scenes and characters, they have given a local habitation to those which are merely illustrative. The houses of Dives and Lazarus are objects of special interest; they are very much alike in their out- ward appearance, having each a balconied window project- ing well into the street. Can it be supposed that Lazarus, with a house of his own, not a stone's throw from that of his rich neighbour, was accustomed to sit in the gutter, while the street dogs, hungry and numerous enough in all con- science, licked his sores, while Dives, clothed in purple and fine linen, sat up aloft in the little balconied window enjoy- ing the spectacle? Such must be the conception of the relicmongers, if they have any conception at all beyond emptying the pockets of their poor dupes, and filling their bellies with chaff. Most of the objects I have enumerated lie to the east, but, returning along the Via Dolorosa, we ascend its narrow open street running west, and come to one side of the Holy Sepulchre, at the corner of Christian-street. I am almost heart-sick with the above recital, but must pile up the agony a little further to show the mendacity of the Greek, Roman, and Armenian relic-mongers. The following are a few of the things crowded together beneath the roof of that one church, which I dotted down as we went from shrine to shrine in the so-called "holy places." 1. The stone on which the body of Jesus was anointed. 2. The place where the women received the anointing, several yards away. 3. The stone that was rolled away from the sepulchre. 4. The very tomb said to be hewn out of the rock, but built of marble without any appearance of rock. 5. The place where Christ appeared to Mary Magdalene. 6. The pillar of scourging, through a peep-hole in the dark—shown, too, in a blacksmith's shop at the foot of the street, also in the city of Rome, and many other places. 7. Two prints of Christ's feet—date, fifteenth century. 8. Where they parted His raiment. 9. Where He was crowned with thorns. 10. The place, in a sort of opened vault, where the three crosses were found. 11. The balcony from which Queen Helena witnessed the finding of them. 12. The tombs of Joseph of Arimathea, Nicodemus, Melchisedek, and Adam. I have no doubt they would exhibit the tomb of the old serpent himself if they did not find it more to their advan- tage to keep him alive. But, taking Adam as the climax, will it be believed that anything so blasphemous in its audacious lying could be invented as that "the place of a skull " meant Adam's skull, and that the blood of Christ trickling through the stone restored the first man to life? These things and a hundred others are exhibited in this crowded peep-show, before whose shrines hundreds and thousands of pilgrims in the course of the year bolt, and cross, and kiss, and kneel; and then travel back to their homes over seas and continents, feeling half- way nearer heaven. History says that the site of this church in the fourth century had a statue of Jupiter erected upon it, probably to commemorate and rnark the position of some stronghold taken and reduced by Titus in the siege of Jerusalem. Constantine, about that date—the fourth century—instituted a search for the sepulchre of Christ. Instead of finding it outside the city—" without the camp "—be found it inside, probably in entire ignorance of Paul's allusion (Rom. xvi,); and, in his burning desire to turn the tables upon his idolatrous subjects, found no diffi- culty in accepting this site as the genuine one. His zealous mother, the Queen Helena improving upon his wonderful sagacity, seems to have discovered site after site, relic after relic, finding them, or having them found for her, exactly where she wanted them, after the manner of all will-wor- shippers; and thus it was that priestcraft, in its chrysalis state till then, burst under royal sunshine into vigorous life, and has continued ever since, adding one absurd story and object of veneration to another, until the city and its edifices are full of them. We were thankful to escape the Holy Sepulchre's oppressive atmosphere, and breathed freely as we felt we could come away without a particle of faith in one of these inventions, and be rich in our poverty. We have said again and again on our journey, that God, in His wonder-working providence, has made it impossible to find a single spot of earth on which it could be said positively that the Redeemer's foot had pressed, or a tenement he occupied in life, death, or resurrection. Had such a mark ' of His presence been left properly authenticated, how great the incentive to idolatry. Not only over the credulous and superstitious, but also over the minds of the pure and the devout. But, after rejecting all these so-called holy places and things, there is no reason why we should turn away from the city in disappointment and disgust, for how much remains, even in the neglected and desecrated sites in and about Jerusalem, to draw out the soul, and to awaken emotion to its deepest depths! In these we have a hundred times more of real, veritable relinquice of the dead past than we reject. Take, for instance, the grand temple area within the city, or the sacred road to Bethany without; take the pool of Siloam without; relics impossible to enclose within their money-making shrines, and, therefore, leftwt h its one and s d remnantseso ati no.f ancient Take the Via Jerusalemwithin, Dolorosa, or the steep road leading down from St. Stephen's Gate to Gethsemane without. Then have we not the old un- changing hills—the hoary Olivet with its ancient companions; the age-worn valleys from Gihon, through Hinnom to the vale of Jehoshaphat ? What a weight of throbbing interest attaches to every one Of these ! How the eye kindles with rapture or melts into tears as you • realise at one moment the glory, and at another the shame that gathers around them ; when you realise that, within the compass of this mile or two of earth, the light of God shone with clearer and more concentrated rays than on any other spot of the earth's surface; or mark the desolation which for eighteen centnnes has followed the averting of His countenance and the baring of His avenging arm. I wish I could impart to my readers as clear an impression of Jerusalem and its surroundings as there is imprinted on my own mind at this moment. Of course no description of my poor pen can do it, but I would bespeak indulgence while I attempt a little amateur chaperon- ing through the city,and beyond its walls as far as Bethany. It shall be by a way we have partly travelled before—the Via Dolorosa. Let us think of the city as lying four square,

walled all round and with deep valleys encircling it on three sides, west, south, east; the northern outskirts rising a little above the level of the city, and stretching away without any adjacent valley. From these northern outskirts we en- ter the city by the Damascus gate. But we are about to take our departure from the Latin convent at the western wall, and to walk down the Via Dolorosa. Casting our thoughts outside the city we have, as we proceed, the northern plateau to our left; behind us is the Talley of Gition flanked by the Hill of Offence; the Valley of Hiss- nom, surrounded by the Hill of Evil Counsel, is on the right, while directly before us we have the Valley of JehoshaPhat and the Mount of Olives, to which we are bound. As we go down the narrow street with its rugged pavement, the first opening we come to on the right is Christian-street, the most business- like thoroughfare in the city, although that is not saying very much. Just at the corner of Christian-street is one side of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre; on which, hav- ing bestowed more than its share of attention, we merely give a passing glance. Advancing, we have the shops of olive-wood manufactures on each side, and, at the foot of the hill, we enter the dark archway, from which runs to the left the two streets which I said, on first entering the city, branched off from the Damascus Gate at an angle of 30 or 35 degrees. Assuming that the direction of the streets has not greatly altered, although the streets themselves may, we are probably treadinr, under arched houses or between narrow balconied buildings, otherwise destitute of any windows to the street, the ancient line of road along which the Divine Sufferer was dragged, pale and haggard, to execu- tion. Up one of these ways to the left he must have turned to reach the only elevated ground outside the city, and, climbing up towards the Damascus Gate, he may have met Simon coming in from the country. When we come to the second street, the Via Dolorosa forms part of it, and runs up for about 100 yards, then turns, and runs eastward again towards St. Stephen's Gate. After making this turn, we soon come to the Church of Ecce Homo on the left, while before us is the Arch of Ecce Homo spanning the street and seem- ing to rest against the side of a house. Within the church is shown a very ancient gate ray supposed to be the entrance to the Preetorium. Upon the arch outside they say it was that Pilate led forth Christ and exclaimed, "Ecce Homo!" "Behold the Man ! " After passing under this arch we soon come to a fragment of the tower of Antonio, understood to be a veritable relic of ancient Jerusalem. A little further on we gain an entrance to the barracks, from whose walls we obtain a commanding view of the Temple area stretching to the right. Before we dare to enter within the sacred en- closure we must have a military escort, so, for the present, we descend the steps of the barfacks and leave it behind. Passing beneath the walls of the Temple area, we approach the gate through which it is said Stephen was dragged forth to martyrdom, and which bears his name. Just before we reach St. Stephen's Gate, we have, on the right, the pool of Bethesda so called, now apparently, a receptacle for the city's refuse. We have now gone from the western to the eastern walls of the city, and, passing through St. Stephen's Gate, we look out upon the Mount of Olives, and down into the Valley of Jehoshaphat from a narrow ridge, over which are scattered a great number of Moslem tombs, many of them, indeed, "whited sepulchres," being besmeared with clay and whitewashed. Whatever doubt may rest on other scenes and other sites, we are quite safe in standing here, and taking in the full inspiration of assured conviction that along the paths that wind through the valley, and run like belts over the hill in front of us, the feet of the Holy One ,fttimes trod on his way to and from Bethany and his Galilean home. Turning gently to the right, we descend a steep and broken path which leads down to the bed of the brook Cedron, now generally dry, and we shall probably meet a number, fewer or greater, of Russian pilgrims, men mad women, staff in hand, plodding up the hill. Of these Rvssian pilgrims we must speak hereafter. Crossing the bed of the Cedron we come to a closed-in garden, from whose corner branch off two roads to Bethany, one right up the face of Olivet, the other winding round to the right. The garden is " Gethsamene." (To be continued next week.)

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. H. S. Hall.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. H. S. Hall.

A DISTURBANCE IN LUGSDALE-ROAD.—Michael Doyle was charged with having been guilty of a breach of the peace in Lugsdale-road.—An officer gave evidence to the effect that on Saturday night defendant made a considerable dis- turbance in the road by swearing and shouting.—Defendant was bound over to keep the peace for one month, himself in £lO, and one surety in £5. WEDNESDAY.—Before Colonel Gamble (chairman) and Mr. F. H. Gossage. A SATURDAY NIGHT DISTURBANCE IN LUGSDALE-ROAD. —Frank Lahey and John Dolan were charged, on remand, with resisting P.C. Brydges in the execution of his duty, and having been drunk and disorderly.—The officer stated , that on Saturday night, about a quarter past eleven, Lahey was causing a great disturbance in Lugsdale-road by fight- ing with a man named McCue. On offering to take Lahey into custody, he tried to throw him down, and resisted very violently. Dolan struck him (witness) a blow, and also at- tempted to throw him, but failing in this, he got hold of him by the arms and pulled him about violently. Dolan said to the crowd " Is there a man amongst you that will allow Frank to be taken ?" ; and also cried out to Lahey, "Frank, show yourself a man for once, and don't go." He struggled with the prisoners for about half an hour, and it was only with the assistance of the Inspector and other officers that they were taken to the police station. P.C. Skinner gave corroborative evidence, and said there was a crowd of nearly 100 people assembled at the time of the disturbance.—lnspector Barnett stated that he heard of what was taking place, and ran to the spot. He found the crowd exciting one another to rescue the prisoner Lahey; and the officers were nearly exhausted through their efforts to keep hold of him. It took three policemen to bring Lahey to the station, and he fought all the way, and, in the end, had to be carried.—Mr. Swift, jun., defended Lahey, and said that about eleven o'clock at night his client and Dolan le une out of Tilley's public-house, and just as they were bidding "Good night" to one another, the man McCue rushed up, and, without any provocation, struck Lahey a violent blow. Lahey defended himself, as he had a perfect right to do under such circumstances, and whilst he was doing so the officers came up and took him into custody. He told them his name over and over again, stated that be worked at Messrs. Pilkington's, and that he had to be at his work on the following morning at six o'clock. All that Dolan did was to say to the officers "Let him go; his name kis Frank Lahey; be lives at 12, Bedford-street, and has got to go to his work." There was no doubt that it would have been very much better if Lahey had gone to the station quietly, but he thought he should show the Bench that his criminality had not been very great, and cause them to come to the conclusion that he had been more than sufficiently punished by being kept in custody several days.—Thomas Burns, who was some short time ago one of the school attendance officers to the Widnes School Board; and was now in custody charged with being concerned in the row, he having, it was alleged, resisted the police in the execution of their duty, was then called as a witness by Mr. Swift. He said that on Saturday night, just about closing time, he came out of his own house, and seeing that there was a fight at the corner of Anne-street West, he went there. The quarrel was not between the two men now charged, and the fight terminated just as two police officers came up. A short time after some scuffling took place some thirty yards down the same road, and again he went up to the scene of the quarrel. He saw an officer named Montgomery take hold of one of the men, on which he. took upon him to give him some instructions to the effect that he ought not to seize him, but simply take his name and address. Barnett came up at this time, and pointing to him (witness) said "that is one of them." Then about half a dozen officers got round Lahey and kicked him and abused him most shamefully. Cross-examined by I Superintendent Barker: You have been a police constable? Yes, in the Widnes force.—Yes, and you were dismissed for misconduct ? I was dismissed "for getting a glass of refresh- ments."—Michael Bohan, St. Helens, a girl named Mary Ann Heegan, Elizabeth Keogh, of Wareing-street, and John Sweeney, with other witnesses, were also called to support the statement for the defence. Mr. Swift informed the Bench that Dolan had lived 18 months and Dahey about a year in Widnes. Previous to that Dolan had resided in St Helens about 26 years. Each of the prisoners was fined ss. and 6s. 6d. costs for the drunkenness; Dolan I.oe. and Gs. 6d. costs for resisting the police, and Dahey 20s. and 6s. 6d. costs for the like offence. In default of payment they were ordered to be imprisoned three weeks.—Thomas Burns, the witness above mentioned, who said he was now a labourer, but held a good testimonial from the Widnes School Board, was next charged with resisting the officer Brydges, during the disturbance. Brydges gave evidence to the effect that the prisoner got hold of him whilst struggling with Lahey, and ordered him to let him go. Burns also seized Skinner and put himself in a fighting attitude. The prisoner caused some amusement by the rather smart way in which he cross- I examined the witness. He told the magistrates that he was nat guilty, and alleged that the police had a spiteful feeling against him because. he was not now connected with the force. The Chairman slid the Bench had no doubt that the prisoner tried to rescue the man and also joined in the dis- turbance. He would accordingly be fined 103. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. Burns asked to be allowed a week's time in which to pay the money and the Chairman requested Superintendent Barker to grant him a little time for that purpose. 4 NEOLECTING TO SUPPORT A CHILD IN A REFORMA- TORY.—Patrick McCreese was summoned to show cause , why he should not pay 198. 6d. arrears owing by him as a ' weekly contribution to the maintenance of his child, who is in a reformatory. Evidence was called by Superintendent Barker, to show that defendants' wages for the last fifteen weeks had been 15s. sd. per week, and that he had a lodger, and one of his children was earning a weekly wage of Bs. He was ordered to pay is. 6d. per week until the arrears were paid off. LIVELY DOINGS AT HALTON VIEW.—The court was occu- pied a considerable time in hearing some cases of assault in which several people well dressed and evidently occupying a respectable position in the social scale, were concerned. —ln the first case Mr. John Hunt was charged by Mrs. Martha Burrell with having assaulted her on the 13th inst. —Mr. Yearsley appeared for the complainant, and defen- dant was represented by Mr. Swift, jun.—Complainant said she heard a noise at her front door, on the night of the 13th iunssedtanst 0, maendfioltnh ygoilnago gtohaegree, withstruohke rh her a uoguh ttehre, defendshoul daenrt, caught hold of her arm, and pushed her down the steps. His wife then came up and took charge of him—Mr. Swift denied the complainant's statement, and said that since Mr. Hunt put her husband in the County Court she had never ceased to annoy him, though in the past

div.head: TIIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 27, 188 L
div.p: TIIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 27, 188 L

/they had been great " friesds." On the night I referred to Mr. Hunt went to Mr. Burrell's for some meat, on which complainant called him a very wicked name, and put up her hands to strike him. All that defendant did was to raise his hand for the purpose of keeping off the blow.—Witnesses were heard on both sides. —A summons was next considered in which Mr. Burrell was charged with using certain false and defamatory lan- guage to Mrs. Jane Hunt, on the 13th instant. The same legal gentleman appeared in this case as in the last.—Mr. Swift, for complainant, alleged that defendant called his client a thief, and added a strong adjective to the substan- tive; alleged that Mr. Kershaw was pointing her house for the Special purpose of gaining her favour; that her money was obtained by robbing people, and that "she was too thick" with a certain county court bailiff named Atwell.—Com- plainant indignantly denied that there was any truth in any of these allegations. After she had been examined, the defendant was put in the box, and utterly denied . the truthfulness of Mrs. Hunt's statements.—The Chairman said there had evidently been some words between the people in the cases just heard, but the magistrates did not think they had been properly made out, and the summonses would be all dismissed. "CONSCIENCE MARES COWARDS OF 'CS ALL."—James Heath was charged with stealing a glass bottle, value 2s. 6d., the property of Mr. John Anderson, of the Railway Hotel, Victoria-road.—The wife of the prosecutor said the prisoner entered the house and asked to be served with some porter, but, as she did not consider he was in a fit state, she declined to serve him. He then told her that if she did not give him the porter he would go away with the bottle, which he did. —P.C. Murray at this part of the proceedings entered the box, but no sooner had he done so, than prisoner went into what appeared to be a violent fit, and had to be assisted out of court by several policemen.—The prosecutrix said she had no wish to press the case, and the prisoner was dis- charged. At the time this pleasant intelligence should have been told to him he was, apparently, in a state of cata-

1 epsv. INSULTING AN OLD SoLmEß.—James Birch, for using some very coarse language to John Townsend, an old soldier, and threatening to kick him, was ordered to enter into his owu recognizances in £5 and one surety in £5 to keep the peace. "Boys WILL BE Boys."—A youth named Peter Noon was summoned for rather violently assaulting another lad named John A. Tansey.—Defendant was ordered to pay S. 6,1. including costs.

which he sold to Mr. Lightburn, and he now actually ap- plied to the Bench to have a full license given to his own house, which was in the very same street. The Magistrates, without leaving the court to consider the matter, said they had decided to refuse the application. Mr. Fletcher said that perhaps the Bench would permit him to apply for a wine license that day. There were about 100 bowlers attending Mr. Hayes's green who often asked for claret and light wines in preference to beer. It was rather a hardship that they were not able to obtain anything but beer. The Chairman : But you said just now that the beer was so good. (Laughter.) Mr. Fletcher: Yes, but heavy—(renewed laughter) ;—too good, perhaps. Mr. Lake objected to the application being entertained that day on the ground that the notices given did not apply to it. The Chairman said the magistrates, without considering the point raised as to the notices, must refuse the applica- tion upon its merits.

RENEWAL OF THE LICENSE TO THE THEATRE ROYAL.— Mr. Thomas James, the owner and responsible manager of the Theatre Royal, applied for a renewal of the license to the building. Superintendent Williamson said he had no objection to offer, and on Messrs. W. R. Wass and Henry Coward enterinz into the necessary bond for the observance of the rules established for the management of theatres, the application was granted. I Before Messrs. S. B. Chadwick (chairman) and Henry Reynolds. WAYWARDEN'S LICENSE.—On the application of Mr. Henry Linaker, clerk to the Daresbury Highway Board, Mr. William Eaton was granted a licence to cart materials for the Board.
FLIGHT BY MOON LIGHT.—John Edward Filkin, a boat- - - -

, man, was summoned for having clandestinely removed his household goods to avoid distraint for rent by Mr. Stringer. —Defendant said be had had permission to remove the things, but evidence was called of the untruthfulness or this statement, and Filkin was ordered to pay 10s. 5d., the amount due for rent, and 12s. 6d. costs. THE _BUILDER AND THE IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.

—Mr. Henry White, builder, was summoned by the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners for infringing their building bye-laws. An adjournment was asked for a fortnight, and as Mr. Barker, surveyor to the Board, offered no opposition, the Bench granted the application. A Row AT THE SWAN BEHRHOUSE.—The court were occupied a considerable time in hearing a case in which John Ogden, keeper of the Swan beenhouse, was charged with having permitted drunkenness on his premises on the 10th inst.—Mr. C. H. Lewin defended, and the case excited considerable interest owing to the fact that in his annual report Superintendent Williamson had alluded to defendant having been previously convicted,—to which statement Mr. Lewin objected—and the large number of witnesses called for the defence.—lnspector Hollingworth said that about half-past ten at night he visited the defendant's house in company with Sergeant Whalley. In the front room they found a boatman named Joseph Bell, his wife' another man, and the landlady. Bell was very drunk, and he called the attention of the landlady to the fact, and asked her how it was that she had served the man with drink whilst he was in such a state. She said Bell had only had two quarts of beer, and she had several times asked him to leave. On the table were two glasses full of beer, and a quart jue. The landlady said to Bell, "Drink up your beer and go out ; I have asked you several times before to go out." Bell shortly afterwards went out, but he was so drunk that he had to be assisted down the street by his Wife. Information had been laid against him for drunkenness, but owing to his having been off on a trip with his boat, the police had not been able to serve him.—Sergeant Whalley corroborated the In- spector's statement—Mr. Lewin said he most distinctly denied, on the part of his client, that he had permitted drunkenness, for he had not supplied Bell with drink, nor had any been paid for him whilst he was in the house. Under these circumstances, it would be impossible, accord— ing to a recent decision from the Home Office, for the Bench to convict. The officers admitted that there were other men in the room at the time, and the beer on the table belonged to them. The police had not stated in their evidence that Bell had drunk any of the beer.—Selina Ogden, wife of defendant, said Bell and his wife, who declined to

go on the boat with her husband, and so caused a fierce quarrel, had been in the house about five minutes when the inspector and ser- geant entered. Bell had asked to be supplied with the beer, bat she had refused to let him have any.—Sarah Pettifor, mother of the landlady, said the two glasses of beer on the table had been filled for a couple of musicians. She drew all the beer that night, and none was supplied to the boat- man.—David Ogden, a violinist, said that he and Lewis Done, who combines the pursuit of a joiner with that of a violinist, were in the house, and he heard the landlady re- fuse to serve Bell, and desire him and his wife to go away. but they would not.—Lewis Done corroborated.—Joseph Bell was called, and stoutly maintained that he was sober when he went into the house, and though he was willing to admit be was "a bit agitated," it was owing to his wife being so stupid, and not through drink, of which he had never tasted that night. The landlady declined to serve him, and told him that "she had been had once, and a burned child dreaded the fire."—Margaret Bell supported ' the statement made by her husband.—The Chairman : Although we think this a very proper case for the police to have brought before us, yet we think there is a very grave doubt about it, and we dismiss the summons. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst.

A \Vatic CASE.—Luke Cavanagh wan charged with steal- ing 2s. belonging to Patrick Armstrong.—P.C. Motter said that about a quarter to eleven o'clock on the previous night the prisoner was given in charge, and on being questioned at first he denied all knowledge of the theft, but be after- wards acknowledged that he saw the money knocked out of the prosecutor's hand. He then put his foot upon it, and a woman who was standing near picked it up. Witness had seen the woman, and she said she knew nothing about the money.—Supt. Williamson observed that he had spoken to the prosecutor, who did not now appear, and he told him that he only landed in England a few days ago and was afraid to stop in the town. He told Armstrong that he must stay, but now he could not be found. There was no doubt the man had been robbed, and the prisoner had brought what had happened to him upon himself.—Prisoner was discharged.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit (chairman), Rev. E. A. P. Campbell, Messrs. S. B. Chadwick, Henry Reynolds, James Reynolds, A. Thomas, and C. W. Hazlehurst. BREWSTER SESSIONS. This was the day appointed for the Brewster Sessions. . Superintendent Williamson read his annual report, which was as follows :—" Gentlemen,—' have the honour to re- port for your information that in the Runcorn Petty Ses- sional Division there are the following licensed victuallers: —Runcorn 37, Weston 5, Halton 2, Sutton 1, total 45. There are also the following beerhouses licensed to sell on or off the premises, viz, Runcorn 46, Halton 5, Weston 2, total 53. Seven licenses are held in Runcorn by druggists. grocers, and confectioners: Ito sell spirits, wine and beer, 3 to sell wine, 2 to sell beer off the premises, and 1 to sell wine on the premise, total 7, making the total number of licenses held in this division 105. The population of the Runcorn Petty Ses- sional Division, according to the last census, was 19,111, being 182 persons to each licensed house. In the past year only one licensed victualler has been proceeded against, and the case was dismissed. Two beerhouse keepers have been summoned and convicted for permitting drunkenness. One has since left the house, and the other is summoned before your worships to-day for a second offence. The Masons' Arms beeerhouse in Church-street, Runcorn, after being closed for some time, is now occupied as a provision shop, and no beer is sold on or off the premises, no transfer of the license having been made to the present occupier. During the past year 122 persons have been proceeded against for drunkenness, viz., 80 males and 42 females. Of these 115 have been convicted, and seven dismissed or discharged,' as against 146 in the preceding year, showing a decrease of 24 persons in the number proceeded against during the past twelve months. There is to-day one application for a spirit license, by George Hayes, beerhouse keeper, Ashridge-street, Runcorn.—I have the honour to remain, gentlemen, your obedient servant, SAMUEL WILLIAMSON, superintendent." The bench granted the following transfers:—Public-houses: —Wellington Inn, from Samuel Dagnall to William Roger Wass; Queen's Hotel, from Thomas Walker to Robert Hoyle; Wilson's Hotel, from John Knowles to Henry Jack- son; Navigation Inn, from 'Henry Jackson to Thomas Wal- ker ; Halton Castle Inn, Halton, from John James Scott to William Phillips; George and Dragon Inn, from Jane Griffiths to Alfred Ledyard. Beer-houses :—Welsh Harp, from Samuel Dunbavand to William Waterworth ; Feathers' Inn, from George Green to Michael Phillips; Shamrock Tavern, from George Waight to Jane Griffiths. The Chairman said all the licenses would be renewed with the exception of the Masons' Arms and that of John Ogden, of the Swan Inn, Shaw-street, who had been convicted during the past twelve months for permitting drunkenness, and against whom the Bench heard there was a case for their consideration that day. In the case of the two referred to the owners of the licenses would have to appear before the magistrates at the adjourned licensing meeting on the 19th September. He might state that it was very gratifying to the Bench to hear that there was such a reduction in the number of the cases of drunkenness brought before them during the year as compared with those of the previous 12 months, and that only those holders of licenses referred to in Superintendent Williamson's report had been proceeded against. This showed that the police had been doing their duty, and also, perhaps, exercising a little clemency by urging people under the influence of drink to go home rather than be brought up when there was really no occasion for their being so. Mr. Fletcher, of Northwich, eppeared on behalf of Mr. George Hayes, of the Bridge Inn beerhouse, Ashridge-street, to apply for a spirit license. As the application has now been made at each annual licensing meeting, it will lot be necessary for us to enter at great length into the case. Mr. Fletcher remarked that he might venture to say that the house which his client had kept for a con- siderable time had been well conducted, and so as to afford no ground of complaint on the part of the police. He (the speaker) cordially concurred in the congratulatory remarks Iwhich Mr. Brundrit had given utterance to in regard to the ' report presented by the superintendent, but he hoped the chairman would pardon him for saving that he was of opinion the 105 licensed victuallers in the division ought to receive some commendation for the manner in which they had kept their houses during that period. The facts re- vealed in the report as to the few holders of licenses who had been summoned, clearly showed that the licensed vie- tuallers of Runcorn valued their licenses and co-operated with the police in trying to produce order and reduce drun- kenness. In making the application he was bound to satisfy their worships of three things, after doing which he pre- snmed that their duties became of a purely ministerial character. The first of these was as to the requirements of tke district; secondly, as to the suitability of the premises; and thirdly, as to the respectability of the applicant. He took it that, to some extent at any lute, those three points had already been admitted by the Bench, for he could con- ceive no grounds on which a beerhouse license should be granted which should not apply, with equal force, to the granting of a spirit license. It would be some encourage- ment to the beerhouse keepers of the district to find that, after having been tried with a beerhouse license, and found to be fit and proper persons to hold such a license, the Bench would enlarge it, and so improve the character of the house, and give it a lift in the scale of respectability. Opposite Bridgewater-street there was a large plot of land on which building had been going on for some time. There were in fact 715 houses en the property, inhabited by a respectable class of people. He was told that the popula- tion in these dwellings numbered 3,572, and upon the estate in question there was not a single licensed house. When he stated this, and also that the occupiers were prevented by the terms of their leases from having a licensed house upon the property, he must say he considered he had made out a case on behalf of his client. He understood that his friend , Mr. Lake would oppose the granting of a spirit license to I Mr. Hayes, on behalf of Mr. J. W. Lightburn, who had an interest in a neighbouring public-house. Surely, however, Mr. Lake's client did not claim a monopoly in the district. He understood there was a little feeling on the part of Mr. Lightburn, owing to the fact that Mr. Hayes, who sold very good beer, had taken away some of his customers. Then there was another point which ought to be taken into con- sideration, viz., that the Bridge Inn was nearer to the Run- corn railway footbridge than any other beerhouse in the neighbourhood. It was hardly necessary that he should refer to the respectability of his client. He' might remind the magistrates that in previous years, at the Brewster Ses- sions, deputations from bodies who were concerned for the ' morality of the district had attended, but this year they were not represented, and he looked upon their silence as assenting to the granting of this particular license. He held in his hand a memorial signed by 78 respectable People re? 'siding on the estate, and from the terms of the document it would appear the license was needed and that the people had confidence in Mr. Hayes's ability to supply „them with a good article. Mr. Lake said he had to oppose the application on behalf of Mr. Lightburn, the owner of the Devonshire Hotel, Ash- ridge-street, and Messrs. Gaskarth, wine merchants, Altrin- charn, the owners of the George and Dragon Hotel, Egerton- street. As their worships were aware, the application of Mr. Hayes for a full license to his house was a very old one, it having been before them from time to time. He appeared to oppose the application at the last licensing sessions, when they were told by Mr. W. H. Linaker that the population of the district was 3,000, but now, according to Mr. Fletcher, it had risen to 3,572. After making the usual deductions, this would leave about 714 male adults for whom accommo- dation was required. Then the memorial was only signed by 78 out of a population of 3,572. From his (the speaker's) own knowledge there had only been 19 new houses built in the Duke's-field district during the year: and he did not think anything had arisen to cause. the Bench to alter the decision at which they had arrived in previous years in res- pect to the application. He called the attention of the magistrates to the nearness of Mr. Hayes's house to the South Bank and Devonshire Hotels, which were both fully licensed houses. Not far away was the Darwell's vaults, another beerhouse in Rutland-street, and the Georee and Dragon public-house in Egerton-street. Mr. Fletcher had said there was a little personal feeling between Mr. Light- burn and the applicant. He would not deny that there might be a little; and he !bought it was •.-cry natural, see- ing that Mr. Hayes at one time owned the Devonshire

div.head: AN ABSCONDING RUNCORN TRAVELLER.
div.p: AN ABSCONDING RUNCORN TRAVELLER.

Mr. Joseph Clough, Stanley-street, aged 28 years, and respectably connected, was charged with having, on the 18th inst., feloniously and fraudulently embezzled the sums of £1 10s., LI 159., and £1 Is., the moneys of his employer, Mr. Henry Handle, draper, Bridge.street.—A considerable number of respectably dressed people were present to watch the proceedings. The prisoner appeared to be in a half dazed condition.—The prosecutor said that Clough had been in his employ since the Ist of March last as assistant and country traveller. Prior to engaging him he had known him ten years. Prisoner left his place a Cosiness on Wed- nesday evening in the previous week, to go upon his round, land he gave him twenty shillings worth of silver for change. He supposed that he would start for Dunham-on-the-Hill at about seven o'clock the following morning. He had been employed a day or two in searching for Cough, who he I was in hopes had merely got upon the :Tree at some place and not done anything criminally wrong Mr. place, deputy magistrates' clerk, asked the prosecu- tor what it was aroused his suspioions..—Nlr. Handles said his suspicions were aroused on Saturday evening when be found that the prisoner had not come home, as he ought to have finished his journey and come to the place of business on Friday evening, for the purpose of delivering up the money he had received. However 39, Friday was a wet day, he was led to believe that he had not been able to complete his round, and had decided to stay in the country, and re- turn on the Saturday. He then made enquiries and found that Clough had not been home on Friday. Mrs. Clough came to see him on the Saturday, and, as the result of en- quiries, he took out a warrant against the young man. He had certainly indulged the hope that Clough would turn up. —Superintendent Williamson said that in consequence of information received from Mr. Handle, on Tuesday, ha wired to tile Dover police, who apprehended the prisoner the same evening at the post office of that city. He at once despatched an officer for him, but he only re-- turned that morning, a little after six o'clock. Ofl, that evidence he asked the magistrates to re- mand the prison.n. until Monday, as such cases often took a considerable time to put into a proper state for being placed lbefore the Bench. He did not for one moment wish to be I bard with the prisoner, but he had a public duty to perfOrm. —ln reply to Mr. Johnson, Mr. Randle said he bad made 1 enquiries which proved that the sums the prisoner was I charged with embezzling had been received. He had'not seen the receipts, but he had the prisoner's cash book, which he found in a publichouse at Alyanley, in which the item of 355. was put down as having been received by linn. He knew Clough's hand writing very well. A friend of prisoner's went in search of him on Sunday,land found he had received two sums for which he had not accounted. Might he (wit- ness) be allowed to plead on behalf of the prisoner?—Mr. Johnson said the prosecutor could not do so then, as there was only a remand asked for at the time.—The Bench ac- cordingly remanded the prisoner until Monday next.—lt is stated that the total amount of the prisoner's embezzlements amount to between £5O and £7O. THURSDAY.—Before Messrs. W. Bankes (chairmart) and S. B. Chadwick.

ROBBING A WIDNES MAN.—Hugh Rowley, a man about 30 years of age, was charged with stealing 13s. ed. froml Thomas Toole.—The evidence was to the effect that on Monday night the men walked over from Widnes together, Toole paying Rowley's fare, and treating him with beer at nselered al Drury, a tid On went arriving to hi sa t houseß u nc Runcorn, Mill-street, where they net a man they had a gallon of beer. Immediately before sending for the beer, Toole counted his money, and found that he had 15s. t3d. The beer was is. 10d., and after they had finished it, Toole lay down on a folm in the kitchen and went to sleep, He fell from the form to the floor, and the prisoner lay beside him. Shortly afterwards he was awoke by feeling Rowley's hand in his pocket. He asked him for his money/ on which Rowley professed to be very indignant:Prosecutor which they got in the street, where P. C. Noden took then seized Rowley by the neck, arid they had a struggle, gnto custody. On being eTamined at the police station, dhuimrin i Ps. fid. was found upon the prisoner, who now denied his gull t. —A witness named John Drury having given evidoce, the prisoner was sent to gaol for 14 days.

Mr. DEACON. expressed his opinion that the tables were more complete than had hitherto been the case. The num- bers of one table corresponded exactly with those which had been got out in previous years ;, and he had compared those of the present year with the table presented to the Board in 1878: The number of houses was shown to be 14.8 per cent. more than in 1878.; but in inhabited dwellings it , only showed 5.8 per cent. increase. The number of houses in course of erection was 50 per cent. less. As to the school accommodation for the children in the east and south dis- tricts it was the same; in the west it had increased. The number of children between 3 and /3 in the east district had actually decreased. In Warrington-road the number of children in 1878 was 939, and at present only 863, showing a decrease-of rather more than tf per cent.; whilst in the west district the number had augmented by 436, or very nearly 17 per cent. In the south district the number had increased about 15 ,per cent.—The CHAIRMAN asked what provision was being made for the children in excess of the accommo- dation. He observed that a new school was being built at St. Mary's.—Mr. Bnansuaw.said he saw from the news- paper reports on the matter that there would be accommoda- tion for about 500 additional children.—The CHAIRMAN: Then there will be no lack of accommodation.—Mr. DEACON: No, there will be an excess of accommodation for about 260.—Mr. Slam was-not sure that the lack of accom- modation would be met in the way. suggested. Did it

necessarily follow that the schotars would be drafted into St. Mary's school ?—Mr. DEACON observed that from number four table it seemed that the enumerators made 36 more children in the town .than was shown by the census returns; but this might be accounted for by the fact that the names of many children were kept on the rolls after they had left the town. He moved that the tables be adorated.—The motion was seconded by the CHAIRMAN, and carried.

M. DAVIES read this report, which was adopted. It con- tained a recommendation that the resignation of Mr. D. A. JOnesy assistant master in the senior boys' department, be accepted from September 30th.
THE MEMBER& AND THE LOCAL BOADD.

The Sites and Building Committee's minutes, which were read by Mr. Brock, stated that the digging had hem com- pleted round the Simm's Cross schools by the Local Board, with the exception of a small piece in front of the care- taker's house door and the entrance to the infant school.—lt was recommended that a letter be sent to the Local Board, calling their attention to the matter, and requesting their early notice of it.—Mr. Brock having made some remarks on the subject which elicited a short disrassion, Mr. Suaw said: I think it would be much better that, under the cir- cumstances, the Local Board should do the work.—The CHAIRMAN : Legllhr, I believe, we cannot compel them to do it, but I think that in equity they ought to.—Mr. Sitew : We have the rensody in our own hands, Mr. Cbairmaa, be.

cause we can compel it to be done by taking in the land be- longing to us. I should certainly support the adoption of that course, if the Chairman of the Sites and Building Com- mittee was agreeable to it being pursued.—The CHAImmAN : No, no—The CLERK: Theu you weuld have to take the I I flagging up again, Mr. Shaw P—Mr. SHAW: Oh, yes.—The CHAIRMAN : But I should not cara for us to do that ; but if the feeling of the Board coincide with the proposition, I should be quite willing that a letter be written, to them stating the members are of opinion that they ought to do it.—Mr. BROCK : When I saw that they had not done it, I was so satisfied that they had agreed to do it, that I wrote to the Local 'Board without consulting any other member of the committee.—The CLERK was instructed to draw up a draft letter to the Board to be submitted to Mr. Brock, expressing the surpcise of the members that they had not carried out their agreement, and also drawing their at- tention to the fact that in this special matter they allowed three years to elapse without doing anything. THE REV. GEORGE HOLLOWAY'S EX?ERIENCE AS A.ti,
THE STATE OF THE CROPS.
The following reports, as to the state of the crops in Lancashire and Cheshire, have been supplied by our cor- respondents in the places mentioned below :
CHESHIRE.

LT-sm.—The crop of clover bay has been very good, but meadow land has, with few exceptions, been very light. Wheat is very good; we should say as good as could be expected. Oats are also a fair crop. Potatoes have been very prolific, and, so far, free from disease. Turnips look fairly well; mangolds also look fair, but in a few cases are spoiled with fly. Beans, few grown, but they are looking well. On the whole crops are very fair, both in quality and quantity.

GRAPPENIIALL.—Oats are good, and stand well, likely to be of average quality and yield, but during the last few days the chaff has got dark and much discoloured with the smoke falling upon it along with the small misty rain that has fallen at times during the past week. The greatest part of them will have fallen before the reaping machine with another fine day or two. Wheat is rather late, looks well, but is thin upon the ground. It will be below an average this year in quality and yield per acre, so far as can be seen at present. Fine weather is most essential just now, both for condition, quality, and colour. Potatoes, the early ones, are all dug up. They have been a light crop, but those going to market now are good, with fair sized tubers, and up to now free from disease. Late ones are looking very promising. Hay: This crop has been generally light, the quality very good, and has been secured with very little trouble and expense. After-grass also is light, but has much improved during the last week, only a lew fields, which are in a high state of cultivation, will be worth mowing a second time. Pastures are bare, but now improving both in bite and colour. Mangolds, planted after early potatoes, are doing well, although the young plants at first suffered much from I the attack of insects and grubs in the leaves, which retarded their growth. Swede turnips are looking well, but will not be a heavy crop. Market turnips, sown after early potatoes, have come up well, and promise to make up in some degree for the deficiency of the first crop. APPLETON. Wheat is generally short in straw, and below the average in Wilk, but promises to be good in quality. Oats vary; some are good, the largest proportion are light in straw, but well fed. Those on what we call " leys,' or fresh tilled land, are generally the be,st. Grass during the early part of the season has been short, owing to cold and late spring. Hay crops below the average in quantity, but good in quality. After-grass promises to be plentiful. Potatoes, moderate in crop, and at present sound. Turnips have been much troubled with the"fly," but are growing well now, and promise to be- a fair crop. Mangolds have been much infested with " grub " in the leaf, but on the whole are moderate. RONCOB.N.—On the whole the various farm crops in the district lying between Warrington, Frodsham, and Runcorn are satisfactory. With very few exceptions the hay crop is now all stacked, and has been housed in very good condi- tion, having been mown tolerably early, and the weather having been dry with no very great amount of scorching sun. The crop, however, is light, as it is throughout Eng- land, and will, probably, not average very much over a ton to the statute acre. Pastures are full of grass, and the present showery weather will be of great advantage both to them and to the root crops if succeeded by a fine autumn. Turnips are looking well, and planted swedes especially so, but in a few instances we observe patches where they are clubbed. Mangolds do not look quite so well, and are again troubled with the leaf-boring grub, which checks their growth very mach. The early potatoes are mostly got up, and have not been a heavy crop, nor have they realised much money. Late potatoes, however, look most promising so far. Oats are now pretty freely cut; they are good, full crop, and stand well. Wheat is looking healthy, but not particularly thick on the ground. We have seen none that is very forward for cutting. Taken altogether the crops look well, and prospects are brighter; but it will take many good seasons to make up the losses of the past three or four years. PRESTON BROOK.—On well farmed land only, wheat well fed, but thin on other land. Oats very short in the straw but the grain good, not an average. Clover first crop an average, second crop very short and light, want of sun and heat to force it on. Hey not much over half a crop. Swedes healthy but late, second crop after early potatoes grow slowly, can- not make much. Mangolds nearly a complete failure, all more or less damaged by fly and maggot. DARESBURY ATTO THE NEIGHBOURHOOD.—Oats are not an average crop, and wheat is thin on the ground; the grain will be good if suitable weather is obtained. The grass has been light. Early potatoes light; late ones are looking very well and very promising. Turnips and man- golds are late, but if it is a tine back end they may come out a fair crop.

The Rev. GEOROE HOLLOWAY stated that the othet day, when driving out near Warrington Roard Schools, he saw about 30 children who ought to have been at school. On another day he saw about seven youngsters, whom, he sup- posed belonged to his own school, and ;le made up to them with the object of speaking to them. On perceiving his aim, the rascals set upon him and pelted him with stones t (Laughter.)--The CHAIRMAN (humourously): Mr. Iloilo, way, I hope they were not your children.—Mr HOLLOWAY: No ; I think I know whose children they were, c)r they wade off itt the direction of Appleton, (Laughte,,..)

div.head: LtLCASHIRE.
div.p: LtLCASHIRE.

Hmswoon —Cern is below the average; wheat as a rule I not being well filled, and oats light and short in the, straw. Very little barley and beans grow here. Grass has been fairly good, and of excellent quality. Root crops are look- ing remarkably well. HUTTON AND ROBT.—Wheat appears to be quite an average. Barley is little grown in this neighbourhood; what there is looks very good. Oats are certainly below an average, being very short in the straw, and the yield very likely to be indifferent. Grass: the hay crop has been very light, but has been secured in excellent condition. Meadows have also been very light. Turnips are looking well, and likely to produce a full average crop. Mangolds, which at first looked very disappointing, are very much benefited by the late rains, and seem likely to produce a fair crop. Potatoes are an excellent crop, and the bulbs at the roots numerous; at present very few are affected by disease. NEWTON, GOLRORNR, HA.TDOCK, AND ADdOINING DIDTRICT —Wheat :generally thin on land, but well headed. Bar-. ley: very little grown here. Oats: good average crop. Beans: average. Mangolds : much under average; plant suffered mush in early stage from maggot. Swedes: very good. Hay-: under average, but well got in. WINDLE (Sr. HELENS).—Hay crop: generally light; little more than half the average. Wheat crop: generally thin on the land ; suffered a great deal from the severe . winter; the ears not well filled; far short of an average. Oat crop: great deficiency in the straw, and many fields quite a failure; little more than half in proportion to last year's. Barley: an average crop. Clover, second crop: generally light. Potatoes :- a good average crop, but not nearly so good as last year's. Mangold wurtzel : a good average crop. Turnips: good; more than an average.

WCSOLSTON.—Grass very fair; early potatoes very good, and late ones look well ; corn looking well. LirrLu WOOLTON.—Wheat will scarcely reach an average. Oats are a quarter less. than last year. Barley very little grown in this district but that little of fair quality. Grass: Old meadow not more than half a crop. Clover a fair first crop, second in many places not worth cutting. Potatoes looking well. Turnips good. Mangolds poor.

The gloomiest acoonnts are being received in London from the home counties. of the effect on the harvest of the almost incessant rain of the last few days. In parts of Kent sandoo Surrey h r esof farmerst e weather-whoseonlywill, ihto is said, hope ofti dcomplete r the the orntiinmoo times lay in getting in a good harvest this year. While our farmers are being ruined through excessive rain, the agriculturalists in some parts of the United-States are suffering severely for want of it. Private advices from lowa describe the wheat crop in that State as an almost total failure. On one farm in Cass County possessing some of the best soil in the State a field of 100 acres only gave four bushels to the acre, and many farms around, showed a like result. The Indian corn crop, too, which in lowa is generally very strong, is likely this year to be pour, in con- sequence of the late spring and the want of rain. Prices are pretty certain to be high for what is obtained, but this will be a poor consolation for farmers, who will hardly have enough wheat for bread, who will be compelled to buy seed wheat for next year's sowing, and who in many cases will be short of corn for their live stock. It is reported that the extraordinary thunderstorm which passed over South Staffordshire on Tuesday has caused considerable damage to the growing crops, and has flooded the low-lying lands. Hannah Tinsley, West Brom- wich, was struck by lightning and lost her speech. At Her.. borne, a teacher at the Parish Church School was struck while engaged with her class and rendered insensible. About eleven o'clock on Tuesday, a thunderstorm broke over Worcester. The claps of thunder were deafening, and the lightning intensely vivid. Councillor Bozward was pass- ing through .Bull Entry carrying an umbrella, when he was surrounded by what appeared to be a sheet of fire, and lifted two feet into the air and thrown against the wall on one side of the entry. RI7NCORN IMPROVEMENT ACT, 1852.—ELECTION OF COMMISSIONERS. NOTICE is hereby Given, that a meeting of Persons Entitled to Vote at the Election of Commissioners under the above-mentioned Act will be held at the PUBLIC OFFICES, FRIDGE-STREET, RUNCORN, on THURSDAY, the let day of SEP- TEMBER, 18S1, for the ELECTION of FIVE COMMISSIONERS in the place of Messrs. Joseph J. Speakman, John Robert Frith, George Marshall, James Dobson. and Samuel Taylor, who then retire from office, but are eligible for re-election. The voting will commence at nine o'clock in the forenoon, and close at four o'clock in the afternoon. W. BROOKES, Secretary to the said Commissioners. Public Offices, Runcorn, August 24th, 1881.

APPOINTMENTS.—The House-Surgeons and House Physicians, the Obstetric Residents, Clinical Assistants and Dressers, are selected from the Students, according to merit and without payment. There are also a large number of Junior Appoint- ments, every part of the Hospital practice being systematically employed for instruction. ENTRANCE SCHOLARSHIPS,—Open Scholarship, of One Hun- dred and Twenty-five Guineas, in Classics, Mathematics, and Modern Languages. Open Scholarships, of One Hundred and Twenty-five Guineas, in Chemistry, Physics, Botany, and Zoology. PRIZES, Ac.—Six Scholarships, varying in value from £lO to £5O each, for general proficiency in Medical Study. The Trea- surer's Gold Medal in Medicine ; the Treasurer's Gold Medal in Surgery; the Gurney Hoare prize of £25, for Clinical Study; the Heaney prize of 30 guineas, for Pathology ; the Bands Cox Scholarship of els per annum for three years, for Physiology and Physics; the Michael Harris Prize os £lO, for Anatomy. For further information, apply to the Dean, Dr. F. TAYLOR. Guy's Hospital, London, S.E., August. 1381.

TESTIMONIALS. 6111,—A short time since I was induced by the novelty of the title to send for a bottle of your Liebig's Extract of Meat and Malt Wine. I was perfectly acquainted with the value of the Extractum (Darn's, and not quite a stranger to the invigorating and fortifying properties of malt wine, and, therefore, felt a natural curiosity to test them when combined. Men who work hard as I do, not muscular hard work, but that which is quite as exhausting, viz., brain work, very often experience the need of, and have sometimes an , almost irre- sistible *raving for a "pick me up," and very often the panacea for a time for lassitude, and that state of mind which renders work irksome, are alcAolic stimulants, the use of which must sooner or later end disastrously. The man who can furnish a remedy sure, certain, and harm- less, for the lassitude which follows constant brain work, is a benefactor of his species, and may be said to have added many years of usefulness to the lives of useful men. Your extract, if a success, and when more generally known. will be used by all toilers of the mind. Yours faithfully, 0. D. RAY. Thorpe Hamlet, Norwich, February 23rd, Ig2l.

STEWARD will offer for SALE BY AUCTION, at WILSON'S HOTEL, RUNCORN, on THURS- DAY, the 15th day of SEPTEMBER 1881, at 5 for 6 o'clock in the Afternoon, all that desirable and substantially-built Leasehold DWELLING-HOUSE, with the yard, garden, and outbuildings thereto belonging, comprising, in the whole, about 683 square yards of land, situate on the north-easterly side of the road leading from Runcorn to Halton, and about a mile from the Town Hall, Runcorn, formerly in the occupation of Francis Fairhurst, and lately of Benjamin Simner, but now un- occupied. The•house contains an entrance hall, 2 sitting rooms, large kitchen, pantry, washhouse, and out offices, good dry beer and wine cellars, 5 bedrooms, and 2 attics. The property is also subject to a yearly rent of three half-pence, payable to the Lords of the Manor of Halton. Further particulars may be obtained of the AUCTIONEER, at his offices at Runcorn, Frodsham, or Chester; or of c Messrs. ASHTON and GARRATT, Solicitors, Runcorn and Frodsham.

DUTTON has received instructions from Mrs. Dux- bury (the owner) to SELL BY AITOTION all that partly FREEHOLD and partly COPYHOLD VILLA, called "The Grove House," and situate in Farnworth-street, Farnworth, and now occupied by Mr. Taylor, containing six bedrooms, drawing-room, dining-room, large kitchen, butler's pantry, kitchen pantry, wash-house, copper boiler, coach-house stable, and cellar; also the smithy. To view the property apply to the present tenant, and for further particulars to the AUCTIONEER, 2, Oakland-street, Widnes.

The monthly meeting was held on Thursday. Mr. T. Sutton-Timmis presided, and there were also present the Rev. George Holloway, and Messrs. Bradshaw, Brock, Deacon, Hartland, Shaw, Davies, and Danby (clerk). DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE. This committee's report was adopted, on the motion of Mr. DEACON, seconded by the CHAIRMAN, and stated that during July the number of cases summoned were 422, of which 155 were applications for payment of fees, and 267 for contravention of the Education Act. Fees was recom- mended to be paid in 140 cases, and 15 applications were re- fused. There had been five prosecutions before the magis- trates and an equal number of convictions.—Mr. DEACON remarked that one of the Guardians had been down to see how the fees were distributed, and he had expressed himself as thoroughly satisfied with the course pursued. The excessive rainfall Is proving disastrous to the erOps in Cheshire. The harvest is not finished, and a great deal of the hay which remains to be gathered is sodden with rain and valueless. Corn which is not an average crop at the best, is sprouting everywhere under the influence a the soft forcing rains. Rain has fallen almost continuously in West Scotland since Tuesday night, and the crops are soaked. Wheat has risen in the Glasgow market ss. within the past fortnight. Rain has fallen incessantly near Newcastle. Reports from the agricultural districts of France that a good harvest isbeing gathered in this year. The recen drought has somewhat retarded the growth of maize anu on potatoes, while oats have not yielded largely, hut the other hand, wheat, rye, barley, and beetroot promise an abundant supply. Grapes, except in certain regions where severe frosts prevailed last spring, or where the ph,ll43sera' indicate has been particularly active, are also plentiful.
